cia-0000119736: A September 1956 CIA report from the Eastern Europe series covers the Hungarian situation. The series tracked the whole Soviet bloc, and Hungary was becoming its hottest file. The paper places Budapest's unrest inside that regional picture. Series reporting of this sort built the background against which the October explosion was read, linking one country's unrest to strain across the bloc.
cia-0000132636: The Cuban president touring Latin America and attacking the United States fills a CIA item dated May 3, 1960. President Dorticos held the formal post, while Castro held the real power in Havana. The tour mixed state visits with sharp public attacks on Washington. The short item tracks the trip and the speeches made along the way that spring.
cia-0000135836: One declassified planning paper from the CIA files, dated about January 1954, covers Annex B on para-military work, holding parts two and four of that annex. All of it feeds into PBSUCCESS, the agency operation against the Arbenz government in the months before the June 1954 coup. The paper trail here is small but direct, a single piece of the huge file the operation left behind.
cia-0000135936: Filed on 3 January 1954, this CIA cable concerns urgency about reporting documentation that supports a claim, the heading breaking off mid-thought. As the Lincoln station file, it forms part of PBSUCCESS, the CIA plan that ended with President Arbenz driven out in June 1954. Its worth is in the detail it pins down, one dated piece of a covert war fought largely on paper.
cia-0000136036: One CIA cable dated 4 February 1954 handles instructions about enclosures one through six of an earlier reference, filed as HGGA 793. As the Lincoln station file, it forms part of PBSUCCESS, the CIA plan that ended with President Arbenz driven out in June 1954. Its worth is in the detail it pins down, one dated piece of a covert war fought largely on paper.
cia-0000136136: Dated 1 April 1954, one CIA cable in the open files deals with a pending defection of pilots, men who could bring their planes and their knowledge over. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. What survives is the working paper itself, plain proof of how the mission was run from day to day.
cia-0000136236: Cable in the declassified files, dated 4 May 1954, covers a command message for CADICK assigning full field command, the grant breaking off mid-word. As the Lincoln station file, it forms part of PBSUCCESS, the CIA plan that ended with President Arbenz driven out in June 1954. Its worth is in the detail it pins down, one dated piece of a covert war fought largely on paper.
cia-0000136336: Relay this word to CALLIGERIS, LINCOLN tells CADICK and LANGEVIN in late June 1954. The junta of Diaz, Monzon, and Sanchez has given its word to the American ambassador. It will meet CALLIGERIS in El Salvador. The two sides will discuss terms there. The cable is short. But it marks the turn from fighting to talks in the last days of the operation.
cia-0000136636: Spanish records of Brigade 2506 hold this document, dated 1 February 1961. It shares that date with a companion item in the same release. The brigade, Cuban exiles under CIA direction, was preparing its April invasion. The catalog gives neither document a subject of its own. This one is kept in Spanish as released, identified by its date and its place in the brigade's files.
cia-0000136936: Themes for a planted story on Guatemala arms are listed in April 1954. The asset HBDRILL is part of the plan. One theme quotes Foreign Minister Toriello. For Guatemala, he said, communist-ruled territory is the Soviet Union. Other countries are sovereign. That shows the type of sovereignty he would accept, the theme argues. A second theme targets cheap Soviet arms. If Moscow gives or sells arms cheap, it seeks a foothold. A new satellite would follow. More arms would come after.
cia-0000141136: The body of an American pilot killed in the Bay of Pigs was identified in 1979. These Star and Post clippings report it, eighteen years after the invasion. Thomas Willard Ray was from Center Point, Alabama. He was one of four American pilots killed in the abortive attack. Cuban militiamen shot him after his plane crash-landed. The site lay near Castro's combat headquarters, twenty miles from the invasion beaches. His body was frozen in a Havana morgue for seventeen years. The FBI identified it after Cuba sent it home.
cia-03189336: CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1960/06/15, a CIA publication. Another June briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. The paper lived through the years. It awaits future readers. It retains its place in time. The text survives intact.
cia-03192936: This bulletin dates from May 15, 1955. The intelligence community's daily take on global events, prepared for senior readers. Routine Cold War product. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. This file preserves that declassified paper. Kept for readers.
colquhoun-isis-revelata-1836:
J. C. Colquhoun traces animal magnetism from its origins in Isis Revelata, from 1836, the first English history of mesmerism. Mesmer's baquet in Paris, wandering magnetizers, and hospital trials pass in review. Colquhoun, a Scottish lawyer, writes as a learned and keen believer in the strange science he chronicles.

He follows the craze across Germany, France, and Britain in turn. Cures, scandals, and learned disputes fill his two thick volumes of lore. The book introduced many British readers to Mesmer's world in depth. Enthusiastic and erudite at once, it remains a rich source for the age when magnetism seemed to open a new sense.
cours-de-phrenologie-1836: Cours de phrénologie, 1836. The French course. This book preserves that work. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Tomorrow's readers will find it.
documents-laid-before-the-right-honourab: Documents Laid before Lord Glenelg, 1836. The convict documents. This book preserves that report. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. The paper lived through the years and remains here.
emerson-nature-1836:
Ralph Waldo Emerson published Nature in 1836, the slim book that launched transcendentalism in America. The essay is the founding text of American nature writing and of Emerson's public career in Concord. He published it anonymously, fresh from resigning his Boston pulpit over matters of conscience and rite there.

Emerson urges readers to see nature with fresh eyes, as a child sees the woods and sky. Nature, he argues, is spirit made visible, and the soul can read God in a landscape. The famous transparent eyeball passage claims a moment when self dissolves into universal being in nature. Few slim books have seeded so many movements, from conservation to American self-trust in thought today. It announced a native philosophy, spurning Europe's authority for the soul's own light.
europmc-pmc10094836:
Giorgino and colleagues review knee osteoarthritis in a 2023 update, covering its spread, causes, and the role of stem cells. Osteoarthritis is the most common joint disease, and the knee bears much of its burden. Rates vary widely between studies and places, which the authors work to explain.

The review describes how cartilage breaks down and pain develops over time. It surveys standard care, from exercise and weight control to surgery. It then assesses what mesenchymal stem cells can and cannot yet offer. The update is a practical guide for clinicians.
europmc-pmc10335936:
Chen and a large team reported in 2023 the first full genome of maize, or corn, with no gaps. A genome is the full DNA code of a living thing. Past maize genomes held gaps in hard, repeat-rich parts. The team used two long-read methods to span each chromosome from end to end.

The Mo17 genome runs to 2,178.6 million DNA letters, with over 99.99% accuracy. Chen found repeat arrays up to 235,000 letters long. One region held 2,974 copies of a key gene in a 26.8 million letter array. All ten centromeres, the hubs that split cells, were built in full. The work opens the hardest parts of crop DNA to study.
europmc-pmc10338336:
Nakamura and colleagues found a new way in 2023 to force cancer cells to die. The death type is ferroptosis, in which iron drives fat damage inside the cell. A protein called FSP1 can block this death and shield tumours. The team screened small compounds to find one that stops FSP1.

Their lead compound, icFSP1, works in a fresh way. It does not block the protein head-on. It pulls FSP1 off the cell membrane and makes it clump into droplets. That clumping needs a fatty tag and loose parts of the protein. In mice, icFSP1 slowed tumour growth. Paired with a drug that blocks a second shield, GPX4, the death effect grew stronger.
europmc-pmc10416536:
Araghi and a team of co-authors updated the state of targeted therapy for a major lung cancer in 2023. The cancer is non-small cell lung cancer, the most common form of lung cancer. Lung cancer still leads cancer deaths across the world. Targeted drugs attack the genes or proteins that let a tumour grow, while sparing normal cells.

The review lists the main tumour targets and the drugs built for each one. Araghi also sums up trial results for patients on these drugs. Gains in survival and in quality of life drive the fast pace of work. New targets keep joining the list as gene studies of tumours grow.
europmc-pmc10445636:
Zeng led a large team in 2023 to present version 2 of DeePMD-kit, a software pack for atom studies. The pack runs simulations of how atoms move, using machine-learned energy models. Those models, called Deep Potentials, mimic costly physics math at a fraction of the cost. The pack first came out in 2017 and spread across physics, chemistry, and materials work.

Version 2 adds richer ways to describe an atom's neighbourhood, Zeng reports. It can fit stretch traits of materials and can be squeezed into smaller, faster models. It also runs on graphics chips and offers screens and code hooks for ease of use. The team gives a full sample run and tests of speed and accuracy for each model type.
europmc-pmc10700136:
Oh and co-authors showed in 2023 that each organ ages at its own pace, and blood proteins can reveal it. The team read proteins that leak from set organs into blood plasma. Machine learning turned those levels into an age score for 11 major organs. Scores held up across five groups with 5,676 adults in all.

Near 20% of people had one organ ageing far faster than the rest. Oh found that fast organ ageing raised death risk by 20 to 50%. A fast-ageing heart came with a 250% higher risk of heart failure. Fast brain and vessel ageing foretold Alzheimer's decline as well as the best blood mark. The method needs just a blood draw.
europmc-pmc10733136:
Boiko and co-authors built Coscientist in 2023, an AI system that plans and runs chemistry experiments on its own. The system runs on GPT-4, a large language model. It pairs that model with web search, code running, and lab automation tools. Most past AI help in labs stopped at advice or single steps.

Coscientist took on six varied tasks end to end. Its prize run tuned a palladium-driven reaction, a staple bond-forming step in chemistry. Boiko reports that the system designed the tests, ran them, and read the results with little human input. The team stresses that its steps can be traced and explained. Such systems may speed research across many fields.
europmc-pmc10967436:
Hong, Boiti, Vallone, and Foulkes review oxygen-based signals that can both harm and help cells in this 2024 paper. Reactive oxygen species are unstable oxygen molecules formed when cells use oxygen for energy. For decades they were seen mainly as a source of cell damage. Work since shows they also act as signals that steer many cell processes.

The review covers how these molecules are made and how cells neutralise them with defence systems. It then maps the main signal paths they sway and the gene switches they control. Such control looks ancient and shared across most life forms. Yet animals in extreme habitats show the system can bend and vary, the authors note. They ask how this flexibility arose over evolution.
europmc-pmc11701636:
UniProt Consortium describes the 2025 state of the Universal Protein Knowledgebase in this paper. The knowledgebase aims to give users a full, high-quality, free set of protein sequences with functional notes. Output is now limited to high-quality reference proteomes, one clean, non-redundant protein set per species. Expert curation of the literature continues to add the latest functional data.

Machine learning aids the curation, and community curation is encouraged so that key papers are not missed. The update details the automatic methods that predict data for entries not yet reviewed, which describe unstudied proteins. Website updates include a new tab linking each protein to genomic data. The resource now holds Global Core Biodata Resource status, a mark of essential infrastructure.
europmc-pmc1283536:
Jones and Wilson recorded two rat brain regions during a maze memory task in 2005. The hippocampus encodes spatial information about places. The prefrontal cortex must blend that with route and task rules. Electrodes recorded both regions at the same time.

Correlated firing between regions rose during memory-demanding behavior. Coupling also strengthened in the theta rhythm band, 4 to 12 hertz. That rhythm may coordinate timing across brain structures. Structures can then encode alone yet interact on demand. Jones proposes theta coordination as a general control mechanism. Recordings came from tetrode arrays in both regions at once.
europmc-pmc1550236:
Chronic pelvic pain burdens many women, yet its scale was murky. Latthe and co-authors reviewed world studies in 2006 for the World Health Organization. They gathered 178 studies with nearly 460,000 women, covering period pain, pain during sex, and steady noncyclic pain.

Data came mostly from rich countries; just a fifth of less developed nations had any. Rates swung with study quality. Among 40 high-quality studies, period pain hit 16 to 91 percent of women depending on place and method. Latthe calls the patchy data a planning blind spot for women's health services. The review was a World Health Organization project.
europmc-pmc1564136:
Wikis, blogs, and podcasts were reshaping how health workers learn together in 2006. Boulos, Maramba, and Wheeler surveyed that Web 2.0 wave. Wikis are pages anyone can edit. Blogs are online journals rich in media. Podcasts push audio and video to subscribers for learning anywhere.

Free and open versions fueled fast growth of all three. The same openness creates a weakness: anyone can alter content, so accuracy is hard to gauge. Boulos notes teamwork can act like selection, letting the fittest content survive. They see strong promise for clinical training if quality checks keep pace.
europmc-pmc1761136:
Honeybees carry a strikingly thin toolkit for detoxifying chemicals. Claudianos and co-authors counted the genes in 2006: the bee genome holds about 11,000 genes, fewer than fly or mosquito. Three detox families shrank the most.

Bees have roughly half as many glutathione-S-transferases, P450 enzymes, and esterases as other insects. Some clades tied to insecticide resistance in other species are ten-fold smaller. The deficit may explain bee sensitivity to pesticides. A few detox clades did expand recently, perhaps tied to the social and chemical life of the hive. Claudianos links genome content to the bee's ecological niche.
europmc-pmc1892036:
Grissa, Vergnaud and Pourcel built CRISPRdb in 2007, a database of the bacterial defense elements called CRISPRs. These repeated DNA stretches store short spacer pieces taken from invaders, and the array may target invading DNA for destruction, much like RNA interference. New spacer units are added at one end, so arrays record infection history.

Their program CRISPRFinder locates CRISPRs in genome sequences and pulls out each repeat and spacer. The database refreshes automatically each month from newly released genomes. Extra tools align the DNA flanking each array to hunt for kinship between sites, and build dictionaries of spacers and repeats for comparison. The resource was made to support study of how CRISPRs are born and evolve as genome data pours in.
europmc-pmc1925136:
Kloosterman, Plasterk and co-authors devised in 2007 a quick way to switch off single microRNAs in developing zebrafish. MicroRNAs are tiny gene regulators, but removing them one by one had rarely shown clear effects. Their tool is a morpholino, a synthetic strand that blocks the cutting steps which mature a microRNA.

Morpholinos aimed at either the first long transcript or the hairpin precursor blocked production, while others blocked the mature microRNA itself. The team knocked down 13 microRNAs shared by zebrafish and mammals. Most knockdowns caused no visible flaw. Blocking miR-375, though, wrecked the shape of the pancreatic islet, the hormone-making cell cluster. The islet held together at one day but its cells scattered later. Independent control strands gave the same result, ruling out off-target effects.
europmc-pmc1934936:
Winter, Provart and co-authors built in 2007 a browser that paints large biology datasets onto pictures of the samples themselves. Gene chips and other high-throughput projects yield floods of numbers that non-specialists find hard to read. A picture of a plant or tissue, colored by measured values, is far more intuitive.

The tool is called the electronic Fluorescent Pictograph, or eFP Browser. It maps each value onto the matching spot in a drawing of the experiment's source material. Examples include Arabidopsis gene activity painted onto plant organs, protein locations painted onto a cell diagram, and mouse gene activity painted onto a tissue atlas. The engine adapts to datasets from any organism. Its purpose is hypothesis generation: letting a researcher see patterns at a glance and decide what to test next.
europmc-pmc2124536: A medical paper on the ratio between heart weight and body weight in various animals. The hearts, weighed. This article preserves that comparative anatomy. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2126336: A medical paper on a characteristic localization of Bacillus abortus in the bovine fetal membranes. The cattle germ's home. This article preserves that veterinary bacteriology. The historical record keeps it. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
europmc-pmc2128336: A medical paper on changes in small blood lymphocytes following ligation. The tied vessels. This article preserves that hematology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2131436: A medical paper on the antigenic complex of Streptococcus haemolyticus, anaphylaxis. The strep's antigens. This article preserves that immunology. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2242836:
Koh and co-workers tested in 2008 what lets the fungus Candida albicans spread from the gut into the bloodstream. In cancer patients, gut colonisation plus chemotherapy is thought to precede bloodstream invasion. The team built a mouse model with stable gut colonisation after antibiotics cleared resident bacteria. They then applied single insults and combinations: chemotherapy, neutrophil depletion, macrophage depletion, lymphocyte loss, or gut lining damage.

Chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide caused 100 percent mortality in colonised mice. Each single immune depletion or gut damage alone caused no deaths. Combining neutrophil depletion with gut mucosal damage, however, produced disseminated infection and 100 percent mortality. Spread also required the fungus to switch from yeast to hyphal form, its thread-like growth mode. Both a breached gut lining and missing neutrophils are necessary.
europmc-pmc2323236:
Huse and co-authors measured the error rate of a fast DNA reading machine in 2007. The machine, the Roche GS20, reads many short DNA pieces at once by a method called pyrosequencing. It promised far more data than older methods, but early reports put its accuracy near 96% per letter.

The team read a known stretch of bacterial gene and counted the mistakes. They found that a small share of low-quality reads caused most errors. Those bad reads likely came from beads that carried more than one DNA template at once. By spotting and removing such reads, accuracy rose to 99.75% or better, a level they judged good for surveys of microbe communities.
europmc-pmc2323736: Acid and gelatin combine in proportions worth measuring twice, which is what this paper did with fresh determinations. The laboratory repeated the union under controlled conditions. The second look at an old reaction, reported. The article preserves that biochemistry research for future readers.
europmc-pmc2359936:
de Azambuja and co-authors pooled studies of the Ki-67 marker in early breast cancer in 2007. Ki-67 is a protein found in cells that are actively dividing, so it gauges how fast a tumor grows. Doctors wanted to know whether high Ki-67 meant a worse outlook for patients.

The meta-analysis covered 46 studies with 12,155 patients. Tumors scored positive for Ki-67 carried a higher risk of the cancer coming back, with a hazard ratio of 1.93, and that held whether or not lymph nodes were involved. Survival was also worse, with a hazard ratio of 1.95, and the pattern was similar in node-negative and node-positive groups. The authors concluded that Ki-67 positivity marks patients who face higher relapse risk and poorer survival.
europmc-pmc2551736:
Ghosh, Rho, McIntosh, Kötter, and Jirsa used a computer model in 2008 to explain the brain's resting activity. Even with no task, groups of brain regions pulse together in patterns called resting state networks, which overlap the networks used during directed thought. Oddly, similar patterns appear under deep anaesthesia, when there is no consciousness at all.

The team simulated dynamics on a realistic map of primate brain connections. Anatomy alone did not produce the resting networks. Adding neural noise, the brain's background randomness, plus the time delays of signals travelling along fibres, made the familiar patterns emerge on their own. Activity unfolded across fast and ultraslow rhythms at once. The authors argue noise lets the brain explore its range of possible states.
europmc-pmc2553836:
Schommer and colleagues uncovered in 2008 how a small RNA in plants links leaf growth to leaf ageing. The RNA, miR319, reins in a family of transcription factors called TCPs, proteins that switch genes on and off. Working out what those factors do downstream had been a gap, so the team traced their direct effects in developing leaves.

They found that TCPs control production of jasmonic acid, a plant hormone. The factors switch on a gene needed to make the hormone, and plants with altered TCP activity changed their jasmonate levels accordingly. TCPs also promoted leaf senescence, the ageing and yellowing of leaves, a process jasmonic acid was already suspected to drive. The authors propose that miR319 and its TCP targets coordinate two stages of a leaf's life: growth first, then ageing.
europmc-pmc2582336:
Henderson and colleagues sorted young children's wheezing into patterns in 2008 and asked which patterns point toward asthma. They used records from 6,265 children in the ALSPAC birth cohort, with wheeze reports at seven points from birth to age seven. A statistical technique called latent class analysis grouped the children, and allergy tests, lung function, and airway responsiveness were measured at ages seven to nine.

Six wheezing phenotypes emerged. Wheeze starting at 18 months carried the strongest links to allergy, with odds of 8.36 against the rarely wheezing group, and to twitchy airways. Wheeze beginning after 42 months also tracked allergy and responsiveness. Early wheeze that faded showed no allergy link, only weak airway effects. The authors say onset after 18 months marks when environmental influences may trigger atopic wheezing.
europmc-pmc2582436:
Grützmann and a large team of collaborators validated in 2008 a blood test for colorectal cancer based on altered DNA in plasma. Colorectal cancer is the second leading cause of cancer death, yet fewer than 45 percent of at-risk Americans screen regularly. The test looks for heavy methylation, a chemical silencing mark, on the septin 9 gene in DNA floating in blood.

In a training study of 354 samples the test caught 48 percent of cancers with 7 percent false positives. A blinded validation on 309 samples caught 58 percent, and adding a repeat measurement lifted detection to 72 percent while holding specificity at 90 percent overall. It also found about 20 percent of large polyps, the growths that precede cancer. Rates in other cancers and non-cancer conditions stayed low.
europmc-pmc2614436:
Jones and colleagues introduced software called CellProfiler Analyst in 2008 for exploring the flood of data from image-based cell screens. Automated microscopes can measure hundreds of features per cell, for hundreds of millions of cells in one experiment. That is far more than researchers can inspect by eye. Their open-source system is built for interactive exploration of exactly this kind of multidimensional data.

Analyst lets users plot, filter, and classify cells on the fly, linking every data point back to its image. Crucially, it automates the scoring of complex phenotypes, cell appearances that no single measurement captures but that combinations of features define. A biologist can train the classifier by example, marking cells of interest, and the software then scores the whole screen. The authors present it as a companion to automated image analysis pipelines.
europmc-pmc2633336:
Westman and colleagues compared two diets for type 2 diabetes in a 24-week randomised trial published in 2008. Carbohydrate is the main driver of blood sugar after meals, so the team tested whether cutting it harder beats a gentler approach. Eighty-four community volunteers, all with obesity and type 2 diabetes, took part. One group got a low-carbohydrate ketogenic diet, under 20 grams of carbohydrate daily. The other got a low-glycemic-index diet with a 500-calorie daily deficit.

Forty-nine participants finished the study. Both diets improved blood sugar control, fasting insulin, and weight. The ketogenic group did better on each measure. Their haemoglobin A1c, a three-month sugar average, fell by 1.5 percent against 0.5 percent. They lost 11.1 kilograms against 6.9 in the comparison group. Diabetes medicines were reduced or stopped in 95.2 percent of the ketogenic group versus 62 percent.
europmc-pmc2660436:
McDonnell and Abbott explored in 2009 a strange effect called stochastic resonance, in which adding random noise makes a weak signal easier, not harder, to detect. The effect shows up in physics, in electronics, and in nerve cells. Yet the term means different things in different fields, and the fuzziness has bred confusion and debate.

The deepest open question is whether the brain itself uses noise on purpose, as part of its code. Indirect proof abounds, the authors note, but brain scientists have largely ignored the debate. They argue the brain would be stranger to waste free randomness than to put noise to work. They urge a broad working definition, centered on noise benefits, and call for experiments that test directly whether random variation helps living systems process signals.
europmc-pmc2687936:
Samuels and Szabadi laid out in 2008 the basic wiring of the locus coeruleus, the brain's main source of noradrenaline, a chemical that promotes wakefulness. This small nucleus reaches nearly the whole brain. Part one of their review explains how its connections let it control both arousal and the body's automatic functions.

To keep us alert, the nucleus excites wide areas of the cortex, the thalamus relay, and other arousal centers. At the same time it silences sleep-promoting cells, a pincer move that enforces wakefulness. For body control, it projects down the spinal cord and to a string of automatic control centers, from the vagus nucleus to the amygdala. Turning the nucleus up raises sympathetic, fight-or-flight activity and lowers parasympathetic, rest-and-digest activity. Any change in its firing, they show, ripples out as a whole-brain pattern.
europmc-pmc2689936:
Howie, Donnelly, and Marchini described in 2009 IMPUTE v2, a program that fills in unmeasured DNA variants in genome-wide disease studies. Chips read only a sample of a person's variants. Imputation guesses the rest from reference panels of fully read people, and bigger panels, from projects reading thousands of genomes, were on the way.

The new version's edge is flexibility: it can weave several reference panels, typed on different chips, into one model and stay fast enough for real studies. Against HapMap data alone it already beat rival methods. With panels expanded to thousands of chromosomes, accuracy jumped for rare and common variants alike, with error rates 15 to 20 percent below the nearest competitor. Better guesses mean more power to spot the small genetic effects behind common disease, without typing a single extra sample.
europmc-pmc2698136:
Yan and colleagues charted in 2009, day by day and region by region, what happens in a standard mouse model of gut inflammation. The model feeds mice a chemical, DSS, in their drinking water, damaging the colon lining in a way that mimics human inflammatory bowel disease. It is used everywhere to test new therapies, yet its timeline was loosely mapped.

Mice lost weight, their colons shortened, and stools turned bloody, as expected. Tissue checks showed crypts shrinking and vanishing while immune cells flooded in, then healing once the chemical stopped. One inflammation marker, MPO, stayed very high even during recovery, a lag worth knowing. The gut wall leaked more during treatment but resealed afterward. Inflammatory signals rose and fell with the damage, but not evenly: the far end of the colon reacted differently from the near end. Timing and sampling spot, the authors show, can tilt results.
europmc-pmc2716536:
Ramos and co-authors used new sequencing tools in 2009 to find hundreds of thousands of pig DNA markers and build a dense testing chip. Single nucleotide polymorphisms, one-letter DNA differences, are needed in large numbers to map traits that matter to pig farming. No high-density pig chip existed before this work.

Sequencing samples from four pig breeds and wild boar found over three hundred seventy thousand new markers. From a larger pool they built a commercial chip holding over sixty-four thousand markers. Testing the same animals gave a high call rate, and most scored markers proved truly variable. The chip gives pig genetics a standard tool for trait and diversity studies.
europmc-pmc2727536:
Marshall, Altman, Holder, and Royston gave guidance in 2009 on combining results in prognostic studies that use multiple imputation, a method that fills missing data several times to reflect uncertainty. Prognostic models predict patient outcomes from traits and disease features, and missing trait data are common. Each filled data set gives its own estimate, which must then be merged fairly.

Their literature review found that methods for merging were poorly reported, and when stated, most teams used Rubin's rules with no transformation at all. Those rules assume a normal spread, which fits some measures poorly, such as predicted survival chances. Their simple guidelines match the merging method to the measure, which should widen sound use of imputation.
europmc-pmc2742736:
Balgi and co-authors screened in 2009 over three thousand five hundred chemicals for compounds that boost autophagy, the cell self-eating process, by blocking mTORC1 signaling. mTORC1 is a kinase complex that senses nutrients and normally suppresses autophagy when food is plentiful. Drugs with useful properties were needed to test mTORC1 control in diseases such as cancer and diabetes.

Four compounds raised autophagy markers fast, including three approved drugs: perhexiline, niclosamide, and amiodarone. They blocked signaling to mTORC1 without blocking its sister complex, and most effects reversed when the drug was washed out. Brief exposure killed starved cells but not fed cells, which contrasts with rapamycin, whose block is lasting and nonselective in that test.
europmc-pmc2815736:
Palacios and colleagues showed in 2009 that a mitochondria-based enzyme called SIRT3 answers to both exercise and diet in mouse skeletal muscle. Mitochondria are the cell's energy units, and SIRT3 sits inside them, removing chemical tags from proteins. The team asked what daily signals turn its levels up or down.

Training raised SIRT3 levels in muscle, alongside rises in two partner factors, CREB activity and PGC-1alpha, which drives new mitochondria building. Slow, endurance-type muscle carried more SIRT3 than fast muscle. Fasting and calorie restriction raised levels, while a high-fat diet lowered them. In mice lacking SIRT3, those partner factors fell, placing the enzyme upstream in the muscle's energy response chain.
europmc-pmc2835736:
Price, Dehal, and Arkin released FastTree 2 in 2010, a program that builds evolutionary trees from huge sets of aligned sequences. Tree building slows brutally as datasets grow, yet the largest gene families now hold hundreds of thousands of members. The update keeps the original speed while closing its accuracy gap.

New tree-shuffling moves and a per-site rate estimate sharpen the search. On test data the program edged out a standard likelihood tool. It also ran one hundred to one thousand times faster on large inputs, though the very slowest, most careful methods still beat it slightly. As a proof, it built a tree from nearly two hundred thirty-eight thousand ribosomal RNA sequences on a desktop in twenty-two hours.
europmc-pmc2841636:
Mullin and colleagues surveyed pesticide residues in North American beehives in 2010, during a period when about a third of United States colonies were dying each winter. Samples of wax, pollen, bees, and hive material came from beekeepers across twenty-three states and one Canadian province over two growing seasons.

They found one hundred twenty-one different pesticides and breakdown products across eight hundred eighty-seven samples. Nearly every wax sample, ninety-eight percent, carried two mite-killing chemicals beekeepers themselves apply, often at high levels, alongside farm fungicides. Pollen, the food of young bees, held cocktails reaching parts-per-million levels. The authors warn that such mixtures, heavy with nerve agents, may erode bee fitness even when no single chemical kills outright.
europmc-pmc2854736:
Engel, Miodovnik, Canfield, Zhu, Silva, Calafat, and Wolff followed a New York City birth cohort in 2010. They tested whether phthalates, chemicals leaching from plastics and personal care products, affect children's behavior before birth. Mothers gave urine samples late in pregnancy, and one hundred eighty-eight children were tested repeatedly between ages four and nine for behavior and executive function, the mind's self-control system.

Higher levels of low-molecular-weight phthalate traces in mothers predicted worse scores in their children across aggression, conduct problems, attention, and depression scales. The same exposure tracked poorer overall executive function and weaker emotional control. The affected areas mirror those disturbed in children diagnosed with conduct and attention disorders, the authors note.
europmc-pmc2882336:
Titov and co-authors ran in 2010 an Australian trial asking whether a trained technician can guide online therapy for depression as well as a clinician can. The therapy was internet cognitive behavioral therapy, six lessons with weekly homework over eight weeks. One hundred forty-one volunteers with major depression were assigned by chance to clinician guidance, technician guidance, or a waiting group.

Completion ran high in both guided groups. By the end of treatment, both groups had cut their depression scores sharply compared with waiting, and the two forms of guidance did not differ from each other. Gains were large by standard effect measures. Skilled technicians offering structure and encouragement, without clinical advice, may free scarce clinicians for the patients who need them most.
europmc-pmc2892436:
Spiess and Neumeyer demonstrated in 2010, through intensive computer simulation, that a beloved fit statistic misleads scientists who fit curved models to data. The statistic, R2, works tolerably for straight-line models but was long suspected to fail for nonlinear ones common in pharmacology and biochemistry. The pair generated data from known true models and watched what R2 reported.

Even when the evidence favoring the true model was overwhelming by modern information criteria, R2 budged only in its third to fifth decimal place. A bias-corrected version still leaned toward needlessly complex models. Two alternatives built for model choice performed far better in the same tests. Reviewers and researchers should drop R2 as proof of a nonlinear model's worth, the authors conclude.
europmc-pmc2908536:
Szajnik and co-authors showed in 2010 that tumors shed tiny membrane bubbles that recruit the immune system's own peacekeepers to protect the tumor. The bubbles, called tumor-derived microvesicles, float in patients' body fluids. Regulatory T cells, which suppress immune attacks, are already known to be more numerous and more active in cancer patients, and the team tested whether the bubbles drive that.

Bubbles from tumor cells, but not from normal cells, created fresh regulatory T cells from ordinary ones and expanded existing ones. The resulting cells carried more suppressor weapons, including IL-10 and TGF-beta signals, and shut down other immune cells more strongly. Blocking those two signals largely stopped the expansion. Tumors appear to manufacture their own immune shield at a distance.
europmc-pmc2936536:
Bigham and a large team scanned the genomes of Tibetan and Andean highlanders in 2010, hunting signs of adaptation to thin mountain air. Both peoples have lived for thousands of years where oxygen is scarce, and each shows distinct body responses.

Applying four statistical tests for natural selection to dense genome data, they flagged candidate genes in each group separately. The two patterns proved largely different, with selection marking different genes and regions in each population. One shared thread involved a gene tied to sensing oxygen inside cells. The results show mountain adaptation evolved along separate paths.
europmc-pmc2956736:
Cox, Peterson, and Biggs presented SolexaQA, a software package for checking the quality of Illumina sequencing runs, in a 2010 article. The machines dominate modern DNA reading, yet quick standard quality checks were lacking.

The package produces detailed statistics and simple graphics within minutes, so lanes and runs can be compared on the same footing. A companion tool trims reads dynamically, cutting weak bases guided by each read's own quality scores. Because errors climb steeply along each read in this technology, such at-a-glance diagnostics help users decide how to clean data before analysis.
europmc-pmc2984136:
Sobrova and co-authors reviewed deoxynivalenol, a toxin made by Fusarium fungi that infect grain in fields and storage, in a 2010 article. People meet it in cereal foods directly, or through milk, eggs, and meat from exposed animals.

It turns up in wheat, corn, oats, barley, rice, and many processed foods from flour and bread to beer and baby food. Short-term exposure brings nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, stomach pain, headache, and fever. The review also covers harms to reproduction and how this toxin amplifies or offsets the effects of other fungal poisons eaten together.
europmc-pmc3002336:
Brase, Wuttig, Kuner, and Sültmann reviewed blood-borne microRNAs as gentle cancer markers in a 2010 article. These tiny RNA molecules steer gene activity, go astray in tumours, and survive surprisingly well in serum and other fluids.

Studies across tumour types had begun reporting distinct circulating signatures that separate patients from healthy people and may forecast course. The review also covers how the molecules escape cells, whether in tiny vesicles or bound to proteins, and what jobs they might do once travelling. Hurdles remain in standardising measurement before clinics can rely on such tests.
europmc-pmc3075236:
Mohapatra and the Million Death Study team produced in 2011 the first solid national count of snakebite deaths in India. Hospital reports had put the yearly toll anywhere from a little over a thousand to fifty thousand, a useless range. The team instead interviewed families about more than one hundred twenty thousand deaths in randomly chosen areas across the country, with doctors coding causes independently.

Snakebite accounted for close to forty six thousand deaths a year in the early two thousands by their estimate, far above official counts. Deaths clustered in villages, struck young adults most, and peaked in the monsoon months. Three states carried the largest burdens. The authors say global snakebite totals are likely underestimated too, since India holds such a share. Better antivenom distribution, staff training, and community teaching in the worst hit states could cut the toll sharply.
europmc-pmc3091536:
Bults and colleagues tracked in 2011 how the Dutch public perceived and responded to the new swine flu during its first months, using three online surveys of a representative panel. The first ran days after the outbreak made news in spring 2009, with follow ups in early and late summer. They measured knowledge, worry, trust in government information, and what precautions people actually took.

Knowledge rose steadily, while the flu came to seem less severe and trust in official information slipped. Worry eased early, then leveled off. By late summer far more people were taking preventive steps than in June, even as concern fell. Taking steps tracked with high anxiety, confidence in one's own precautions, and close attention to media coverage. A strong intent to follow future official advice tracked with age and trust. The authors call the public response calm and largely compliant.
europmc-pmc3101336:
Burton and Jauniaux reviewed in 2011 how oxidative stress shapes the placenta and the complications of human pregnancy. Oxidative stress occurs when reactive oxygen molecules outrun the body's defenses. At low levels these molecules serve as useful signals inside cells. At high levels they damage fats, proteins, and DNA indiscriminately.

The chapter explains how the placenta makes and detoxifies these molecules across pregnancy, and the roles they play in its normal growth. It then traces their hand in troubles ranging from miscarriage to preeclampsia, the dangerous blood pressure disorder of pregnancy, and early rupture of the membranes before labor. The placenta's shift to oxygen rich blood early in pregnancy is a natural stress test that usually passes safely. When defenses falter, the authors show, the same chemistry turns destructive. Their review anchors a fast growing research focus.
europmc-pmc3160336:
Camilo Mora and colleagues estimated how many species live on Earth in a 2011 paper in PLoS Biology. Counting every species directly is impossible, and earlier guesses swung wildly. The team noticed instead that the ladder of classification above species, from genus up to phylum, fills in at a predictable pace as naming advances. That pace can then forecast the missing species below.

Checked against groups whose species are nearly all known, the method held up. Applied worldwide, it predicts close to nine million complex-life species, about a quarter of them marine. With just over a million species catalogued after two and a half centuries, the great majority on land and nearly all in the ocean still await description. The authors call for renewed exploration and naming work.
europmc-pmc3234236:
Cheng Huang and colleagues dissected how a SARS coronavirus protein silences host cells in this 2011 paper in PLoS Pathogens. The viral protein nsp1 clamps onto ribosomes, blocks protein production, and triggers destruction of the cell's messenger RNAs. The team used cell-free systems to learn exactly where the cuts fall and which RNAs are spared.

Nsp1 cut host-like messages mainly near their starting end. It also cut inside the ribosome-loading regions of some viral-style entry elements, but not others. There was no strict sequence preference at the cut sites. Remarkably, the virus's own messages escaped cutting entirely, because their leader sequence at the front end protects them. The authors argue this self-protection lets viral messages and proteins accumulate efficiently while the host's defenses are dismantled.
europmc-pmc3249036:
Stuart Baker reviewed the primate reticulospinal tract, a brainstem pathway for movement, in this 2011 paper in the Journal of Physiology. Textbooks cast this tract as a controller of trunk and shoulder muscles for posture, reaching, and walking, leaving fine finger control to the corticospinal tract. Baker argues recent evidence gives it a real, if secondary, role in hand movements.

Experiments he discusses show the pathway can reach the motor neurons of hand muscles, and that spinal circuits blend its input with corticospinal input, including in circuits serving the fingers. That matters after stroke damages the main pathway: surviving reticulospinal connections could carry part of the recovery. Baker urges deeper study of how the reticular formation handles sensation and movement, so rehabilitation can be designed around what this backup system can actually do.
europmc-pmc3276136:
Julian Catchen and colleagues introduced Stacks, software for building genetic markers directly from short sequencing reads, in this 2011 paper in G3. Cheap sequencing made it possible to genotype tens of thousands of markers in hundreds of individuals, but no software automated the calling. Stacks fills that gap for data from reduced-representation methods such as RAD-tags, which sample the genome at enzyme cut sites.

Given the piled-up reads at each site, the program assembles loci either from scratch or against a reference genome and calls genotypes with a likelihood-based model. The authors verified it on simulated stickleback data and rebuilt a zebrafish linkage map, improving on the original. They present Stacks as a route to ultra-dense maps, population history studies, and help with genome assembly, especially for little-studied species.
europmc-pmc3310436:
Kirkbride and colleagues reviewed sixty years of studies on how often psychotic illness begins in England, publishing in 2012. Rates of new cases matter for planning mental health services, but studies used different methods and covered different groups. The team gathered work published between 1950 and 2009 on first onset psychosis in adults, including schizophrenia and mood disorders with psychotic features.

Across studies, about thirty two people per hundred thousand developed a psychotic disorder each year, with schizophrenia accounting for roughly half that rate. Rates were far from uniform. They varied by age and sex, with a second peak for women after middle age. Rates also ran several times higher among people of Black Caribbean, African, or South Asian backgrounds than in the white British population. Overall rates showed no clear change over time.
europmc-pmc3312336:
Luckheeram, Zhou, Verma, and Xia reviewed how helper T cells choose their specialized forms, in a 2012 article. These white blood cells, marked by a protein called CD4, coordinate immune attacks against germs. Fresh helper cells start uncommitted and, once they meet their target, mature into one of several types depending on the chemical signals around them.

Alongside the classic two types, researchers now recognize several more, including types that fight fungi and bacteria, types that calm the immune system, and types that help antibody production. Each type needs its own chain of signals, master switch proteins, and lasting marks on its genes, and each releases its own set of messenger chemicals. The review maps those pathways as a guide to how balanced immune responses are built.
europmc-pmc3348936:
Celis-Morales and colleagues compared two ways of measuring how active people are: motion sensors worn on the body and a widely used self-report questionnaire. Working with several hundred adults, they set out to see which approach better captured links between activity and markers of health risk.

Among 317 adults, the questionnaire and the accelerometer told different stories. People tended to describe their activity in ways that blurred its true relationship with risk markers, so associations looked weaker than they were. Objective monitoring recovered stronger, clearer links. The authors warn that studies relying on self-reported activity alone may underestimate how much movement matters for health.
europmc-pmc3351736:
Khangura and her team described how their Knowledge to Action research programme produced quick evidence summaries for health decision makers. Managers often need synthesised research faster than a full systematic review allows, so the group formalised a rapid review product and reported their experience openly.

Their eight-step approach was refined through feedback from the managers who requested the summaries. Between November 2009 and March 2011 the team delivered eleven summaries spanning clinical effectiveness and health system questions. Users judged them timely and valuable for decisions. The authors argue that rapid products can stay trustworthy if their shortcuts are transparent and systematically reported.
europmc-pmc3369436:
Jaggupilli and Elkord took a critical look in 2012 at two surface markers widely used to hunt cancer stem cells. These rare cells are blamed for starting tumors, spreading them, and resisting treatment. CD44 sits on almost every tumor cell, while CD24 appears on many tumor types.

The review weighs reports from breast, lung, pancreas, prostate, and other cancers, alone and paired with other markers. Again and again the pair's value for picking out true tumor-starting cells proves inconsistent. No marker set has yet been confirmed as the best across cancers. The authors urge caution before treatment plans rest on these labels alone.
europmc-pmc3429036:
Mitchell and colleagues reviewed in 2012 how aging shrinks and weakens human muscle, separating loss of mass from loss of strength. The mass loss, sarcopenia, has drawn two decades of attention, but weakness, called dynapenia, tracks disability more closely. The two decline on different schedules, which forces the idea of muscle quality: force per unit of muscle.

Across studies, adults past seventy-five lose mass at well under one percent a year, while strength drains several times faster. Studies measuring both in the same people confirm strength falls two to five times quicker. Weakness, more than size, predicts disability and death. The review covers the tissue changes behind both declines and what drives them.
europmc-pmc3476336:
Plagnol and colleagues built a better way to spot missing or extra chunks of DNA in exome data, reporting in Bioinformatics in 2012. Exome sequencing reads only the protein-coding parts of the genome and finds many disease mutations. Larger deletions and duplications also cause disease, but uneven lab handling makes them hard to call from read counts without false alarms.

Their method, ExomeDepth, models read counts robustly and picks a tailored reference set for each sample. It proved able to catch even single-exon, half-strength deletions across many kinds of datasets. Applied to patients with immune disorders, it found new disease-causing deletions in two genes. Plagnol's team released the method as a free software package.

fbi-vault-al-capone-al-capone-part-18-of: Part eighteen of the FBI's Al Capone records. The 1931 trial brought the gangster down. These pages preserve more of that story. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
fbi-vault-al-capone-al-capone-part-19-of: Part nineteen of the FBI's Al Capone case file. Prison at Alcatraz ended Scarface's empire. This section continues the Bureau's account. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
fbi-vault-al-capone-al-capone-part-2-of-: Part two of the FBI's Al Capone records. The young Bureau took on Chicago's most famous criminal. These pages hold the early case. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
fbi-vault-special-counsel-mueller-invest: The Russia probe's evidence filled volume after volume; part thirty-six of the FBI Vault's Mueller records continues the release. Hundreds of interviews backed the special counsel's findings. These pages preserve more. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
frus-1861-d136:
On 6 July 1861, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote a second letter to William Dayton. It is document 136 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Paired letters let Seward sort Paris business point by point. One file might hold law, the next a claim or a name. The second letter of 6 July shows the same neat hand at work in the French file as in the London one. Neat clerk work of this sort kept a vast record clear under wartime strain. A clear record is a gift to every later reader of a crowded year.
frus-1861-d236:
8 June 1861 is the date on a dispatch from James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands to William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 236 in the President's message volume for 1861. By then, in the opening months of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d36:
Thomas Corwin received a letter from William H. Seward on 6 April 1861, as he set out for Mexico. Corwin was the new American minister to Mexico. The letter is document 36 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Mexico mattered to Washington for its long border with Texas and its own deep debts in Europe. Corwin, a famed speaker and former Treasury chief, carried weight in Mexico City. Seward's April letter sent him south with the war only days from its start. Corwin's fame as an orator made him a strong voice with the Mexican government of Benito Juárez.
frus-1862-d136:
Charles Francis Adams reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in a dispatch dated 4 September 1862. The printed record keeps it as Document 136 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. It was written in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d236:
Two Seward letters to William Stuart bear the date 11 September 1862, and the first is Document 236 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Stuart was acting head of the British legation in Washington that year.

By 11 September, Union and Confederate armies were closing on each other in Maryland, days from Antietam. Foreign policy waited on the result more openly than either side admitted. Seward's letters of that week kept the Department's business with the legation current. So that no small dispute could grow while the great question was decided by arms. The channel stayed open through the whole war, which was itself a kind of success.
frus-1862-d336:
On 20 October 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent William L. Dayton a dispatch printed as Document 336 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The letter came late in a heavy month of Paris mail.

Late October found the truce proposal stalled in London and France unwilling to act alone. Seward's letters in this stretch could afford a calmer tone than September's, though the danger was not past. This dispatch shows the Department working to convert a reprieve into a durable result, keeping pressure on Paris while tempers cooled. French public opinion ran warmer for the Union after the emancipation news arrived.
frus-1862-d36:
Charles Francis Adams reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in a dispatch dated 20 March 1862. The printed record keeps it as Document 36 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. It was written in the winter of the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d436:
Gabriel García Tassara sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 26 August 1862. It appears as Document 436 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, out of strict date order in the printed Spanish file.

The printed volume groups letters by subject as well as by date, so Tassara's August note sits among the autumn papers. Its place in the file is a reminder that the Spanish correspondence ran on several tracks at once. Those tracks were Mexico, Cuba, and maritime rights. They also included the daily courtesies between two governments at peace. Reading the Tassara notes in sequence gives a clear view of how a resident minister worked, and how much of foreign policy was routine care.
frus-1862-d536:
On 19 June 1862 Roest van Limburg wrote again to Secretary of State William H. Seward, ten days after the first burst of Dutch notes. His letter is Document 536 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

The mid-June note shows the Dutch business settling into its longer rhythm after the intense first week. Van Limburg continued to represent a government whose ships, colonies, and carrying trade gave it a permanent interest in American maritime practice. Seward's department dealt with The Hague on two tracks, through Pike abroad and Van Limburg at home. The letter belongs to the home track, where questions arrived in writing and were answered in kind, on the record.
frus-1862-d636:
On 8 May 1861 Townsend Harris addressed this dispatch from Japan to the Secretary of State, by then William H. Seward in the new Lincoln administration. It is Document 636 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Harris wrote a month after Fort Sumter, though no word of the war could yet have reached him. His subject was Japan. There he remained the solitary American minister. The address to the office rather than the man suits a dispatch sent across a change of government. His reports from Edo in 1861 describe a treaty system still fragile and a minister worn by isolation and ill health. The letter opens the Civil War-era Japanese file in the volume.
frus-1863p1-d136:
On 28 March 1863, William H. Seward sent this second letter of the day to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 136 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

A same-day Adams letter sits right after this one in the volume, so the pens crossed in print as they did at sea. Seward's second sheet of 28 March held its own head of the brief, as his pairs always did. Adams would read it ten days on, beside the news of the hour. The letter is a stitch in the tightest-woven part of the file, the spring of 1863.
frus-1863p1-d236:
To guide his minister in London, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote these orders on 14 July 1863 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. They stand as document 236 of the 1863 volume. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

The chief aim behind such orders was simple: keep Britain from treating the Confederacy as a nation. Every instruction from Washington served that goal in some way. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d336:
On 10 December 1862, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It appears as document 336 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Cases in these notes can look small, one ship or one arrested man, yet each tested the rules of neutrality. Both governments treated the precedents as serious business. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d36:
On 14 August 1862, Judah P. Benjamin wrote to A. Dudley Mann. Benjamin ran the Confederate state office in Richmond; Mann was one of the South's first agents sent to win backing in Europe. The letter is document 36 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Mann had roamed the courts of Europe since 1861, seeking a nod for the South's cause. Benjamin's letters kept such agents stocked with claims, facts, and hope. This one predates the others in its group, a look at the South's pitch in the summer of 1862. Printed in the Union's volume, it lets readers hear the other side in its own words.
frus-1863p1-d436:
Secretary William H. Seward wrote this official letter to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington on 1 April 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d536:
Dated 27 May 1863, document 536 is a letter from F. W. Seward to Lord Lyons. F. W. Seward was the Assistant Secretary of State, writing here to Britain's minister in Washington. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d636:
Among the day's business on 8 October 1863 was a letter from Charles Francis Adams to William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. Adams in London was the Union's front line in Britain, pressing its case with the British government week after week.

Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. Adams's task was to make the Union's case where it counted, inside the British capital, while Seward set the line from Washington. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d136: Minister Kirk wrote to the Secretary of State from Cairo on November 17, 1943, five days before the conference opened in his city. The dispatch is Document 136 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Host-city reporting in the final days mixed politics with roofs, guards, and telephones, though this record names no topic. It is printed in the Foreign Relations series, in the arrival run of papers.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d236:
Joint Staff Planners drafted a proposed agenda, marked Enclosure B, for President Roosevelt's first meeting with Prime Minister Churchill at Cairo. Prepared aboard the Iowa between 15 and 19 November 1943, the short secret paper went directly to the President without Joint Chiefs of Staff approval.

Command questions head the list: the urgency of naming an overall commander, a commander for Overlord, a commander for the Mediterranean, and a unified strategic bomber command in Europe. Other items cover the Rankin plans for a German collapse. They also cover the American refusal to join operations in the eastern Mediterranean and Balkans, Soviet cooperation from bombing to Turkey and Sweden, and American facilities in the Azores.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d336:
Assistant Secretary of War John McCloy sent Secretary of War Henry Stimson a second secret priority telegram from Cairo on 27 November 1943, numbered 10065. It follows his longer report of the same day on the civil affairs talks.

McCloy says he has spoken with the Joint Chiefs and the British, and with Roosevelt, Winant, and Eden as well. If the British confirm the agreement set out in his telegram 10064, he feels the Americans will have gained all they set out to win on civil affairs. He adds a glimpse of the wider conference: though he stood only at the fringe of the strategy talks, every important decision was plainly being held up. All waited until the Eastern conference, at Tehran, reported back. He had been asked to stay on at Cairo pending the party's return.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d36: Roosevelt wrote to Churchill on October 4, 1943, the same day he wrote to Stalin. The Churchill letter is Document 36 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Paired letters like these let the president keep both allies moving in the same week, a habit of his summit diplomacy. No topic is given in the record. The message can be read in the Foreign Relations volume, where the October papers thicken quickly.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d436:
On December 3, 1943, the American and British chiefs of staff met in Cairo. They sat as the Combined Chiefs of Staff. That joint body ran the shared war effort of the two countries. The meeting came two days after the Tehran Conference ended. It came one day before the Second Cairo Conference opened. The State Department later printed the minutes in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Minutes of this kind record who attended the session. They note which plans were argued over. They also note what the chiefs settled. The chiefs then reported those points to Roosevelt and Churchill. Read beside later sessions, the record shows summit work in detail. Broad pledges made at Tehran became orders, dates, and forces. Commands could then act on them.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d536:
Prime Minister Churchill opened the new year with a message to President Roosevelt on January 2, 1944. The two men had parted after the Cairo conferences in December, Churchill falling ill on his journey home. The State Department printed the message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

New Year messages between the leaders set the tone for the decisive year of the war in Europe. Their correspondence now had to turn Tehran and Cairo decisions into the Normandy invasion and the final campaigns. For readers, this letter stands at the hinge of the volume: the summit season behind, and the year of action ahead, in the words of the alliance's most tireless writer.
frus-1944-quebec-d136:
On September 8, 1944, Roosevelt sent Secretary of War Henry Stimson a short memorandum on Italy. It followed General O'Dwyer's report to the president that same day. The supply situation in Italy, Roosevelt wrote, was critical after years of Fascist and Nazi rule and the destruction of battles fought on Italian soil.

The order is direct and leaves no room for delay. The War Department was to take immediate action to make available the additional essential civilian supplies and shipping needed to remedy the condition. The memorandum is a clear example of a briefing paper turning, within hours, into a presidential instruction to a cabinet department.
frus-1944-quebec-d236:
Schoenfeld cabled from London on September 16, 1944, transmitting an appeal from Warsaw's Council of National Unity. Dated September 15 and addressed to Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin, the appeal reached London through Premier Mikołajczyk. It was the forty-fifth day of the Warsaw struggle, and the first Soviet supply drop had just brought, in the council's words, great relief.

The council affirmed the inflexible will of Warsaw and Poland to fight to the end. It fervently appealed for continuous dropping of arms, ammunition, and food, for permanent air cover, and for bombing of German concentrations. The enemy was attacking with reinforced formations, and without quick, effective succor a catastrophe might follow. Mikołajczyk noted weather had recently impeded the American shuttle service and British flights from Italy.
frus-1944-quebec-d36:
The American minister in London, named Reed in the heading, wrote to Harry Hopkins on August 29, 1944. A message from an embassy officer straight to the President's aide shows how many side channels fed the White House that summer. It appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Late August was arrangement season: the Quebec Conference was a fortnight off, and London was both a partner capital and a staging post for the journey. Staff messages like Reed's handled the questions that could not wait for the leaders. For readers, the note shows the conference being prepared from the British end of the alliance's wiring.
frus-1945-50-intel-d136: A memorandum of conversation dated 16 April 1948 is the latest-dated paper in the intelligence volume. Memoranda of conversation record a talk between officials, who met, what each side said. What was left open. So that spoken words cannot later be denied. The title names neither party. So the record stands on its date and its place at the volume's end. By then the National Security Act of 1947 had replaced the old system with the Central Intelligence Agency.
frus-1945-50-intel-d236:
A letter from Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter reached the Director of the Bureau of the Budget (Webb) on 15 December 1948. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 236, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. An outside survey team led by Allen Dulles was then reviewing the CIA, and its findings would drive a round of reform debate.

A formal letter was a step above a memo: it put a request or a stance on record under the writer's signature. The files around it hold the answer it drew, and often the draft that came before it. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d336:
A text titled "National Security Council Resolution" bears the date 13 January 1948. It survives in print as document 336 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. The young CIA was still defining its job, while the Council weighed how far secret action abroad should go.

The form is stiff because it has to be: each line is a rule that a named office can be held to. For a reader, the gain is precision: this is the rule as the ruled were told to obey it. A formal resolution carries more weight than a memo, since it records a choice the Council itself made and stood behind.
frus-1945-50-intel-d36:
General Hull, the Army's assistant chief of staff for operations, wrote to Lovett on 28 October 1945. Hull had appeared in the Potsdam papers as well, a mark of his wide duties. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

Operations and intelligence are the two hands of a general staff. Their chiefs had to agree on how the Army would gather and use secret information. Hull's letter to the air secretary crosses staff lines in a way that shows the question ripening inside the War Department. Readers can watch the Army sorting its own house in these autumn papers, before it faced the other departments across a table. Internal agreement came first; it was rarely easy.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d136:
How much should Germany pay, and in what form? A briefing book paper of 16 January 1945, “Reparation and Restitution Policy Toward Germany,” gives the American answer prepared for Yalta. It is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

Reparation, the paper warns, must never be let to wreck wider aims in Germany and Europe. It should take only the surplus above what a minimum German standard of living and prior charges require. Payment should be mostly in kind, over a short span, five years if possible and never more than ten. Labor services are allowed within reason, with a line drawn between active Nazis and passive Germans. Stolen property that can be traced must go back to its owners.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d236:
Moscow gave its side of the Iran oil quarrel in a letter of 28 December 1944 from Ambassador Gromyko. Addressed to the Secretary of State and received in translation, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It answers an American note of 1 November on the question of Iran.

In September, Gromyko writes, the Soviet government sent an official commission to Iran under Deputy Commissar Kavtaradze. Its task was to negotiate an oil concession in Iran's northern regions. The terms Moscow had in view, he insists, were very profitable and advantageous for Iran. In no degree did they infringe her sovereignty or independence. Prime Minister Saed at first declared his attitude favorable, and the commission began its early work on that basis.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d336:
Germany's treatment headed the plenary session at Yalta on February 5, 1945, and Bohlen's minutes open with Roosevelt framing the day. Political questions on Germany would come first, the President said. The leaders would not roam over the whole map of the world, to Dakar or Indochina. Zones of occupation came first.

Those zones, Roosevelt noted, had already been agreed in the European Advisory Commission. One point stayed open: France wanted a zone of its own and a seat in the control machinery for Germany. He stressed that zones concerned occupation only, not Germany's lasting fate. He then laid a map of the agreed zones on the table.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d36: Roosevelt also wrote to Churchill on 31 December 1944, giving the year two closing messages between them. His letter is document 36 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on Malta and Yalta. Paired with Churchill's note of the same date, it shows both leaders ending 1944 in active consultation, already looking toward their January departure for the Mediterranean.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d436:
Nine subjects crowd Page's minutes of the foreign ministers' meeting of February 10, 1945. Eden presided. Poland's formula led, then the Declaration on Liberated Europe, Yugoslavia, and reparations. The conference communiqué and the world organization followed. Three frontier questions closed the list, with Iran behind them.

On Poland, Stettinius said the American experts and the President had studied the formula closely. The Americans were ready to withdraw the last sentence, which Molotov had objected to. In return, the President would stay free to make any statement he felt necessary, based on his ambassador's reports. Page records the deal being trimmed to fit.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d136:
John Hickerson, acting director of European affairs, routed a small social invitation through Paris on July 11, 1945. His confidential telegram to Ambassador Caffery is document 136 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The message was meant for James Dunn, the assistant secretary traveling with the American delegation.

The British Embassy in Washington had word that Sir Alexander Cadogan, the Foreign Office's permanent head, would reach Terminal early on the afternoon of July 14. Cadogan hoped very much to have an informal talk with Dunn that day. Hickerson asks Caffery to pass the word along. Such quiet advance contacts between the two delegations' senior officials helped shape the conference before the leaders ever sat down together.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d236:
Under Secretary Grew recorded the Italian ambassador's call about declaring war on Japan in a memorandum dated July 6, 1945. The memo is document 236 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Ambassador Tarchiani came that morning with a secret paper from his government.

The new Italian government had decided in a secret meeting to favor declaring war on Japan, Tarchiani said, and wanted the step approved before the Big Three meeting if possible. The United States favored the move, and Cadogan had said Britain would not object. The Soviet government might have to be consulted. Grew said he did not know whether approval could come before the summit; the matter might have to be discussed there. He promised to explore it at once. Italy did declare war on Japan days later, a step toward regaining standing among the victors.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d336:
Money for German exports opens a quarrel in Clayton's letter of June 18, 1945, to McCloy at the War Department. War Department officers had told the State Department that the Army was not responsible for exports from Germany, except where goods served a direct military need. On that view, the Army could not pay for supplies to raise German output for export.

The question had come up over coal. Europe's freed countries needed far more German coal, and producing it took supplies someone had to finance. Clayton's letter presses the War Department to widen its duty, setting up a State-War fight that ran on into the Potsdam briefing.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d36:
Stalin wants the meeting, and would host it near Berlin: Hopkins cabled Truman from Moscow on May 28, 1945. Another long talk with Stalin had ended that night; details would follow in the morning. Stalin had again said he was anxious to meet Truman at any time wished. In the suburbs of Berlin, he said, there would be adequate quarters for such a meeting.
