Hopkins asked whether he should tell Stalin that Truman would like to meet around July 15. Stalin, he judged, would prefer an earlier date, given the many pressing problems to be decided. The cable assumes the Control Council would by then be set up, with American forces in the area. Potsdam enters the record here as a suburb and a date.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d436:
Expulsion of minorities from Czechoslovakia is the subject of a briefing book paper dated June 23, 1945. The Czechoslovak Republic had officially informed the United States that it wished to expel, immediately, the Sudeten German and Hungarian minorities. Washington had voiced sympathy with Prague's concern over its minority problems.

Yet the United States opposed any unilateral action to transfer these minorities. Transfer must wait for a satisfactory agreement with the powers responsible for order and military security in Germany. The paper places the Sudeten question inside the larger problem of German minorities in Poland and other states, fit for the heads of government to settle in an orderly way.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d536:
A post-war lend-lease settlement with Britain is missing, a briefing book paper explains, and it gives the reason. No so-called 3(c) agreement for post-war deliveries of lend-lease has been made with the British. When approached informally in 1944, the British indicated they were unwilling to enter any commitment to make post-war financial settlement for lend-lease goods.

That position rested on Britain's hard outlook. The United Kingdom will emerge from the war in a difficult financial position, with limited supplies of gold and dollar exchange. The British should nevertheless be asked to reconsider, the paper argues. American policy holds that lend-lease is not to be used for post-war purposes, so transfers would be interrupted shortly after V-J Day without a settlement.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d636:
A top secret briefing paper on Syria and Lebanon was prepared for Potsdam, dated June 30, 1945. It is document 636 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The Levant crisis had just brought British troops into Syria against the French.

The paper notes that London and Paris both want the Levant problem settled. It clouds their ties and blocks a general treaty of alliance between them. Britain had proposed five-sided talks with the U.S., Syria, and Lebanon taking part. Washington agreed, but asked that fair French proposals get preference. France then countered with a call for a broad Near East conference of the five major powers. Washington told Paris it did not think such a wide conference would serve the purpose. The brief readies Truman in case Churchill seeks U.S. backing for a British plan.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1036:
Philip Mosely cabled Ambassador Winant from Babelsberg on July 20, 1945, about the additional requirements agreement for Germany. Soviet official Vyshinsky had told him that Moscow approved the agreement, apart from a new title and first paragraph. Those two points should clear shortly, Vyshinsky expected.

Mosely also reports talks with John McCloy and Colonel Cutter on Washington's questions. Their answers stress that Allied representatives means the four commanders, acting both in the Control Council and in their zones. The draft does not assume a central German government exists. Nor can the council act on German property in a power's own country against that power's will, since council rulings must be unanimous. McCloy saw no bar to early War Department clearance.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1136:
Stanislaw Mikolajczyk, deputy prime minister of Poland, sent this memorandum on 24 July 1945. It was the first of three he put forward that day. Mikolajczyk led the non-communist wing of Poland's new joint government, the part that spoke for Poles who hoped for a free vote.

His papers put the Polish case straight before the Potsdam powers. Poland's border and its promised vote were being settled by others, in another country. A deputy premier with no seat at the table had only paper to fight with. This memorandum opens a striking one-day burst of Polish pleading in the record.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1236:
Secretary of War Stimson wrote to the Secretary of State on 16 July 1945, the day before Potsdam opened. The two cabinet chiefs ran the war and the peace talks between them. A letter from the war secretary to the top envoy joined those worlds on paper.

Stimson's concerns spanned the fronts: the forces in Europe and the Pacific war. They also covered the secret work on new weapons, which he alone in the cabinet fully oversaw. His word to Byrnes on the summit's eve helped align the two departments. This message is part of that alignment. It shows the cabinet's senior men closing ranks before the talks.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1336:
General John Hull, the Army's assistant chief of staff for operations, wrote to General Thomas Handy, the deputy chief of staff, on 28 July 1945. Hull ran the War Department's operations desk in Washington. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Staff papers between senior generals show the Army's inner workings while the Potsdam talks went on abroad. Operations officers had to match summit choices with real forces, ships, and plans for the war still being fought against Japan. Readers can follow how orders moved through the wartime Army. The paper trail shows two of its top staff men talking to each other.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-136: Printed after document 710 without a number, this editorial note forms part of the frame of the second Potsdam volume. The Foreign Relations editors used such notes to mark provenance and point out connections. They also flag where a paper survives only in part. The note helps a reader keep bearings among many similar staff documents.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-36:
A United States delegation memorandum sums up the foreign ministers' meeting of July 20, 1945. It is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Its purpose was to fix the afternoon agenda for the heads of government.

Four subjects were recommended in order. First came procedure for peace settlements, hinging on one redrafted paragraph of the Council of Foreign Ministers proposal. The ministers would meet briefly beforehand to try to agree that text. Second came policy toward Italy, on the U.S. paper the President had presented on July 17. Third came the situation in Austria, above all in Vienna. Churchill would speak on it, seeking ratification of the control and zones agreements already approved for Austria. Fourth came the western boundary of Poland, on a Russian paper with a map.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d736:
George Allen, deputy director for Near Eastern and African affairs, wrote to Assistant Secretary James Dunn on July 25, 1945. Document 736 is an internal State Department letter from the Potsdam week. Allen's office watched a region the conference touched only at its edges. His letter moved business between two senior desks.

Internal letters show the Department's daily grain. Officers traded facts and asked for calls on live questions. Allen wrote to a man who stood near the Secretary's door. Readers see how a regional office reached the center. The document adds the home front of diplomacy to the summit's brighter stage.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d836:
Elbridge Durbrow and an acting director named Phelps wrote jointly to Emilio Collado on July 18, 1945. Document 836 is an internal paper linking Eastern European affairs with financial policy. The two offices shared problems where politics met money. Their note went to the director of financial and development policy. It joined the second Potsdam volume.

Joint office papers show the Department thinking across its own walls. Eastern Europe's future turned on loans, trade, and aid as much as on flags. Readers see that link being worked at staff level. The document adds an economist's thread to a volume of envoys and generals. Potsdam's choices needed both kinds of mind.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d936: American staff attached this table to Clayton's statistical paper during the July 1945 Potsdam talks. It values movable factory equipment in Germany at the start of 1945, at prewar prices. Heavy industry, including iron, steel, machinery, and chemicals, totals 6,608 million marks. Only 27 percent of it sits in the eastern zone plus Berlin. Light industry totals 5,686 million marks, with 55 percent in the east. Across all manufacturing, the eastern share comes to about 40 percent.
frus-1947v05-d36: A 1947 FRUS memorandum from the Near East and Africa volume. The Secretary's office weighed Middle Eastern questions. This document holds that memorandum. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
frus-1969-76v01-d36: A 1969-1976 FRUS editorial note from the Foundations of Foreign Policy volume. The Nixon era's doctrine. This note provides that context. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
gao-gaoreports-b-295836: Hospital Klean of Texas doubled its April 2005 protest — two dockets, one cleaning fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Paired filings get one careful answer.
gao-gaoreports-b-295936: Vertol Systems took its April 2005 contract fight to GAO, and the ruling lands the verdict. The systems firm said the award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Rotorcraft contracts get the same fair hearing. Rotorcraft contracts get the same fair hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-296536: Computers Universal took its August 2005 contract fight to GAO again, and this ruling is the verdict on the second claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Repeat filers get the same full hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-296836: Muddy Creek Oil and Gas took its August 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Energy firms get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-297536: American Material Handling took its January 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-310136: This 2007 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Firestorm Wildland Fire Suppression, Inc. The November 26, 2007 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. Its full text is kept in the library next to this description.
gao-gaoreports-b-310436: This 2007 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Recon Optical, Inc. The December 27, 2007 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts. The library keeps it as part of the public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-336: The patent shop's tech plan needed muscle in 2005, and GAO's report says the key gears had to be fixed. The findings demand the upgrades. The report warns that the inventors deserved a working office. The inventors deserved a working office.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-536: Risk retention groups needed common standards in 2005, and GAO's report says uniform rules and greater member protections were required. The findings demand the standards. The report warns that the insured deserved solid backing. The standards had to be common. The insured deserved solid backing.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-736: Share-in-savings contracting was untested in 2005, and GAO's report says the federal initiative had not yet been tried. The findings take the measure. The report warns that the experiment deserved a trial. The initiative had to be tested. The experiment deserved a trial.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-236: Extending the FCC's auction authority had strong support in 2006, and GAO's report says backing existed, though little agreement on other options. The findings map the consensus and the splits. The report warns that the airwaves' sales needed deciding. The authority had to be extended.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-336: Wood waste energy users shared lessons in 2006, and GAO's report says their experiences offered insights for government promotion. The findings gather the wisdom. The report shows the sawdust-to-power pioneers had guidance. The insights had to be used. The sawdust pioneers had guidance.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1036: Hackers were eyeing the computers that run power plants and factories — and GAO's 2007 report says the defense was a work in progress. Plenty of shield programs were rolling, but the holes stayed real. The findings map a race the nation was not yet winning: locking down the industrial brains before someone else reached them.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-136: The IRS's own books got an audit in 2007, and GAO's report grades the tax agency's financial statements for 2006 and 2005. The findings deliver the formal opinion. The report shows the nation's money handler got its own money checked. The collector's books had to balance.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-236: Disability aid was a bureaucratic maze in 2007, and GAO's report says stronger federal oversight could assure the programs' accountability. The findings demand the watch. The report warns that the many helping hands needed one firm grip. The maze needed a map.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-336: The Energy Department's mega-projects needed a readiness yardstick in 2007 — GAO's report says a consistent way to judge new technology was missing. The findings demand the measure. The report's lesson: bet big on tech only after the tech proves itself.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-36: The nuclear weapons complex needed better management in 2007, and GAO's report says more action was required to run the nation's atomic enterprise. The findings demand the discipline. The report warns that the arsenal's stewards needed tighter hands. The bombs' keepers needed watching.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-536: Homeland Security's money systems stayed tangled in 2007 — GAO's report says the department-wide finance merger remained a stubborn challenge. The findings describe the accounting knot left by the rushed mega-merger. The report's refrain: merged departments need merged books, or the numbers never add up.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-736: The 2010 address hunt was improving in 2007 — GAO's report says the Census Bureau's local address update had gotten better, with challenges left. The findings credit the progress and flag the gaps. The report treats every missed address as a missed American.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-836: Drones were crowding the skies in 2007 — GAO's report says the Pentagon needed better coordination and visibility to get the most from unmanned aircraft. The findings call for joined-up drone doctrine. The report's vision: robot wings working as one fleet, not a flock of solo acts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-936: The Army's new-look brigades needed a training doctrine to match in 2007 — GAO's report says the modular-force game plan was half-written. The findings press the service to finish the playbook for its reshaped combat teams. Reorganized troops, the report warns, still need a coherent school.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-136: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on HUD and Treasury Programs: More Information on Leverage Measures' Accuracy and Linkage to Program Goals Is Needed in Assessing Performance. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-336: GAO published its findings on combating Terrorism: State Department's Antiterrorism Program Needs Improved Guidance and More Systematic Assessments of Outcomes Facilities in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-36: GAO warned Congress in 2007 that a bad flu wave would test the crews who keep power, water, and phones alive — and that no joint plan existed. Guarding those lifelines needs government and private firms rowing as one, but GAO found the rowing badly out of sync. The report urges the two sides to plan together before a crisis does the planning for them.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-536: The Government Accountability Office dug into privacy: Alternatives Exist for Enhancing Protection of Personally Identifiable Information in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs. Its full text is kept in the library next to this description.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-936: GAO published its findings on 2010 Census: Census Bureau's Decision to Continue with Handheld Computers for Address Canvassing Makes Planning and Testing Critical in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gogol-inspector-general-1836:
Nikolai Gogol wrote The Inspector General in 1836, a comedy play about corruption in a small Russian town. Local officials hear that a government inspector is coming in secret. They mistake Khlestakov, a poor and vain clerk passing through, for that inspector. Gifts and bribes pour in at once.

Khlestakov plays along, boasts wildly, and takes money from everyone. The mayor hopes to marry his daughter to the supposed great man. A letter read aloud at the end exposes the trick, just as the real inspector arrives. Gogol's satire of greed and fear still plays well. It is a peak of Russian comic drama.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-low-moritz-1013:
Moritz Löw, a Hungarian astronomer, is the subject of a brief entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born at Mako, Hungary, in 1841, he studied at the universities of Leipzig and Vienna. He earned his doctorate from the University of Budapest in 1867. After graduating he worked as an assistant at the Leipzig observatory.

The article records his move to Berlin in 1883. There he became a section chief in the Prussian geodetic institute, with the title of professor. His work joined astronomy to land surveying, fixing exact positions and pole heights. The entry lists his main writings, on planets, passage instruments, and surveys in East Prussia, Helgoland, and the Harz mountains. He died at Steglitz, Berlin, in 1900. Short as it is, the entry preserves a Jewish scientist's place in German state science.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-maccabees-the-g:
Maccabees, the name of the Hasmonean family, is examined in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. The entry explains that Maccabeus was first the surname of Judas alone. He was the third son of Mattathias and the family's most heroic warrior. After he took command, his name spread to all his kin and followers. Hence the title Books of the Maccabees.

The article then hunts for the name's origin. Scholars read it as the hammer, a title earned by Judas's heroism. Others link it to the banner of the tribe of Gad, or to initials of a verse from Exodus. One view takes it from a word meaning the extinguisher. The entry admits the question stays unsettled after all these efforts. It also notes the Talmud never uses the name, calling the family simply the Hasmoneans. The piece shows how a famous name can resist every explanation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-of-mers:
Menahem of Merseburg was a German halakist of the first half of the fifteenth century. Isidore Singer and Gotthold Weil profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jacob Weil praised him as a great and prominent scholar. His collection of legal notes was printed as an appendix to Weil's responsa. It was treated as authoritative across the communities of Saxony. It covered marriage law, the civil code, and communal taxation.

His boldest act concerned the law of mi'un. Under that law, a girl married in her minority could dissolve the union on coming of age, without a divorce. Her mother or brothers had made the marriage. Menahem judged the practice immoral. He repealed the law on his own authority. The next century set that ruling aside. The entry praises his range. Where German Jews of his day debated petty liturgical questions, his book engages everything that concerns Judaism.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-molo-francisco-:
Francisco Molo, a Dutch financier of the seventeenth century, is sketched by Gotthard Deutsch and M. Seligsohn in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In 1679 he settled in Amsterdam as financial agent of John III, king of Poland — though De Barrios, his contemporary, called him a Spanish Jew. His ability made him a power at The Hague.

The Dutch state thanked him with two years' exemption from taxes. His influence with the States General was so great, the entry claims, that Louis XIV was enabled through Molo's mediation to conclude the Treaty of Ryswick in 1697. A short entry, resting on Dutch histories — Koenen, Lamberti, and Wagenaar — for a backstage figure of European diplomacy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-musaf-11236:
Musaf is the additional offering, and the additional prayer that replaced it, in Jewish worship. Cyrus Adler and Julius H. Greenstone wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article on it. In the Temple, extra sacrifices followed the morning offering on Sabbaths, New Moons, and festivals. When the Temple fell, prayer took their place.

The article sets out when Musaf is said, soon after the Torah reading, and how the rabbis made it a duty for every person. Its middle blessing quotes the day's sacrifice from the Book of Numbers. For the New Year it grows into the longest prayer of the year, with the kingship, remembrance, and shofar verses. Through it all runs a prayer for the Temple restored.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nassau-11336:
Nassau was a German dukedom later joined to Prussia. Its entry was written by Gotthard Deutsch for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The article traces Jewish life there from early medieval times. A Jew named Levi of Lorch is named in a record from 1266. In 1865 the dukedom held 6,995 Jews among 465,636 people in all.

Medieval attacks hit towns such as Limburg, Diez, and Montabaur. Jews there paid special taxes for many years. Those taxes ended in the early 1840s, step by step. Nassau then set up district rabbis and a school for Jewish teachers. Full religious freedom came in 1848, with more gains in 1861. The entry names rabbis such as Abraham Geiger of Wiesbaden.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nemenyi-neumann:
Ambrosius Neményi was a Hungarian writer and lawmaker. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Peczel in 1852. Until 1871 he bore the family name Neumann. He studied law at Vienna and Paris.

Neményi worked on the staff of the Pester Lloyd. In 1884 his district sent him to Parliament. He served on committees for economics, transport, and finance. He was secretary of the budget committee as well. His books treat Rabelais and parliamentary discipline. Others cover Hungary's railways, its state, and its offices. From 1896 he edited the Pesti Napló as chief. He died in Budapest on Dec. 13, 1904.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nieto-isaac-115:
Isaac Nieto was haham of London's Portuguese congregation. Joseph Jacobs and E. Slijper wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in 1702, son of David Nieto. He died at London in 1774. In 1733 he was appointed hakam ha-shalem officially.

He gave up that post in 1741 and went abroad. Home again in 1747, he worked as a notary. The congregation recalled him as ab bet din in 1751. A violent dispute over court titles soon arose. He resigned by letter on March 17, 1757. That July he was barred from acting as assessor. His lasting work is his prayer-book translation. Its two volumes ground all later English versions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nyari-alexander:
Alexander Nyári was a Hungarian critic of art. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in 1861 at Zala-Egerszeg. He trained at Vienna and gained a diploma in building in 1884. He then went to Paris and Berlin. There he read in thought and the past of art.

Nyári took his doctor's degree at Leipzig in 1891. His state sent him to hunt for fine old works in Hungary. He sought art from the days of King Matthias. He later held posts at the state museum in Budapest. He also taught the past of art at a trade school. In 1894 he took charge of the state art hall. His chief books treat a portrait painter and a great church.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oppenheim-morri:
Morris Simeon Oppenheim was an English lawyer in London. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in London in the year 1824. He died there on January 3, 1883. His father was clerk to the Great Synagogue.

Morris served as clerk to a Jewish school group first. While in that post, he read for the bar. He was called to the bar in the year 1858. He worked as a pleader on the south east circuit. He gave much time to the work of his flock. In 1869 he joined the Board of Deputies. He sat on its law and Parliament groups there. He wrote on the marriage laws as they touched Jews. He drafted the by-laws for the joint synagogues of London.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pastoureaux-119:
The Pastoureaux were bands of French shepherds who rose in religious frenzy. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Kahn wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The entry covers two outbreaks, one in 1251 and one in 1320. Both waves turned quickly to violence against Jews.

In 1251 a leader called the Master of Hungary preached a crusade in Picardy. His followers attacked towns and robbed Jews at Bourges. The 1320 wave was far worse in the south. Mobs killed the Jews of Toulouse and destroyed many communities. The violence spread into Spain before the King of Aragon crushed it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-perjury-12036:
Perjury is the breaking of an oath or a solemn lie. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Julius H. Greenstone wrote the article. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Bible counts it among the greatest sins.

Yet the Bible sets no human penalty for perjury. God himself is left to punish the liar. A false oath in court or trade is still banned. The rabbis later sorted the sin into four classes. Each class carried its own set punishment. A witting liar faced lashes, an unwitting one an offering.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pick-behrendt-1:
Behrendt Pick was a German scholar of ancient coins. He was born at Posen on December 21, 1861. Isidore Singer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Mommsen himself had trained Pick at Berlin. His doctorate in classical philology came at Berlin in 1884.

On Mommsen's advice Pick chose inscriptions and coins. He taught archaeology at Zurich from 1889. In 1893 he moved to the ducal library at Gotha. He later directed its great coin collection. He also lectured on coins at Jena from 1896. His chief work catalogs the coins of Dacia and Moesia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rahabi-david-12:
David Rahabi was an Indian calendar maker from Cochin. Joseph Jacobs and Frank Cramer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born there in the mid eighteenth century. His father Ezekiel was a wealthy merchant.

The article says David took over the family business in 1771. He still found much time for study. His fame rests on Ohel Dawid, printed at Amsterdam in 1785. That work deals with the origin of the Hebrew calendar. A brief source note ends the entry. Readers meet a merchant scholar whose one book treated a hard dating topic.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ricchi-raphael-:
Immanuel Hay Ricchi was an Italian rabbi, cabalist, and poet born at Ferrara. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Sources give his birth as 1688 or 1693. He was killed near Cento on February 25, 1743.

The article says he lost his father as a small child. An uncle and then a cousin raised the orphan. He studied Talmud under Nathan Pinkerle at Alessandria. He tutored in wealthy homes across northern Italy. At Venice he opened a school of his own. Triest ordained him rabbi in 1717. Love of Cabala drew him to Safed in 1718. There he studied Luria and Hayyim Vital. An epidemic forced him back to Europe in 1720. Pirates captured his ship on the voyage home.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenbach-hyman: Hyman Pollock Rosenbach was an American journalist in Philadelphia, born there on September 16, 1858. Cyrus Adler wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Rosenbach worked for the Public Ledger and other city papers before his early death in 1892. In 1883 he published The Jews of Philadelphia Prior to 1800. The entry calls that book one of the earliest works on American Jewish history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rules-of-hillel:
The Seven Rules of Hillel are the classic guides for interpreting Scripture in rabbinic Judaism. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Hillel I gave them to the sons of Bathyra as chief guides.

By these rules, laws are drawn out of the Torah's own words. One argues from the lesser case to the greater, or back again. Another argues by analogy between passages sharing a word or phrase. Others apply one passage's rule to its kin, or read the general by the particular. The last rule reads a passage by its own context.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salomon-max-130:
Max Salomon was a German physician born at Sleswick on April 5, 1837. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He took his medical degree in 1861 after study at Heidelberg, Berlin, and Kiel.

Salomon served as a Prussian army surgeon from 1866 to 1870. He then practised at Hamburg, and from 1874 in Berlin. His history of glycosuria runs from Hippocrates to the nineteenth century. Other works treat diseases of the nervous system and of the lungs. A late book fights tuberculosis as a disease of the people. Berlin conferred on him the title Sanitätsrath, a medical councilor's rank.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-nath: Samuel ben Nathan was an amora of the early part of the fourth century. Wilhelm Bacher and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He appears mostly as the transmitter of sayings of Hama b. Hanina, in Shabbat and elsewhere. Once the direction reverses: Hama passes on a tradition of Samuel's own. It concerns a journey Samuel made with his father to the baths at Gadar.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schwabach-juliu:
Goodman Lipkind worked with Joseph Jacobs on this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Julius Leopold Schwabach. He was British consul-general in Berlin. Schwabach was born at Breslau in 1831. He died at Berlin on February 23, 1898. At sixteen he entered the banking house of Bleichröder. Twenty years later he became a partner there.

When Baron Gerson von Bleichröder died in 1893, Schwabach became senior partner. He also led the directors of the Berlin Bourse. Later he presided over a standing committee of that exchange. The entry is brief and rests on obituaries. The Jewish Chronicle and The Times both reported his death in February 1898.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-seraiah-13436:
Seraiah is a name shared by several men in the Hebrew Bible. Emil G. Hirsch and Schulim Ochser wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on them. One Seraiah served King David as a scribe. Another was chief priest under Zedekiah, Judah's last king.

The priest Seraiah was put to death by Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah. Yet his line ran on, since Ezra the Scribe counted him as father. Other men of the name appear as warriors, priests, and royal officers. Untangling them takes care with names that shift between books. The entry helps readers keep each Seraiah in his own time and place.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shekel-13536:
Shekel names both a weight and a silver coin used by the Hebrews. Emil G. Hirsch and Wilhelm Nowack wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Israel took its weight system from Babylon, scholars agree. Babylon split the talent into sixty minas of sixty shekels.

That scheme gives a talent of 3,600 shekels in all. Yet Ezekiel's figures seem to point another way. His text suggests fifty shekels to the mina instead. Greeks and Persians also used a fifty-shekel mina. The clash may come from decimal and sexagesimal counting meeting. The entry weighs texts and numbers to pin down how heavy a biblical shekel really was.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-siddim-vale-of-: Siddim is a vale named in Genesis as the meeting place of warring kings. Emil G. Hirsch and E. I. Nathans wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Its name's origin stays uncertain, though one version renders it vale of fields. Genesis links it with the Dead Sea, a claim critics reject as a late gloss. The region was rich in asphalt, Hommel held. A natural upheaval may have flooded it with Dead Sea waters. There the confederation gathered against Chedorlaomer in Abraham's day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simmlein-of-hal:
Simmlein of Halberstadt was a German Talmudist who served as rabbi there from 1620 to 1650. Wilhelm Bacher and A Peiginsky wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. His years matched the Thirty Years' War almost exactly. That war brought great hardship to the Jews of Halberstadt. The hostility of the Diet made their lot still worse.

Simmlein often risked his life for his community. The city government changed hands again and again. He won favor from both the bishop and the Swedish governors. He spent his own fortune to relieve his people. His house stayed open as a home and school for poor orphans.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sokolow-nahum-b:
Nahum ben Joseph Samuel Sokolow was a Russian journalist born in 1859. Isidore Singer and Peter Wiernik wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in Wishograd, in Russian Poland. At ten he was known as a prodigy of learning. He was meant for the rabbinate and studied under Talmudists.

In 1880 Sokolow moved to Warsaw to work in journalism. He joined Slonimski's Hebrew paper Ha-Zefirah in 1884. By 1886 that paper had become a daily under his hand. After Slonimski's death he became its sole editor and owner. He wrote books on geography and on Jew-hatred. He also founded the year-book Ha-Asif and edited it for years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-south-africa-13:
South Africa's Jewish history began before the Cape was even discovered. Joseph Jacobs and Joseph Hermann Hertz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Jewish astronomers helped chart the Portuguese sea route to India. Jews also directed the Dutch East India Company for years. That company ruled the Cape colony for 150 years there.

Full religious equality came to the colony only in 1820. Jews arrived in numbers at Cape Town in the 1820s. Men like Benjamin Norden were commercial pioneers of the interior. The Mosenthal brothers brought Angora goats from Asia in 1856. They thus founded the mohair industry of the Cape. Jews also led in wool, hides, diamonds, and ostrich farming.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stern-moriz-abr:
Moriz Abraham Stern was a German mathematician born in Frankfort in 1807. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born on June 29 of that year. He first studied philology at Heidelberg and trained for the rabbinate. He died at Bern on January 30, 1894.

Stern switched to mathematics at Göttingen and became a lecturer there in 1829. He rose to full professor of mathematics in 1859. In 1887 he retired and settled in Bern near his son Alfred. He took an active part in the Reform movement. His open letters defended reform in the 1840s. His math work covered continued fractions in depth. He also wrote on month names and cuneiform inscriptions. The entry joins a scholarly career with religious debate.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stripes-10336:
Stripes were the only bodily punishment named in the Pentateuch. Wilhelm Bacher and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Judges had to watch the beating take place in person. The law capped the number of blows at forty. Deuteronomy sets out those limits in plain terms.

Where the law only says thou shalt not, courts could impose stripes. A court of three judges handled such cases. Some acts drew stripes plus a money payment instead. The man who slandered his new wife faced both. A plotting witness could be flogged for false testimony. Mishnah rules sort which commands carry stripes and which do not. The entry gives readers the legal logic of an ancient penalty.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sussmann-lob-be:
Löb ben Moses Sussmann was a Hebrew printer of the 1700s. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. In 1750 he set up a Hebrew press in Amsterdam. It worked inside the office of Johann Jansen at first. Baruch Wiener and his sons staffed the press.

Sussmann soon opened an independent printing office. His press issued a Pentateuch with a scribal guide in 1767. It printed the Book of Job with Bahya's commentary. A prayer book with grammar notes came out in 1766. Later he moved to Leyden, then to The Hague. There he published Falaquera's medieval Seeker in partnership. His son later printed law codes at The Hague too. The entry tracks Hebrew printing across three Dutch cities.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tanhuma-midrash:
Midrash Tanhuma is a set of sermon collections on the Pentateuch. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Three collections bear the Tanhuma name. Two survive, and the third lives only in citations. None was truly written by Rabbi Tanhuma himself.

The name stuck because his homilies run through them. Sermons open with the formula Thus began Rabbi Tanhuma. Later preachers in his style filled out the rest. Buber published the oldest collection at Wilna in 1885. He gathered its text from several manuscripts. That version may be the oldest running Pentateuch commentary. Genesis Rabbah itself quotes its rulings. Editors completed it in the fifth century, scholars hold. The entry untangles three books behind one name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-terongi-raphael:
Raphael Benito Terongi was a Jewish martyr burned at Palma, Majorca, in 1691. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He died with his teacher Raphael Valls and his sister Catalina. The charge named them impenitent Jews at an auto da fé.

When the three saw the flames, they strained against their bonds. Terongi broke free and threw himself onto the pyre. Catalina begged to be saved but could not name Jesus. An English witness, James Stanhope, reported the scene to Madrid. He noted that most victims were wealthy householders. The short entry preserves a grim record of persecution in Spain.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-valuation-14636:
Valuation is the act of setting a money price on sacred gifts. Emil G. Hirsch and Eduard König wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The topic comes from chapter twenty seven of Leviticus. There a priest judged what a vowed person or animal was worth. The payment then replaced the gift itself.

The entry works through the Bible rules in detail. A man aged twenty to sixty was valued at fifty shekels of silver. Animals that failed the standard for sacrifice also took a money value. Vows about people who served in the Sanctuary worked the same way. The article shows how set prices mixed with the priest's own judgment.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weill-michel-aa:
Michel Aaron Weill was a French rabbi and author. He was born at Strasburg on July 19, 1814. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He died at Paris on January 6, 1889. He trained at Metz's rabbinical school and the Sorbonne. He taught at Nancy's consistorial school next.

In 1846 Weill became the first French chief rabbi of Algiers. He tried to spread French culture among Algerian Jews. The effort met little success, and he retired in 1864. He returned as rabbi of Toul in 1876. His many books treat Judaism's dogmas and mission. They cover revelation, providence, and Jewish morals at length.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wurzburger-juli:
Julius Wurzburger (1819-1876) was an American news writer born in Bavaria. Cyrus Adler and Abram S. Isaacs wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He studied at the University of Erlangen in his youth. In 1848, the year of revolt, he ran a daily paper.

That paper was the Bayreuth Tageblatt of his home state. He moved to Munich and wrote with a free pen. The state marked his bold views and acts. In 1849 it cast him out of Bavaria for good. He worked as a news man in Italy and France. At last he crossed the sea to America to live. There he joined the New-Yorker Staats-Zeitung staff. He ran its Sunday part with skill for near twenty years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yusuf-ibn-teshu:
Yusuf ibn Teshufin was an Almoravid king of Spain in old times. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He ruled in the 1000s and the early 1100s. He was the sole king of his line who bore hate to Jews.

Once he sought to force the faith of Islam on them. In 1105 he passed through the town of Lucena. He saw its Jews thrive in trade and in peace. He called their heads and laid a hard claim on them. The Prophet, he said, gave Jews free faith for a term. That term was five hundred years from his flight. That term was now at its end, he told them. The Jews bought their way out with large sums of cash.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zemah-jacob-ben:
Jacob ben Hayyim Zemah was a Portuguese cabalist and doctor. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He died at Jerusalem in the late 1600s. He had trained as a doctor in his home land as a Marano.

Near 1619 he fled that land for the town of Safed. There he gave six years to Talmud and law books. He then went to Damascus for a span of eighteen years. There he read the Zohar and the works of two masters. Those masters were Isaac Luria and Hayyim Vital of note. At last he settled at Jerusalem to live and teach. He set up a school for the Zohar in that town. He wrote twenty works in all in his long life. Just two of those works have reached print to date.
lane-manners-customs-modern-egyptians-18:
Edward William Lane lived as an Egyptian to write An Account of the Manners and Customs of the Modern Egyptians, out in 1836. Lane dwelt in Cairo for years, wore its dress, spoke its tongue, and kept its fasts and feasts. He then set down all he saw: faith, home life, births, wed days, death, charms, and tales told at night.

His care and calm set a new bar for such work. The book has stayed in print since its birth. No guest to Egypt can skip it. It is the best guide to that world.
lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-literat:
Lippincott's February 1873 number concludes a Peruvian search. Writers had hunted the quinine-plant through Peru's forests. J. L. T. Phillips glances at Athens's site and antiquities. Constance Fenimore Woolson contributes a story called Commonplace.

Caroline Chesebro's Probationer Leonhard advances through chapters four to nine. Reginald Wynford describes country-house life in England. Will Wallace Harney reports observations and adventures in submarine diving. Prentice Mulford offers glimpses of John Chinaman for the close. The Forest of Arden and Jack the Regular add fiction. A winter reverie and passport comedy close the February contents.

The September 1873 Lippincott's stages a saint's feast. Strahan's New Hyperion reaches The Feast of Saint Athanasius. Mary Stewart Doubleday contributes Two Moods, a poem. Martin I. Griffin versifies the ride of Prince Geraint.

William Black deepens his Princess of Thule in chapters fourteen and fifteen. A friend in need arrives for Sheila in the second. S. C. Clarke reports on Colorado and the South Park. Marie Rowland explains the Patrons of Husbandry to readers. English court festivities and a lotos of the Nile appear. How they keep a hotel in Turkey amuses the gossip readers.
livy-history-rome-books-27-36:
Livy wrote his history of Rome in the age of Augustus, and books twenty-seven through thirty-six cover the strain and glory of the Hannibalic war's last years. The English text here is the version by D. Spillan and Cyrus Edmonds, from Project Gutenberg. These books carry the tale from 210 to 187 BCE.

Scipio takes Spain, wins at Zama, and ends the war with Carthage. Rome then turns east and breaks Philip of Macedon. Livy writes big set speeches and battle pieces with a poet's touch. His history is the grand Roman story of the republic, and these books hold its turning point. The library's Livy set runs on from here.
meyfart-christliche-erinnerung-german-16:
Johann Matthäus Meyfart, a Lutheran theologian, published his Christliche Erinnerung, a Christian reminder, in 1636. The German book addresses powerful rulers directly. Meyfart urges them to proceed soberly and justly in witchcraft cases, at a time when German trials still burned the accused by the score.

He attacks the tortures that manufactured confessions and the greed that fed on confiscations. His plea is pastoral as much as legal. The reminder became the German Protestant protest that helped end the persecutions. Conscience, raised in print against the pyres, speaks in Meyfart's pages. Later reformers treated his book as a landmark of humane theology.
miller-evidence-second-coming-1836:
William Miller was a Baptist farmer in upstate New York who studied Bible prophecy with intense, solitary care. His Evidence from Scripture and History of the Second Coming of Christ, published in 1836, makes his case in full. He concluded that Christ would return about the year 1843.

Miller reads the days of Daniel's prophecies as years, counting forward from ancient decrees to his own century. His lectures drew huge crowds, and his followers built a movement that swept the northeastern states. When the date passed, the Great Disappointment scattered them, but Adventism grew from the ruins of his hope.
openalex-w1985422736:
Arturo Briva, István Vadász, and co-authors ran this lung study. Their paper is dated 2007 in the catalog record. High carbon dioxide levels occur in severe lung disease. The alveoli are the tiny air sacs where gas exchange happens. Their lining cells drive fluid balance in the lung.

The title states the core finding in plain terms. High carbon dioxide impairs those lining cells' function. The harm occurs independently of acidity changes, they report. That split matters for how doctors manage ventilation. Permitting high carbon dioxide may carry direct cell costs. The study warns that gas levels alone can injure lungs.
openalex-w1987982436:
Zeno Bisoffi and co-authors checked tests for a gut worm. Their study came out in a tropical disease journal in 2014. The worm can live in the gut for years, undetected. Stool tests miss many true cases, the team notes. Blood tests are thought to catch far more of them.

No gold standard test exists to judge the blood tests by. The team thus checked five blood tests side by side. They scored how well each test found true cases. They also scored how well each test cleared healthy people. Clear scores help labs pick the best test to use. Good tests matter most when weak immunity turns the worm deadly.
openalex-w2105846236:
Jorg Henseler, Christian Ringle and Marko Sarstedt proposed a new test for survey-based research models. Their paper appeared in 2015. Researchers must show that measured concepts truly differ. That check is called discriminant validity. Standard checks in common use can miss failures.

The team ran large simulation studies. Old criteria failed to detect problems in many cases. Their new ratio compares correlations between concepts. It caught validity problems far more reliably. The ratio builds on a classic multi-method matrix idea. Guidelines explain how to apply the test in practice. The paper quickly became a standard methods reference. It changed reporting practice in management research.
openalex-w2169480336:
Valérie Masson-Delmotte, Shugui Hou, Alexey Ekaykin, and colleagues published this review in the Journal of Climate in 2008. They built a database of isotope ratios in Antarctic surface snow, a record that helps read past climate from ice cores. Snow chemistry varies with temperature and with how moisture travels to the frozen continent.

Over a thousand sampling spots were gathered, though coverage clusters in parts of East Antarctica. The team mapped how snow isotopes shift with height, distance from the coast, temperature, and snowfall. They paid special attention to deuterium excess, a clue to moisture origins. Climate models with isotope physics were then tested against the data to judge how well they capture these patterns.
openalex-w2342602136:
Astride Audirac-Chalifour, Kirvis Torres-Poveda, and Margarita Bahena-Román led this pilot study in PLoS ONE in 2016. They mapped the germs of the cervix and local immune signals across stages of cervical disease. Lasting HPV infection causes this cancer. But local germs shape the signals that let such infections stay.

Gene reading sorted each woman's germs into group types. The mix clearly set healthy women apart from those with pre-cancer lesions and cancer. Cancer samples swung the most from case to case. Healthy cervices were led by guard lactobacilli. Lesions favored Sneathia germs, cancers Fusobacterium. Fusobacterium-led samples also held more of two immune-calming signals. The mix of germs, the authors say, may play a part in this cancer.
openalex-w2488001736:
Varsha Vijay, Stuart L. Pimm, Clinton N. Jenkins, and Sharon J. Smith published this study in PLoS ONE in 2016. It asks how much recent deforestation and biodiversity loss comes from oil palm plantations. Palm oil is the most traded vegetable oil in the world, and demand keeps rising. Almost all oil palm grows on land that was once tropical moist forest.

The team checked sample areas in twenty countries using high-resolution images from Google Earth and Landsat. In Southeast Asia, forty-five percent of sampled plantations replaced forest that stood in 1989. Shares were far lower in Mesoamerica and Africa, at two and seven percent. They also mapped forests suited to future plantations, finding the largest areas at risk in Africa and South America. Those maps can guide efforts to keep new plantations out of rich habitats.
openalex-w2612161536:
Jean Guy LeBlanc, Florian Chain, and Rebeca Martín, with colleagues, wrote this 2017 review in Microbial Cell Factories. It covers how gut and probiotic bacteria help feed their host. These bacteria produce B vitamins and short-chain fatty acids as they ferment food. The review asks how those products affect the host's energy metabolism.

Short-chain fatty acids like acetate, butyrate, and propionate release energy from fibers people cannot digest alone. B vitamins support the chemical machinery that makes ATP, the cell's energy currency. The authors explain the mechanisms behind both contributions. They also present their own measurements of fatty acid and vitamin output from selected probiotic strains. Such producing bacteria, they argue, could serve as tools to recover more energy from food. That idea matters for nutrition science and animal feeding alike.
openalex-w2787384236:
Nathan James Bennett, Tara Sayuri Whitty, and Elena M. Finkbeiner lead a team defining environmental stewardship in Environmental Management in 2018. Money and policy attention are flowing into local stewardship worldwide. Yet the concept itself had never received a clear, shared definition. Without one, judging why stewardship succeeds or fails in different places stays guesswork.

The authors define local stewardship as acts by people, groups, or networks to protect, care for, or wisely use the environment. Motives and capacities vary, and goals mix green with social outcomes. Their framework unpacks the definition's parts: actors, motives, capacity, and context. They point to leverage points where support can strengthen local efforts. The framework can guide descriptive, evaluative, or planning studies. Its aim is to raise stewardship's profile as a broad guide for how people relate to nature.
openalex-w2972407136:
Marielle Saunois, Ann Stavert, Benjamin Poulter, and colleagues published the Global Methane Budget in Earth System Science Data in 2020. It adds up all sources and sinks of methane worldwide for the years 2000 to 2017. Methane is the second most important human-influenced greenhouse gas after carbon dioxide.

Methane levels in the air keep rising, but the gas stays in the atmosphere for a shorter time than carbon dioxide while warming the planet more strongly per unit. That mix makes its budget hard to pin down and its growth rate puzzling. A firm budget is needed to judge realistic paths for slowing climate change. The authors combine many data streams to give that accounting.
openalex-w2985004336:
Roberto Vázquez-Muñoz, Anaid Meza-Villezcas, Pierrick Fournier, and colleagues published this study in PLoS ONE in 2019. It shows how silver nanoparticles can strengthen the germ-killing power of antibiotics. The work responds to a hard problem: microbes keep evolving resistance faster than new drugs appear.

The title names the mechanism the team studied. Silver particles, sized far below the width of a hair, act on the bacterial cell membrane. A weakened membrane lets antibiotics work harder against the microbe inside. The authors measured this boost in antimicrobial activity across their tests. Pairing old antibiotics with silver particles is one proposed route to rescue drugs that resistant bacteria have learned to shrug off.
openalex-w3017264036:
Salomone Di Saverio, Mauro Podda, Belinda De Simone, and colleagues present this guideline update in the World Journal of Emergency Surgery in 2020. It revises the Jerusalem guidelines of the World Society of Emergency Surgery on acute appendicitis. Appendicitis is among the most common causes of sudden belly pain.

The first consensus meeting was held in Jerusalem in 2015, and a second in Nijmegen in 2019 refreshed the advice. Diagnosis remains tricky, and practice varies widely between countries. The update covers clinical scores and imaging, who needs surgery and when, and when antibiotics alone may serve. It also addresses surgical technique, scoring during the operation, and antibiotics around surgery, all tied to the evidence.
openalex-w3032477836:
Eleanor Sterling, Puaʻala Pascua, Amanda Sigouin, and colleagues published this article in Sustainability Science in 2020. It asks how global development goals can be rooted in real places, using the Pacific Islands as the test case. Global goals steer money and programs, but their effects land locally.

The team compared the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals with dimensions of well-being drawn from the Pacific region itself. Those local dimensions embrace social and ecological resilience together. The comparison found overlaps but also significant gaps between regional ideas of a good life and the global list. The authors draw lessons for localizing the goals so they support both human well-being and environmental health.
openalex-w3158511736:
Corey Bradshaw, Kasih Norman, Sean Ulm, and colleagues model how people first spread across Sahul, in Nature Communications in 2021. Sahul was the joined landmass of Australia and New Guinea during the last ice age. When and how fast humans crossed it has stayed hard to pin down from archaeology alone.

The authors built a random, grid-based model driven by known links between hunter-gatherer movement and local energy in the landscape. As its title states, the model supports a rapid peopling of the continent. Work like this gives archaeologists testable routes and timings to compare with sites, tools, and genetic evidence.
openalex-w7155037536: Programs linking high schools with universities may inspire future doctors. This exploratory study tested whether such a collaboration boosted learning drive and career understanding among aspiring medical students in Japan. The authors measured the motivational effects. An education study of planting medical ambitions early.
openalex-w7204852936: Mental health is moving to the center of education debates, and this article maps why. The authors study how the well-being of teachers and students shapes teaching and learning, in both directions. Drawing on current research, they trace the links between a healthy mind and a working classroom. A timely overview for schools realizing that no lesson plan survives a mental health crisis.
openalex-w7204954936: The most dangerous hack often starts with a convincing lie. This paper studies social engineering, manipulating people rather than machines, as both a crime trend and a tool for police intelligence in Para. The authors trace how digital life made human gullibility a prime target for fraud, then examine the applications and legal limits of using these techniques in police work. A sober look at the human weak point in cybersecurity.
openalex-w7204966536: A burst stomach ulcer is a surgical emergency, and surgeons can fix it two ways: open surgery or keyhole surgery through small cuts. This paper compares how patients do after each method, looking at healing, problems, and survival. The authors pull together the evidence as keyhole repair gains ground on the older open approach. A practical comparison for emergency teams that must choose fast.
openalex-w7205007036: In February 2026, Brazil's health agency created the country's first general federal rules for companies growing cannabis for medical use. This article asks what the new regulation really changed, moving from a history of prohibition to national production. The authors parse the resolutions and their practical effects. Essential reading for anyone following how medical cannabis went from banned to regulated in Brazil.
openalex-w7208837836: Brazil's federal institutes were created to give working-class students free technical and higher education. This study reviews academic research on how free-market economic policies have reshaped that mission. Drawing on a systematic review of graduate-level research, the authors map how market-driven reforms affect curricula, funding, and the public role of these schools. It asks whether the original goal of serving workers and communities is surviving.
phrenology-in-connection-with-the-study-: Phrenology in Connection with the Study of Physiognomy, 1836. The twin sciences. This book preserves that work. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
plos-pbio-0020036:
Eric L. Snyder, Bryan R. Meade, Cheryl C. Saenz, and co-workers tested a bold cancer treatment in PLOS Biology in 2004. Peritoneal carcinomatosis is cancer spread across the belly lining, often from ovarian cancer. It resists standard chemotherapy and has a grim outlook.

Their approach uses a peptide, a short protein chain, that can cross into cells and switch on p53. p53 is a guard protein that can push damaged cells to die. Turning it on inside spread tumor cells offers a way to attack the disease at many sites at once. The study is an early proof of concept. It points to cell-penetrating peptides as a delivery route worth refining.
plos-pbio-0020336:
Elise R. Hondorp and Rowena G. Matthews studied a stress weak point in E. coli in PLOS Biology in 2004. The bacterium makes the amino acid methionine with an enzyme called MetE. That enzyme does not need vitamin B12, which makes it valuable when B12 is scarce.

Oxidative stress switches MetE off, the team found, halting methionine supply. The cell must then lean on its B12-based backup enzyme or stop growing. That fragility looks like a design flaw, yet it may serve as a stress sensor. Either way, the result shows how a single enzyme can link air, diet, and growth. It also marks a possible target: germs that depend on MetE could be starved by stress-like drugs.
plos-pone-0000036:
Roberto Cañamero, Hernán Boccalandro, Jorge Casal, and co-authors used a laser to ask whether a leaf's pores run themselves. Stomata are the tiny mouths on a leaf that open and close to trade gases, taking in carbon dioxide and letting out water vapor. Whether each stoma senses light on its own, or obeys orders from the leaf, was unsettled.

Shining a confocal laser on single stomata as the light source, the team showed the pores respond on their own: stomata-autonomous function. Each pore is a tiny sensor as well as a valve. That finding reshapes models of how plants manage water, a question with stakes for crops in a drying climate.
plos-pone-0000136:
Yongli Zhang, Abbye E. McEwen, Donald M. Crothers, and colleagues published this biophysics paper in PLOS ONE in 2006. It studies the Lac repressor, a bacterial protein that switches genes off by gripping DNA and bending it into a loop. The authors analyze this repression inside living cells through the mechanics of the loop itself.

DNA looping is a common way cells control genes, but it is hard to measure in vivo. The authors use the physics of loop formation to explain how strongly the repressor shuts its target genes down. The work links molecular mechanics to gene control, a bridge between physics and genetics.
plos-pone-0000236:
Selma Ugurel, Ranjit K. Thirumaran, Sandra Bloethner, and colleagues published this melanoma study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Two genes, B-RAF and N-RAS, are often mutated in skin cancer. The authors report that these mutations are preserved when tumor cells are grown for a short time in vitro, and that they affect prognosis differently.

Cell lines are only useful models if they keep the tumor's key mutations. This study checks that they do, over short propagation. It also compares what each mutation means for patient outlook. Both points help researchers who use cultured melanoma cells to test drugs.
plos-pone-0000336:
Laurin J. Kasehagen, Ivo Mueller, Benson Kiniboro, and colleagues published this malaria genetics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. The Duffy blood group protein is the door Plasmodium vivax uses to enter red blood cells; people who lack it were thought immune. In Papua New Guinea, the authors report reduced vivax infection in Duffy-negative heterozygotes, people with one copy of the negative variant.

Partial protection in heterozygotes is a subtler picture than total immunity. The finding refines who is at risk of vivax malaria in PNG, where the parasite is common. It also speaks to how this host-parasite relationship is evolving in real populations.
plos-pone-0000436:
Bora E. Baysal reported a recurring mutation found where it was not expected, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The change is a stop-codon mutation in the gene for succinate dehydrogenase subunit B. That protein is part of the cell's energy machinery. Mutations in it are known from certain tumors. Baysal found the same change in normal peripheral blood and in childhood T-cell acute leukemia samples.

A stop codon ends a protein early, usually crippling it. Finding such a change in healthy blood raises questions: is it a harmless inherited variant, an early step toward disease, or an artifact? The paper's value is in flagging the recurrence so others can test what it means.
plos-pone-0000536:
Simon Melov and colleagues connected a signature of brain aging to energy stress in cells, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Tau is a brain protein that becomes hyperphosphorylated, overloaded with phosphate tags, in Alzheimer's disease, where it tangles. The team showed that mitochondrial oxidative stress causes hyperphosphorylation of tau.

Mitochondria are the cell's power plants, and oxidative stress is the damage from their chemical exhaust. Linking that stress directly to tau's change puts failing energy production upstream of a hallmark of Alzheimer's. The finding supports treatments aimed at protecting mitochondria as a way to slow the disease's molecular cascade.
plos-pone-0000636:
Otto Appenzeller, Clifford Qualls, Franca Barbic and co-authors read body rhythms in hair and teeth for PLOS ONE in 2007. Biological rhythms offer insight into normal physiology and disease. They can also serve as biomarkers, measurable signs, in nerve degeneration. Hair and teeth grow in layers, locking in chemical records over time.

The team presents a diverse data set showing stable isotope ratios in these tissues reflect those rhythms. An isotope ratio is the balance between heavier and lighter forms of an element. If tissues keep an extended rhythm record, a strand of hair becomes a timeline. Clinicians could read past physiology from samples that are easy to collect and store.
plos-pone-0000736:
Jeffrey A. Gold, Yoshihiko Hoshino, Marcus B. Jones and colleagues reported a cautionary result on immune therapy for anthrax, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Bacillus anthracis causes inhalational anthrax and can live inside host cells. Even with appropriate antibiotics, mortality from inhaled anthrax approaches 45 percent, underscoring the need for better added therapies. Interferons are immune signals that might seem natural helpers.

Their title states the opposite: giving interferon-alpha and interferon-gamma increased lethality in mice with inhalational anthrax. A therapy that harms instead of helps is vital to know before human use. Negative findings of this clarity protect patients and redirect research.
plos-pone-0000836:
Giulia Somenzi, Giusy Sala, Stefano Rossetti and colleagues showed that vitamin A's active form has two faces, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Retinoic acid, the bioactive derivative of vitamin A, controls transcription through its receptors and exerts a potent antiproliferative effect on human cells. Yet a number of studies show retinoic acid can also promote cell survival and growth. The contradiction needed a mechanism.

By disrupting retinoic acid receptor alpha, the team reveals the growth promoter face of retinoic acid. One receptor apparently carries the brake, while other routes carry growth signals. Separating the faces matters for retinoid drugs in cancer, where pushing growth would be the worst outcome.
plos-pone-0000936:
Zhike Zi and Edda Klipp modeled a major cell signaling route with both constraints and kinetics, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The TGF-beta pathway helps control growth, cell death and specialization. Getting its dynamics right is central to understanding how cells decide their fate.

The authors combine constraint based modeling, which sets the bounds of what a system can do, with kinetic analysis, which follows rates over time. Their target is the Smad dependent branch of the pathway. A model that matches real timing can predict how a cell answers a signal of a given strength. Such predictions guide experiments on cancer and development alike.
plos-pone-0001036:
Jeremy Peirce, Karl Broman, Lu Lu and colleagues offered a simple way to merge gene mapping data from many crosses, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Linkage studies mark chromosome stretches that affect a trait. For many traits, enough separate studies now exist that combining them could sharpen the locations and reveal new ones.

Different crosses and study designs, though, resist simple pooling. The authors present a method for combining such data across experiments. Sharper trait locations mean fewer candidate genes to test by hand. For traits like disease risk or behavior, that narrowing is the step that turns a map into a gene.
plos-pone-0001136:
DNA methylation is a chemical mark that helps control which genes are active. Most marks sit in a symmetrical pattern called CpG, but a smaller share fall in lopsided, non-CpG patterns. Valérie Grandjean, Ruken Yaman, and François Cuzin asked how those odd marks get established, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article.

Their title gives the core finding. An inherited epigenetic mark requires the enzyme DNA methyltransferase 1 to set up a complex pattern of non-CpG methylation from scratch. Epigenetic marks can pass between generations without changing the DNA code itself. The study clarifies how one such mark is written.
plos-pone-0001236:
Scrapie is a fatal brain disease of sheep, and some prion protein variants make sheep susceptible to it. Rami Sawalha and colleagues report a paradox in a 2007 PLOS ONE article: lambs carrying the susceptible genotypes survived better after birth. Susceptibility alleles persist at high frequencies in many flocks despite centuries of selection against them.

That persistence suggests the alleles bring some benefit, or hitchhike with one. The authors' survival finding offers a candidate benefit in early life. It complicates eradication programs based on breeding for resistance, since removing the alleles might remove the advantage too.
plos-pone-0001336:
Learning a new movement, like reaching in an altered force field, uses feedback from vision and from the body's own position sense. David Franklin and colleagues asked whether vision is actually necessary for such learning, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Humans integrate multi-modal sensory feedback to adjust movements and complete tasks successfully.

The authors report, as their title states, that visual feedback is not necessary for the learning of novel dynamics. Proprioception, the sense of limb position, can carry the learning alone. The result reshapes accounts of motor learning that put vision in charge.
plos-pone-0001436:
Rhiannon Biddick, G. Lynn Law, and Elton Young published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on two yeast gene switches. The two switches jointly run many genes that sugar normally keeps off. The team set out to split their roles. They asked which one calls in helper proteins and reshapes the DNA wrapping at each gene.

By testing each switch alone, they gave each a distinct share of the work. One led on some steps, the other on the rest. Fine splits like this show how cells share tasks between like factors. The work grounds models of how yeast adapts when its food source changes.
plos-pone-0001536:
Daphne Ling, Laura Flores, and Lee Riley wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE review of lab tests for lung TB. Hundreds of studies grade tests that copy TB DNA from spit samples. Store bought tests gave more steady results than home built ones. Past pooled reviews found high truth for negatives but shaky rates for spotting cases.

The authors pool the data again and probe what drives the spread in results. Their work gives clinics a firmer read on what these tests can and cannot do. In poor lands where TB is rife, that read guides scarce funds. It also sets bars for the next wave of tests.
plos-pone-0001636:
Navjot S. Sodhi, David Bickford, Arvin C. Diesmos, and their co-authors weighed the causes of the worldwide loss of frogs and other amphibians in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Habitat loss, climate change, over-hunting, and disease have all been blamed. What was not clear is how much each cause counts, and how they act together.

The authors describe their study as the largest global look at the problem to that date. The full text gives the data they gathered across species and regions, and their ranking of the drivers of decline and extinction. Amphibians are often the first group hit by damage to fresh water and land habitats. A clear ranking helps conservation groups decide where effort and money will do the most good.
plos-pone-0001736:
Douglas J. Blackiston, Elena Silva Casey, and Martha R. Weiss asked whether a moth remembers its caterpillar lessons, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Insects with complete metamorphosis rebuild their bodies wholesale, changing both form and lifestyle. Whether larval experience can persist through pupation into adulthood was an open question.

The team trained caterpillars, let them transform, and tested the adult moths for retained learning. They also assessed two mechanisms that could carry memory through the rebuild. The full text gives the training, the adult tests, and the verdict. If memory survives a near-total body rebuild, that says something deep about where memories live in a nervous system.
plos-pone-0001836:
Michael Roberts, Aleksey V. Zimin, Wayne Hayes, and their co-authors improved genome assembly software in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The assembly methods used for whole-genome shotgun data have a major impact on the quality of resulting draft genomes. Shotgun sequencing reads a genome in millions of fragments that software must overlap and join.

Their algorithm generates a set of 'reliable' overlaps by identifying repeat k-mers. Those are short repeated sequences that cause false joins, and the method improves Phrap-based assembly of the rat genome. The full text gives the algorithm and the before-and-after assembly quality. Every genome project of the era depended on such assembly hygiene; one repeat mishandled can scramble whole chromosomes.
plos-pone-0001936:
Johan Rebetz and co-authors compared brain tumor cells to stem cells in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Gliomas are the most common brain tumors, and they range from slow low-grade forms to fast high-grade ones. Some tumor cells act like stem or progenitor cells, the early cells that can grow into many types, and such cells may drive the tumor.

The team took live glioma cells and checked how far they match that early-cell pattern. They also tracked a marker called CD133, and the cells' power to take on nerve-cell traits. High-grade tumors showed more of both. The work may help doctors judge how a tumor will act.
plos-pone-0002036:
Annemarie Surlykke and Elisabeth Kalko measured how loud hunting bats call, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Bats that hunt by echolocation have spread across many habitats and prey types. Much past work charted how the pitch pattern of their calls fits each habitat and hunting style. How loud the calls are had drawn far less study.

As the title states, these bats cry out loud to detect their prey. Loud calls carry farther and return stronger echoes from small insects. Volume, it turns out, is as tuned a part of the bat's sonar as pitch.
plos-pone-0002136:
Matthew Ward, Serkan Erdin, Tuan Tran, and co-authors tackled a pile-up problem in protein science, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Labs keep solving the shapes of proteins whose jobs are unknown, and the list grows faster than anyone can test them one by one. Guessing a protein's job usually means comparing it with proteins whose jobs are known.

The authors asked whether those comparisons get sharper when they focus on the structural features that evolution has kept most stable. By comparing such features in both directions, they aimed to give unknown proteins a family and a likely role. Better guesses mean lab tests can start closer to the truth.
plos-pone-0002236:
Laura Fontana, Micol Fiori, Sonia Albini, and co-authors blocked a small RNA to fight stubborn neuroblastoma, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Neuroblastoma is a childhood cancer of nerve tissue, and some tumors resist therapy. The team had traced a key pathway: the cancer gene MYCN, when overactive, switches on a cluster of microRNAs that includes miR-17-5p.

Those microRNAs suppress two protective proteins, p21 and BIM, letting tumor cells grow unchecked. Blocking miR-17-5p with an antagomir, a molecule built to silence it, abolished the growth of therapy-resistant neuroblastoma in their tests. The result nominates one small RNA as a drug target in a hard cancer.
plos-pone-0002336:
Riffat Naseem and Michelle Webb examined how the breast cancer protein BRCA1 binds DNA, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. BRCA1 helps maintain the integrity of the genome; when it fails, breast and ovarian cancer risk climbs sharply. The exact mechanisms of its guard work remain unclear, despite years of study.

BRCA1 can bind DNA directly, hinting at a hands-on role at the genome itself. The authors analyzed that binding activity and how the tumor suppressor p53, another genome guardian, modulates it. Two famous protective proteins interacting at DNA may explain part of their shared defense, and why losing either opens the door to cancer.
plos-pone-0002436:
Dahiya and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Neetu Dahiya, Cheryl A. Sherman-Baust, Tian-Li Wang, and others. Its subject is microRNA Expression and Identification of Putative miRNA Targets in Ovarian Cancer. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) represent a class of small non-coding RNAs that control gene expression by targeting mRNAs and triggering either translation repression or RNA degradation.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002536:
Led by Inderjit, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Inderjit, Jarrod L. Pollock, Ragan M. Callaway, and others. Its subject is phytotoxic Effects of (±)-Catechin In vitro , in Soil, and in the Field. Exploring the residence time of allelochemicals released by plants into different soils, episodic exposure of plants to allelochemicals.

Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002636:
Work by Yimin Wu and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was phase 1 trial of malaria transmission blocking vaccine candidates pfs25 and pvs25 formulated with montanide ISA 51. Authorship is credited in the record to Yimin Wu and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Pfs25 and Pvs25, surface proteins of mosquito stage of the malaria parasites P. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002736:
Research from Simone Köhler and co-authors, published in PLOS ONE in 2008, covers rheological characterization of the bundling transition in F-Actin solutions induced by methylcellulose. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Simone Köhler, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. In many in vitro experiments Brownian motion hampers quantitative data analysis. The authors add a further point. Therefore, additives are widely used to increase the solvent viscosity. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002836:
Work by Anders F. Andersson and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008, dealing with comparative analysis of human gut microbiota by barcoded pyrosequencing. The catalog record names Anders F. Andersson first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work.
