Humans host complex microbial communities believed to contribute to health maintenance and, when in imbalance, to the development of diseases. The authors add a further point. Determining the microbial composition in patients and healthy controls may thus provide novel therapeutic targets. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002936:
Edwin Michael, Mwele Malecela, Mihail Zervos and co-authors weighed chronic disease care in filariasis eradication in 2008. The global program aimed to end lymphatic filariasis by halting transmission with four to six years of yearly mass drug doses. Costs and management hurdles stood in the way.

Writing in PLOS ONE, they argue for the value of caring for people already living with chronic disease as part of elimination programs. Such care builds trust and keeps communities engaged with drug rounds. The paper speaks to program leaders balancing a finish-line goal against duties to those already harmed.
plos-pone-0003036:
Nora Khaldi and Kenneth Wolfe asked in 2008 where the extra genes of Aspergillus oryzae came from. Sequencing showed this fungus carries about 20 percent more genes than its relatives A. nidulans and A. fumigatus. Such a surplus demands an origin story: duplication, transfer, or something else.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the authors evaluate several possible causes of the elevated gene number. The origins proved elusive, as their title admits. A. oryzae is the mold behind sake and soy sauce fermentations, so its genome history has both industrial and evolutionary interest. The article appeared in PLOS ONE, an open access journal anyone can read free online.
plos-pone-0003136:
Francesca Luca, Giuseppina Bubba, Massimo Basile and colleagues survey variation in the NAT2 gene in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Differences at NAT2 have long been known to change how well people break down a wide range of drugs used in care. The team explored the pattern of that variation in twelve human populations, extending both the map range and the detail of past work.

Their title reports that several amino acid variants in NAT2 look advantageous. Readers get a broad human picture of a gene that shapes drug response. The study may help explain why the same dose can act quite differently in different people and groups.
plos-pone-0003236:
Raik Rönicke, Anja Klemm, Jessica Meinhardt and colleagues question a standard toxicity assay in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The MTT reduction assay is a frequently used and easily reproducible method to measure beta-amyloid toxicity in different types of single cell culture. To the authors' knowledge, the influence of beta-amyloid on MTT reduction itself had not been examined as a possible artefact.

Their title asks whether A-beta mediated diminution of MTT reduction is an artefact of single cell culture. Readers get a methods warning with broad reach, since the assay is used in many labs. If the measure is flawed, many past toxicity readings may need a second look.
plos-pone-0003336:
Chang-Ching Yang, Yang-Hsin Shih, Miau-Hwa Ko and colleagues transplant umbilical stem cells in rats in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Human umbilical mesenchymal stem cells isolated from Wharton's jelly of the umbilical cord can be easily obtained and processed compared with embryonic or bone marrow stem cells. These cells may be a valuable source in repair of spinal cord injury. The team examine effects after complete transection of the rat spinal cord.

Readers get a test of an accessible cell source in the hardest spinal injury model, full cutting of the cord. Any benefit there is notable, though rat recovery often exceeds what patients achieve.
plos-pone-0003436:
Judith X. Becerra and D. Lawrence Venable read the past of a Mexican forest in this 2008 paper. Their subject was the tropical dry forest of Mexico. Some areas birth new species, while others mainly receive them. Knowing which is which could guide where protection money goes.

The authors traced where forest lineages spread and split over time. Certain areas acted as sources of new diversity. Others acted as sinks that collect species made elsewhere. Guarding source areas protects the engine of future diversity, they argue. Dry forests get far less attention than rainforests, though they hold many species found nowhere else.
plos-pone-0003536:
Margaret C. Jackson, Claudia Wolf, and Stephen J. Johnston scanned memory for faces in this 2008 study. Good social life needs face identity and expression held in mind briefly. Visual short-term memory carries that ongoing picture. Angry faces seemed to hold an edge in that memory.

Brain imaging revealed the neural basis of the angry-face advantage. Volunteers remembered angry expressions better than neutral ones. Emotion thus tunes the social memory people use daily. Threat signals may get priority space in the mind's short-term store. Threat faces draw the eye first, which may be why they are kept so well.
plos-pone-0003636:
Gabriel Catano, Hemant Kulkarni, Weijing He, and colleagues published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2008. A large scan had linked gene regions called ZNRD1, HCP5, and HLA-C to slower HIV disease. The team tested which exact gene variants were truly behind those effects.

Their analysis found the effects traced mainly to two other variants, HLA-A10 and HLA-B*57. The first-named regions had largely been markers riding along with these. Sorting out which alleles matter helps focus the search for the body's own defenses against HIV. It also warns against crediting the wrong gene.
plos-pone-0003736:
Sung-Kook Hong and Igor B. Dawid published this development study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Alpha2 macroglobulin is a well-known protein found in blood. A relative of it, called alpha2 macroglobulin-like, had no clear job in building organs. The authors tested its role in zebrafish.

They found the protein is essential for the liver to develop in zebrafish embryos. Without it, liver formation fails. The surprise role gives a familiar blood protein family a new job in organ building, and a fresh handle for studying how the liver forms. The gene now joins the short list of known liver builders.
plos-pone-0003836:
Andrew J. Irwin and Zoe V. Finkel published this ocean study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Chlorophyll in the surface ocean measures the phytoplankton that power marine food webs. Its levels reflect a tangle of physiology, ocean conditions, and ecology. Those plants also drive how much carbon sinks to the deep ocean.

The authors mined a large body of ocean data for the factors that control chlorophyll. Their analysis deduces which environmental conditions set the ocean's greenness in each region. The results link ocean productivity to the physical and chemical setting that sustains it.
plos-pone-0003936:
Julie Cahu, Aurelien Olichon, Christian Hentrich, and co-authors studied a motor protein in dividing cells in 2008. Kinesin-5 motors help build the spindle that separates chromosomes. They crosslink and slide the spindle's microtubule rods. A cell-cycle kinase called Cdk1 marks these motors with phosphate groups.

Their PLOS ONE article tested what that phosphate mark does to the motor Eg5. Marking raised how strongly Eg5 binds to microtubules. Tests ran both in lab mixtures and in frog egg extract spindles. The result explains one way cells tighten spindle assembly as division starts. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004036:
Erika M. C. D'Agata, Myrielle Dupont-Rouzeyrol, Pierre Magal, and co-authors modeled antibiotic use and resistance in 2008. Resistant bacteria are a major and growing public health threat. Infections with them bring higher illness and death rates. How drug regimens drive resistance needs clear analysis.

Their PLOS ONE article compares different antibiotic regimens in a model. It asks which patterns slow or speed resistant strains. Such modeling guides stewardship rules in hospitals. Choosing regimens wisely can preserve drug power for future patients. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read. Each claim in it can be checked in the full text that sits with this record.
plos-pone-0004136:
Xuhua Xia and Martin Holcik published this study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Some messenger RNAs can start protein building at an internal site called an IRES, instead of at the usual front end. The authors set out to test the idea that strong IRES sites in eukaryotes lack folded structure.

They also checked how widely that idea holds. They looked at IRES sites from yeast and the fruit fly, which sit just before the protein-coding section. Comparing strong and weak sites, they link strength to weaker folding in the RNA. The paper gives researchers a structural clue for spotting and designing these internal start sites.
plos-pone-0004236:
Karen Mruk and William Kobertz published this channel study in PLOS ONE in 2009. KCNQ1 is a voltage-gated potassium channel, and it partners with five different KCNE peptides. Each partnership gives the channel different gating behaviour and drug sensitivity, letting one channel serve many roles in the body.

The authors report the discovery of a novel activator of the KCNQ1-KCNE1 channel complex, the pairing found in the heart. A compound that switches this complex on is a tool for studying it and a possible lead for heart rhythm drugs. A switch for this channel had been missing from the toolkit.
plos-pone-0004336:
Annapaola Rizzoli and colleagues published this tick-borne disease study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Western tick-borne encephalitis virus often causes devastating or lethal disease. Across Europe, human cases have risen dramatically over the last decade, risk areas are expanding, and new foci are discovered every year. Early localisation of new risk areas is a public health priority.

The team asked whether forest structure and roe deer abundance predict encephalitis risk in Italy. Deer and woods shape the ticks' lives, so they may map the danger. A predictive map lets health services warn the right valleys first.
plos-pone-0004436:
Ferrets primed with mild, live flu vaccines are the test bed for a 2009 PLOS ONE study by Xing Cheng, Michael Eisenbraun, Qi Xu, and co-authors. The question was how well B cells later respond to a vaccine against H5N1, the bird flu virus feared as a pandemic risk. Live weakened seasonal flu vaccines had already been tested in mice and ferrets with no past flu exposure.

Real people, though, carry some immunity from past flu seasons. The team asked whether that earlier priming helps or hinders the response to an H5N1 vaccine. B cells are the white blood cells that make antibodies, the body's targeted defenses. Knowing how prior exposure shapes their reply helps planners design bird flu vaccines that work in real populations, not just in clean lab animals.
plos-pone-0004536:
A classic computer model of motion vision is put up against human observers by Siddharth Jain in PLOS ONE in 2009. The model, by Watson and Ahumada, aims to sense motion the way the human visual system does. The test stimuli were random dots moving in rotary motion, shown in a ring-shaped field.

Jain compared the model's performance with human psychophysical performance, careful measurements of what people can actually detect. The model matched the human observers in this task. A model that keeps pace with people on turning dot patterns earns trust as a stand-in for the visual system. Such models feed into machine vision, display design, and basic questions about how brains compute movement.
plos-pone-0004636:
Formaldehyde, the fixative used in labs everywhere, needs a minimum time to lock cell structures in place. Lars Schmiedeberg, Pete Skene, Aimee Deaton, and co-authors measured that threshold in PLOS ONE in 2009. The chemical works by crosslinking, tying proteins to each other where they touch.

Labs use it to fix samples for microscopy and for many tests in molecular biology. The method rests on the idea that most real interactions between proteins are kept by this tying. The team found a time threshold: fix for too short a time, and interactions are lost or misread. A measured minimum turns a folk habit into a set method. It also helps explain why some past studies of protein pairs did not agree.
plos-pone-0004736:
Takashi Kobayashi and colleagues showed that an adaptor protein is needed to make a key B cell group, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Sensors of the TNF family guide how B cells grow and switch on. The adaptor TRAF6 carries signals for those sensors, but its role in B cells had not been made clear by past work.

The team found TRAF6 is required for the B-1a cell group to form. It is also needed for antibody responses with and without T cell help. The result fills a gap in how early antibody defense is built. It may inform vaccine and immune illness work.
plos-pone-0004836:
Juho-Antti Junno and colleagues studied temporal trends in vertebral size and shape from medieval to modern day humans, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Human lumbar vertebrae support weight of the upper body. Loads lifted and carried cause significant stress to vertebral bodies. Trauma induced fractures are common especially among elderly people with reduced bone strength and changing activity patterns over recent centuries.

Comparing eras shows how lifestyle reshapes skeletons. Modern vertebrae differ in robustness from medieval ones. Trends inform fracture risk and ergonomics. Archaeology meets clinical medicine here. Further tests can show how widely the pattern holds beyond the cases studied here.
plos-pone-0004936:
In early Alzheimer's disease, memory fails early. Toxic clumps of beta-amyloid damage the synapses where brain cells connect. Celia Williams and co-authors studied those synapses directly. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They prepared synaptoneurosomes, tiny fragments of synapses, from human prefrontal cortex. Then they read which genes were active inside.

The readout flags genes tied to neuroplasticity. Neuroplasticity is the brain's ability to rewire itself. Those genes were switched on more strongly in incipient Alzheimer's disease. They may mark the immediate changes that follow amyloid binding. They are also candidate early markers for a disease usually caught late.
plos-pone-0005036:
Building a protein is a race along a genetic message. Some stretches are read fast, others slowly. The choice of synonymous codons helps set the pace. Gong Zhang and Zoya Ignatova built a tool to predict it. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. The result is a generic algorithm for translation speed.

The algorithm evaluates the relative rate of elongation. It allows large-scale comparisons across genes. Speed matters because it shapes the finished protein. Folding can depend on pauses during building. The tool helps explain those effects. It turns codon choice from a curiosity into a measurable force in protein biogenesis.
plos-pone-0005136:
BAG3 is a protein that shields cells from death. It protects client proteins, such as AKT, from destruction. Victoria Virador and colleagues studied the limits on that shield in PLOS ONE in 2009. Two systems regulate protein stability. Caspases cut proteins apart. The proteasome grinds up tagged ones.

Both systems restrict BAG3's anti-death activity. Caspases snip it, and the proteasome degrades it. The cell keeps its protector on a leash. That layered control tunes the survival switch. Cancers often overproduce BAG3 to resist death. Knowing its brakes could help release them. The finding maps how survival and death machinery negotiate.
plos-pone-0005236:
Chunks of DNA that are gained or lost, called copy number variants, cover much of the human genome. They can shape evolution and underlie disease, but their exact structure is hard to read. Luo and colleagues read them in single sperm cells in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Each sperm carries one shuffled copy of the genome, so genotyping single sperm reveals variant structure cleanly. The approach shows how these variants are organized and passed on. That clarity helps geneticists judge which variants are harmless and which may drive disease. Sperm cells are easy to get and hold one copy of each gene, which makes them a neat tool for this kind of map work.
plos-pone-0005336:
Seasonal flu vaccines must be updated yearly because the virus keeps changing its surface. A vaccine that also covers bird flu strains would be a major advance. Alsharifi and colleagues tested an intranasal flu vaccine in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Given through the nose, the vaccine protected against seasonal influenza infections. It also protected against H5N1 avian influenza, the bird flu strain feared for its severity. Broad protection from a needle-free vaccine is exactly what pandemic planning calls for. A shot that guards both the flu of each year. A bird flu that could spark a world outbreak would ease the yearly race to guess which strain comes next.
plos-pone-0005436:
Hongye Liu and Issac Kohane mapped small RNA patterns across body tissues in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Tiny RNAs called microRNAs help set how much protein each gene makes in each tissue. Their binding sites on other RNAs vary with the length of the target and the tissue involved.

The authors studied how microRNAs and their target RNAs rise and fall together in growing and adult tissues. They also looked at the same links in cancer. The patterns show that microRNA control depends on context, which matters for using these small RNAs as disease markers or drug targets.
plos-pone-0005536:
Si Brask Sonne and co-authors refined a method for picking single cell types out of testis tissue, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. The testis holds many kinds of cells packed together. When workers measure gene activity in the whole tissue, signals from other cells drown out the type they care about.

Laser tools can cut out chosen cells, but the tissue must be stained first without harming its RNA. The team tuned staining steps for several cell types, including early tumour cells. Cleaner samples mean clearer answers about fertility and testis cancer.
plos-pone-0005636:
Adam Osborne and co-authors presented a method for reading single mitochondrial genomes in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Changes in mitochondrial DNA are tied to many diseases of aging, including Alzheimer's and diabetes. Much evidence rests on the share of altered copies within a person's cells.

Their PCR method can read the sequence from a single molecule, one at a time. Counting changes molecule by molecule is far more exact than averaging a whole sample. That precision can settle whether a change truly tracks with disease. Single-molecule counts could also settle disputes where group averages have hidden the real change.
plos-pone-0005736:
Garima Agarwal and co-authors used protein shape in 2009 to sort the cupin family and guess each member's job. Cupins share a barrel-like fold, yet do wildly different work across life. Their sequences vary so much that family ties are hard to read from letters alone.

The team built a tree from three-dimensional shapes instead of raw sequence. Shapes change more slowly than sequences, so deep kinship shows through. Sorting members by shape helped link form to function. The method offers a way to classify other vast, varied protein families where sequence alone misleads.
plos-pone-0005836:
Wesley Beckstead and co-authors tested in 2009 whether a variant in a mitochondrial gene fits with longer life under calorie restriction. The electron transport chain burns food energy and is tied to aging. Its core proteins vary slightly between people and strains.

The variant studied changes one amino acid in cytochrome b. Evolutionary pressure on that gene, the team found, matches a role for the variant in lifespan when calories are cut. Such diet-gene interplay may explain why restriction extends life in some strains and not others. The paper links deep evolution to a live aging question.
plos-pone-0005936:
When a predator looms, some tadpoles swell into a bulgy shape that is harder to swallow. Tsukasa Mori, Hiroko Kawachi, Chiharu Imai and colleagues hunted the gene behind that trick in 2009. They studied tadpoles of the frog Rana pirica, which grow the bulgy form when salamander larvae threaten them, then shrink back when danger passes.

Using a gene chip scan, the team found a new gene much like uromodulin tied to the bulgy change. Linking one gene to a whole-body defense gives the trait a firm base in biology. The study shows how a prey animal's shape can be switched by a signal from its enemy, and it names a gene future work can test.
plos-pone-0006036:
Watching two cell signals at once usually means switching lights back and forth. Yusuke Niino, Kohji Hotta and Kotaro Oka removed that shuffle in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper builds dual FRET sensors, glowing protein pairs that report cell signals, so that both can be imaged in one living cell under a single excitation light.

Earlier dual methods needed alternating excitation, which slows the view and complicates the gear. A single light source makes the setup simpler and the timing cleaner. The advance helps cell biologists watch two conversations inside a cell at the same moment, a need that grows as signaling maps grow more detailed.
plos-pone-0006136:
The enzymes that fix nitrogen feed the living world, and they come in three metal flavors. Alexander Glazer and Katerina Kechris compared all three in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper examines the alpha subunits of sixty-nine full-length nitrogenase sequences, the molybdenum, vanadium and iron-only forms, using alignments and pattern checks to find conserved sequence features.

Features shared across all three forms mark the parts evolution could not afford to change. That conservation maps the working core of one of life's most vital machines. The comparison also sharpens the family tree of nitrogen fixation, knowledge that feeds efforts to give crops some of the skill that legumes get from their bacteria.
plos-pone-0006236:
Seabirds and other marine migrants cross whole oceans and many national borders each year. Raul Ramos and colleagues used natural chemical markers inside the animals to trace those journeys, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Overfishing, bycatch, pollution, and warming all threaten migrants during their long trips.

Body tissues carry built-in records of where an animal has fed and travelled. Reading those records reveals routes that tracking devices may miss. Knowing the routes shows which waters and nations share care of each species. Conservation can then target the places migrants truly depend on.
plos-pone-0006336:
Tropomyosin is a long coiled protein that lies along actin filaments and helps govern muscle contraction. Abhishek Singh and Sarah Hitchcock-DeGregori examined how it binds and unfolds on actin in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Subtle variations along its coil let it interact with actin and other proteins.

Actin binding globally stabilises tropomyosin, the authors note, and the interaction repeats periodically along its length. Watching binding and unfolding together reveals the protein's working cycle. The details matter for understanding muscle regulation and its diseases. They also serve the basic physics of coiled proteins.
plos-pone-0006436:
Paul Macey and colleagues scanned the brains of children with a rare breathing disorder for PLOS ONE in 2009. The disorder, congenital central hypoventilation syndrome, is genetic. Children with it have a weak drive to breathe during sleep and sense carbon dioxide poorly. Brain scans had already shown structural and functional changes in these patients.

The team focused on the hippocampus, a brain area key to memory. Their title reports that its volume is reduced in these children. A smaller hippocampus could help explain thinking problems seen with the syndrome. The finding links a breathing disorder to brain development. It may guide care and follow-up for affected children.
plos-pone-0006536:
Guanghui Hu and Pankaj Agarwal built a disease-drug network from gene data in PLOS ONE in 2009. Drug repositioning offers faster development times and reduced risks in drug discovery. It finds new uses for existing drugs. With high-throughput technologies, genomic expression profiles have become widely available.

The authors built a human disease-drug network based on those expression profiles. Diseases and drugs that produce opposite profiles may be treatment matches. A network view reveals links no single study would show. Such maps can prioritize which old drugs to test against which diseases. The work is computational, using public expression data.
plos-pone-0006636:
Salomé Pinho, Celso Reis, Fátima Gärtner, and colleagues compared adhesion changes in mammary tumors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The process of metastasis involves a series of steps and interactions between the tumor embolus and the microenvironment. Key alterations in adhesion molecules are known to occur. The team studied molecular plasticity of E-cadherin and sialyl Lewis X expression in two comparative models of mammary tumorigenesis.

E-cadherin holds epithelial cells together; losing it frees cells to spread. Sialyl Lewis X helps cells stick to vessel walls during spread. Tracking both shows how tumors toggle adhesion. Two models guard against model-specific quirks.
plos-pone-0006736:
Dana S. F. Homsi, Vineet Gupta, and Gary D. Stormo modeled how precisely DNA-binding proteins choose their sites in PLOS ONE in 2009. Transcription factors bind specific DNA spots to control genes. That binding anchors every regulatory network in the cell. Predicting binding sites requires a model of each factor's specificity. Such models are usually built from example binding sites.

The authors focused on quantitative specificity, not just yes-or-no binding. A factor may bind one site strongly and another weakly. Their model captures those graded preferences from examples. Better predictions sharpen maps of gene regulation across genomes. The method serves anyone decoding how a genome's switches are wired.
plos-pone-0006836:
Janne Pitkäniemi and his team built a fuller math tool for gene risk work in PLOS ONE in 2009. Rare, tangled diseases are often traced through state lists of cases. Kin are found through all new cases in a set span of years. The age when the disease starts shifts a lot, which clouds risk counts. Past work often glossed over how the kin were found.

Their tool uses all the facts at once: the case lists and the land's age data. It counts the search path in full, not in part. Age at start is built in, not brushed aside. Sounder math gives sounder risk counts for kin. The tool serves any list-based hunt for rare disease in kin groups.
plos-pone-0006936:
Petra van der Lelij, Barbara Godthelp, Wouter van Zon, and colleagues examined cells from Roberts syndrome patients in PLOS ONE in 2009. Healthy cells hold sister chromatids together until division, a process called cohesion. In budding yeast, an enzyme named Eco1 sets up that cohesion. Humans have two related enzymes, and one is ESCO2, the gene faulty in Roberts syndrome.

The team added working ESCO2 into patient fibroblast cells. They then recorded how the cells' appearance and behavior changed. Comparing rescued and untreated cells reveals what the missing enzyme normally does. That helps explain the birth defects and growth problems seen in this rare syndrome.
plos-pone-0007036:
Anaïs Estrada-Gelonch, Jose Aramburu, and Cristina López-Rodríguez followed a stress factor through cell division in PLOS ONE in 2009. NFAT5 switches on genes that protect cells from salty, hypertonic stress. Under such stress it moves into the nucleus and binds gene control regions. It also helps cells keep dividing.

The team found NFAT5 is shut out of the chromosomes during mitosis. That eviction resets where the factor sits when division ends. The reset may help daughter cells start with a clean distribution. It shows how stress defenses are rewired at every cell division.
plos-pone-0007136:
Banzragch Battur, Damdinsuren Boldbaatar, Rika Umemiya-Shirafuji, and colleagues studied a metabolic enzyme in ticks in PLOS ONE in 2009. The enzyme pair LKR/SDH runs the first steps of lysine breakdown. In plants and mammals it is well known. In ticks, the lysine pathway and this enzyme's jobs were a blank.

The team followed the enzyme across the tick life cycle. It stayed important through every stage, including a long starvation period. Ticks endure months without a blood meal, so survival metabolism matters. An enzyme they cannot do without is a candidate target for tick control.
plos-pone-0007236:
Trine Welløv Boesgaard, Anette Prior Gjesing, Niels Grarup, and colleagues examined a diabetes-linked gene variant in 2009. A large combined analysis had found six new type 2 diabetes loci. Later studies asked how those variants affect insulin release and insulin sensitivity in the body.

The authors study a variant near the gene ADAMTS9 in offspring of diabetes patients. The work comes from the EUGENE2 study. They relate the variant to insulin resistance in those offspring. Their results help separate variants that harm insulin production from variants that harm insulin action.
plos-pone-0007336:
Heather R. L. Lerner, Jeff A. Johnson, Alec R. Lindsay, and colleagues measured genetic diversity in the harpy eagle in 2009. The harpy eagle is the largest Neotropical bird of prey. It is threatened by human persecution and by habitat loss and fragmentation across Central and South American forests.

Conservation strategies include education, captive rearing, reintroduction, and habitat protection. The authors assess genetic diversity and differentiation across populations. They report high levels of both. Their title argues it is not too late for the species. Strong genetic variety can fuel the conservation programs already under way.
plos-pone-0007436:
Alexandre Costa, Eric Jan, and Peter Sarnow published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how fruit flies defend themselves against viruses. The fruit fly is a favorite model for studying innate immunity, the built-in first line of defense. One of its defense pathways, called Imd, was known mainly for fighting bacteria. The team tested whether it also answers viral attack.

They infected flies with cricket paralysis virus, an RNA virus that attacks insects. The Imd pathway switched on and contributed to the antiviral response. That result overturns the tidy division between antibacterial and antiviral defenses in the fly. It also strengthens the fly's value as a model for immunity in other animals. A pathway once filed under bacteria turns out to guard against viruses too.
plos-pone-0007536:
Naoyuki Sato and Yoko Yamaguchi published a computational study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on human episodic memory, our memory for events. In rats, place cells fire in a shifting pattern against the brain's theta rhythm, a phenomenon called phase precession. That timing pattern is thought to help form memories. The authors built a network model on this principle and asked whether it could predict human memory behavior.

The model, driven by theta phase precession and timing-based learning rules, predicts how episodes get encoded. Turning a rat phenomenon into a human theory is the paper's ambition. A working predictor gives experiments something concrete to test. If the model holds, the theta rhythm is a shared scaffold for memory across species. The study bridges animal neurophysiology and human cognition through mathematics.
plos-pone-0007636:
Han Hu and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 establishing a cell line from a dairy cow's mammary gland. Milk production is studied best in living animals, but a lab model allows controlled experiments. The team took mammary tissue from a three-year-old lactating Chinese Holstein cow. They built a culture system for its epithelial cells and characterized the resulting line in detail.

A stable mammary cell line gives researchers a window into bovine milk biology. The cells can be tested for how they respond to hormones, feed factors, and infection. That serves both dairy science and basic cell biology. The characterization work proves the line keeps the traits of the tissue it came from. Without that proof, results in a dish would mean little. The paper delivers a tool other labs can build on.
plos-pone-0007736:
Youlin Xia and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It concerns Helicobacter pylori, a bacterium that infects the stomach. Long-term infection is tied to ulcers, stomach cancer and lymphoma. One bacterial protein, CagA, is a prime suspect in that damage.

The authors ran a wide analysis of the tail end of the CagA protein. They compared its sequence across strains and matched it to disease outcomes. Parts of that tail vary in ways that track how harmful a strain is. The work helps explain why some infections stay mild while others turn dangerous.
plos-pone-0007836:
Guadalupe Ayora-Talavera and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It finds mutations that let H5N1 bird flu grip human airway cells. The study appeared the year a swine-origin H1N1 virus caused a pandemic. H5N1 itself infects people rarely, but kills often when it does.

A key barrier is binding: the bird virus prefers bird cell surfaces. The team identified changes in its hemagglutinin protein that confer binding to human tracheal airway tissue. Each such change is a warning sign for pandemic risk. Surveillance programs watch for exactly these mutations.
plos-pone-0007936:
Joseph Abrajano and colleagues studied two gene silencers that shape nerve cells, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The silencers, REST and its partner CoREST, switch off sets of genes by calling in other proteins. REST is known as a master brake on nerve gene programs.

The team showed the pair do more than brake. They help decide which kind of neuron a young cell becomes, guide its growth, and keep its settled form in place. That broad role makes the pair key editors of brain cell identity, with effects that last from early growth into adult life.
plos-pone-0008036:
John Coates and Lionel Page took a hard look at how traders are scored in PLOS ONE in 2009. Traders are judged by the money they make set against the risk they take, a balance captured by the Sharpe ratio. Market theory says lasting edges should be rare, since prices already hold most news.

Drawing on real trading records, the authors checked what typical scores look like and how much of them could be luck. A lucky streak can mimic skill for a long while. Their note warns bosses and backers to demand long records before paying for what may be chance.
plos-pone-0008136:
Abhay Sharma and colleagues compared male and female flies in a seizure-like model in PLOS ONE in 2009. The drug pentylenetetrazole, fed over time, makes fruit flies develop movement faults like those of epilepsy models, and standard seizure drugs can prevent them. The first model was built in males only.

Gene activity over time told a different story in females. The sexes reached like faults by partly unlike gene paths. Epilepsy research that pools the sexes, or studies one and assumes the other, may miss real effects; even the fly insists on being counted by sex.
plos-pone-0008236:
Jingyu Zhang and colleagues studied plant hormone control in Arabidopsis in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Cytokinins are hormones that guide plant growth and development. They have been known for decades, yet control of their levels inside plants stayed murky. The team characterized two genes, AtSOFL1 and AtSOFL2. These genes belong to a family named for its first known members.

Both genes acted as positive modulators of specific cytokinins. They also overlapped, so one could partly cover for the other. That redundancy shows how plants keep hormone levels steady. The findings help explain growth regulation in this model plant.
plos-pone-0008336:
Joseph L. Spencer and S. Raghu asked whether a biofuel crop shelters a crop pest in PLOS ONE in 2009. Interest in biomass crops grows as global demand for biofuel rises. Miscanthus x giganteus is a tall grass promoted for the United States Corn Belt. It would grow on marginal land mixed among farm fields. The crop is a relative of maize and may host its pests.

The authors weighed whether Miscanthus serves as refuge or reservoir for a major maize pest. A reservoir would build pest numbers and threaten corn. A refuge could instead help manage resistance. The answer matters for planting decisions.
plos-pone-0008436:
Mathieu Kerbiriou and co-authors wrote a 2009 PLOS ONE paper on cystic fibrosis, a disease of mucus and glands. Most cases come from a flawed protein called CFTR. The flawed form folds the wrong way. It gets stuck in a part of the cell called the endoplasmic reticulum. Past work tied that flaw to a stress response in the cell.

The team trace a chain of enzymes that leads to cell death. The chain runs through calpain and two caspases, numbered 12 and 3. In cells with the flawed CFTR, that chain works in a changed way. The findings help explain cell loss in this disease.
plos-pone-0008536:
Maria Karrlander and co-authors test a blood protein against brain tumors in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Malignant glioma grows extensive new blood vessels. That process, angiogenesis, feeds the tumor's rapid growth. Several anti-angiogenic drugs targeting VEGF are in clinical trials. VEGF is the main signal for new vessel growth. The team study histidine-rich glycoprotein, a protein found in blood plasma.

They test if this protein can prevent experimental glioblastoma in mice. Glioblastoma is the most malignant form of glioma. The protein shows a preventive effect in their model. A natural blood protein that curbs vessel growth could inspire new glioma therapies.
plos-pone-0008636:
Nemuri Todaka and co-authors analyze wood-digesting genes in termites in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Xylophagous termites thrive on a wood diet thanks to symbiosis. Protists resident in their hindguts handle essential steps of lignocellulose degradation. That partnership is a textbook example of symbiosis. Genes for cellulolytic enzymes come from both host and symbionts. The team perform phylogenetic analysis of those enzyme genes. Lineages include representative termites and a related cockroach.

Their trees trace where each cellulolytic gene originated. Some enzymes evolved in the termite lineage itself, others came from gut protists. That history explains how wood feeding was assembled evolutionarily. It also informs efforts to copy termite digestion for biofuels.
plos-pone-0008736:
Iona Cheng, John Witte, Steven Jacobsen, and colleagues weighed infection history against prostate cancer risk. Their study drew on the California Men's Health Study. Earlier small studies linked prostate inflammation and sexually transmitted diseases with higher cancer risk. Larger, forward-looking studies gave mixed answers. A big cohort offered a cleaner test of the claim.

Men reported past prostatitis and sexually transmitted infections in surveys. Researchers then tracked who developed prostate cancer over time. Any link, or lack of one, sharpens prevention advice. The work helps separate true risk factors from artifacts of small study designs.
plos-pone-0008836:
Lea Gregersen, Anders Jacobsen, Lisa Frankel, and colleagues named the targets of a tumor-fighting small RNA in colon cancer. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. MicroRNAs tune gene activity by binding gene messages. One of them, miR-145, drops in several cancer types. Its loss likely frees growth-promoting genes. Which genes it restrains in colon cancer was the gap.

Two targets stood out: YES, a signaling enzyme, and STAT1, a gene switch. Restoring miR-145 lowered both in colon cancer cells. Named targets explain part of the RNA's tumor suppression. They also suggest points where therapy could mimic its effect.
plos-pone-0008936:
Stefanie Obermüller and co-authors studied mice missing a protein called chromogranin-B, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Chromogranins sit inside the tiny storage sacs that hormone-making cells use. The pancreas releases insulin and other hormones from such sacs, called secretory granules. Scientists had long debated what chromogranins actually do there.

Mice bred without chromogranin-B released their islet hormones poorly. Their pancreatic islets, the cell clusters that make insulin, secreted less than normal islets did. The defect showed the protein is needed for proper hormone release, not just a passenger. The result speaks to diabetes research, where insulin release is the central problem.
plos-pone-0009036:
Neelkamal Chaudhary, Janet Staab, and Kieren Marr mapped how healthy people's T cells answer a common mould, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Aspergillus fumigatus spores float in ordinary air and are breathed in daily. Healthy lungs clear them quietly; weak immune systems can suffer invasive disease. Others develop allergic lung disease from the same mould.

The team exposed T cells from healthy donors to the mould's antigens. Spores and the thread-like growth form provoked different responses. Knowing the normal response sets the baseline for patients who get sick. It also helps design immune therapies against this stubborn fungus.
plos-pone-0009136:
Paul Bentley and co-authors ran a very large gene survey of stroke. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2010 and compared stroke with heart disease. Ischemic stroke and ischemic heart disease share blocked-artery roots in the body. How far their genetic causes overlap was poorly understood before this work.

The team pooled the studies of gene variants linked to ischemic stroke. They then compared the stroke list against heart disease factors and blood measures. Some risk genes were shared, while others belonged to stroke alone. The map clarifies which prevention lessons can cross from heart to brain.
plos-pone-0009236:
Robin Freeman and colleagues published this seabird tracking study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Black petrels are vulnerable seabirds that roam wide stretches of ocean. Where they feed matters for protecting them, yet their elusive life at sea made them hard to follow. New satellite tracking tools finally made that follow possible.

The team fitted black petrels with GPS trackers and recorded their foraging trips. The birds patrolled the shelf-break, the edge where shallow coastal water drops into deep ocean. That edge is rich in food, which explains the patrol routes. Knowing the hotspot lets conservation planners protect the waters these birds depend on.
plos-pone-0009336:
Giovanni Di Pasquale and co-authors published this virus study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bovine adeno-associated virus, or BAAV, is a small virus used as a delivery tool in research. Sugars on cell surfaces help viruses get inside cells. BAAV was known to use membrane gangliosides to infect.

The team found the virus can also cross cell layers whole, a route called transcytosis. That crossing requires contact with a sugar chain ending in glucosamine. It also requires a cell protein called gp96. A virus that can slip across barriers intact is a promising courier for delivering genes to hard-to-reach tissues.
plos-pone-0009436:
Marta Rodriguez-Garcia and co-authors studied people with HIV for a report in PLOS ONE in 2010. The body makes small proteins called defensins that can kill germs. Dendritic cells, which help start immune responses, can make three forms of alpha defensin. The team checked how much of these proteins patients made.

Higher output from dendritic cells went with slower progress of HIV disease. That link held across the group they studied. It hints that the body's own germ killing proteins help hold the virus back. Raising that natural defense could one day support care for people with HIV.
plos-pone-0009536:
Michelle Lee and colleagues tested a safer way to track tiny drug carriers in PLOS ONE in 2010. Iron oxide nanoparticles can carry drugs or imaging agents in the body. One design joins them to chlorotoxin, a scorpion venom protein that seeks tumors. To learn where carriers go, scientists usually add radioactive tags. The team tried tracking the particles without radioactivity.

They used the particles' magnetic traits to follow them in animals. The method gave quick data on how fast the particles cleared and where they settled. Such data decide whether a carrier is safe and useful. A non radioactive route makes those early tests simpler and cheaper.
plos-pone-0009636:
Alka Potdar and co-authors tracked single human cells on the move in PLOS ONE in 2010. Animals foraging for food often follow random walk paths with a mix of short and long steps. The team asked whether single cells move in a like way. They filmed human mammary epithelial cells, which line milk ducts, and measured their paths step by step.

The cells followed a random walk with two modes, switching between slow local wandering and faster runs. That bimodal pattern had not been shown for single cells before. It extends a law of animal movement down to the cell scale. The link may help explain how cells explore tissue during growth and healing.
plos-pone-0009836:
A short course of antibiotics can leave long marks on the bacteria that live in us. Hedvig Jakobsson and colleagues tracked those marks in the human throat and gut. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Most of those bacteria are harmless or helpful.

The microbiome is the community of microbes living in a body site. The team found that short-term treatment had differing long-term impacts at the two sites. Some communities bounced back while others stayed changed. Lasting shifts matter because gut and throat microbes support health. The throat and gut reacted on different timetables.
plos-pone-0009936:
Epidemic HIV strains spread worldwide in the early twentieth century, and timing may explain why. João Dinis de Sousa and colleagues linked that spread to genital ulcer disease rates. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

GUD, genital ulcer disease, causes sores that make HIV far easier to transmit. High GUD incidence in the early 1900s created a particularly permissive time window. In that window, epidemic strains could originate and gain their first foothold. The argument ties HIV's history to the disease landscape of its era. The strains studied were the ancestors of today's epidemic lines.
plos-pone-0010036:
The authors were Jimmy Ong, Mark Chen, Alex Cook, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study tracked flu in Singapore during the 2009 H1N1 outbreak. Reports of flu-like illness came from family doctor clinics across the city. Such reports can reflect real epidemic activity as it happens, with little setup.

The team used those clinic reports to monitor the epidemic and forecast its course in real time. Fast forecasts help health officials time warnings, staffing, and supplies. The authors note the same low-cost approach could serve countries with fewer resources.
plos-pone-0010136:
The authors were Paras Anand, Ellis Anand, Christopher Bleck, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study examined tiny sacs called exosomes and immune alarm. Cells release exosomes when inner compartments fuse with the outer membrane. Exosomes from cells infected with mycobacteria had already been shown to stir inflammation.

The team focused on Hsp70, a stress protein found inside those exosomes. They showed exosomal Hsp70 drives a pro-inflammatory response to foreign particles, mycobacteria included. That pathway may help the body rally against tuberculosis, whose cause is a mycobacterium. The study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.
plos-pone-0010236:
The authors were Yari Ciribilli, Virginia Andreotti, Daniel Menendez, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study looked at joint gene control by two major regulators. The guard protein p53 and the estrogen receptor can act on the same gene switch. At one DNA variant in the FLT1 gene promoter, that shared control creates a new p53 response site.

The team showed the coordinated control is specific to certain triggers. It responded to genotoxic stress, which damages DNA, and to an estrogenic compound. Such variant-specific control may explain why the same DNA change matters only under some conditions.
plos-pone-0010436:
Adam Cohen and co-workers used an antibody to rally immunity against melanoma in mice, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2010. A surface switch called GITR can boost T cells that attack tumors. Flipping it had helped anti-tumor immunity before, but the details were murky. Especially unclear was what happens to regulatory T cells, which normally calm attacks. The team gave the antibody to mice with melanoma and watched both cell types.

The treatment changed the stability and location of the regulatory cells inside tumors. With the brakes loosened, killer T cells could work better. Melanoma is a strong test case for immune therapy in mice. Results like these helped pave the way toward human immune treatments. The study clarifies how one switch can retune a tumor's immune balance.
plos-pone-0010536:
Dennis Halterman and colleagues showed that rival weapons from the potato blight pathogen can backfire on the pathogen in PLOS ONE in 2010. Late blight, caused by Phytophthora infestans, still devastates potato crops. Breeders have fought it for decades with resistance genes in the plants. The pathogen counters with effector proteins that disarm plant defenses. This team studied what happens when two of its effectors compete.

Instead of helping, the competition made the pathogen more aggressive on plants with broad resistance in some settings; the interactions proved complex. Effector battles inside the pathogen shape how disease plays out. Breeders need that detail to build resistance that lasts. The study warns that single-gene defenses face a moving, quarreling opponent. Blight remains an evolutionary chess game.
plos-pone-0010636:
Sriram Narayanan and colleagues described a hard-working subset of human helper T cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Helper T cells coordinate immune attacks. A surface marker called CD300a appears on some memory helpers but not others, raising the question of what sets those cells apart.

Cells carrying CD300a did several jobs at once when stimulated. They made multiple signaling molecules together, a trait called polyfunctionality. They also switched on a gene controller named Eomesodermin. Polyfunctional cells are prized in vaccine research because they fight harder. This marker may help scientists find and study them more easily.
plos-pone-0010736:
Lei Gao and colleagues pooled studies of HIV and tuberculosis co-infection in mainland China, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Each disease worsens the other, and they overlap in many regions. China needed a national estimate to plan testing and treatment, since single studies covered single cities or groups.

The meta-analysis combined published surveys from across the mainland. Co-infection rates varied widely by group and place, with the highest rates in the hardest-hit groups. Pooled numbers give planners a defensible baseline. They also expose where data are missing, which is itself a planning result: provinces without surveys cannot know their burden.
plos-pone-0010836:
Pamela Austin, Markus Heller, David Williams and colleagues published this cell study in PLOS ONE in 2010. They examined neopetrosiamide A, a small peptide first taken from a marine sponge because it slowed tumor cell invasion. How it worked was unknown, so the team watched its effects on cancer cells in culture.

The peptide loosened tumor cell grip, pulling apart the anchor points that attach cells to surfaces, and lowered a key adhesion protein on the cell surface. Treated cells also sprouted shifting, membrane-bound protrusions and shed tiny vesicles carrying receptors and adhesion proteins into the medium. Tests suggested those vesicles budded straight from the protrusions. Austin and colleagues outline a fresh way a natural compound can stop cells from sticking, a step cancer needs in order to spread.
plos-pone-0010936:
Adaikkalam Vellaichamy, Zoltán Dezső, Lellean JeBailey and co-authors published this prostate cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Prostate tumors often shrink under hormone-blocking treatment, then return in a form that no longer needs male hormones. The team wanted the system-wide changes that follow hormone stimulation, as a route to understanding that escape.

They treated prostate cancer cells with a synthetic androgen and measured gene activity and protein levels at the same time. Instead of just listing what rose, they scored molecules by their position in interaction networks, a concept they call topological significance. Vellaichamy and colleagues argue that the most connected changed molecules are the likeliest levers of hormone response. Their approach aims at mechanisms of treatment resistance, the problem that makes advanced prostate cancer deadly.
plos-pone-0011036:
Béatrice Labrosse, Mathieu Tourdjman, Raphaël Porcher and co-authors published this flu immunity study in PLOS ONE in 2010. When the 2009 pandemic H1N1 virus appeared, a pressing question arose. Did earlier seasonal flu infections or shots already protect people against it? The authors measured cross-reacting antibodies with a sensitive lab test using stand-in viruses.

Many people who had never met the pandemic virus still carried high levels of antibodies able to block it. Blocking strength against the pandemic strain tracked strength against a standard seasonal strain. People given a seasonal flu shot in 2008 showed higher levels against the pandemic virus. Labrosse and colleagues demonstrate broad cross-blocking between seasonal and pandemic viruses. Their result helps explain why the 2009 pandemic spared many older adults and informs how vaccine stockpiles are judged.
plos-pone-0011136:
Ajslev, Andersen, Ingstrup and colleagues linked mother and child health in PLOS ONE in 2010. They studied women who felt strong distress after giving birth. The question was whether that early distress tracks with the child later becoming overweight.

The team found a link between a mother's post birth distress and her child's weight in childhood. That suggests early family stress can shape later body health. It argues for treating new mothers' mental health as part of child health care too. Support in the first months may pay off years later in lower obesity risk.
plos-pone-0011236:
Ota, Monsey, Wu and colleagues traced fear learning in rats for PLOS ONE in 2010. After fear conditioning, connections in the amygdala, the brain's alarm center, grow stronger on both sides of the synapse. The team linked those changes to a gas based signaling chain inside the cells.

The chain helped drive changes both where signals are sent and where they are received. That mechanism shows how a frightening event rewires the alarm circuit for the long term. It matters for research on trauma disorders, where such wiring stays too strong. Blocking or softening the chain could aid future fear extinction therapies.
plos-pone-0011336:
Jaap van Buul and co-workers studied in 2010 how white blood cells cross the wall of a blood vessel. To exit the blood, the cells must stick to a docking protein on the vessel lining and then push through. Inflammation signals make the lining ready for this exit, but how the lining itself controls the docking protein was not well understood.

The team showed that signals from inside the lining cell reshape how the docking protein clusters and moves. That inside-out control helps gather the protein where a white cell is trying to cross. The finding adds a missing piece to the story of inflammation. If the docking step can be tuned, doctors might one day ease diseases where too many white cells flood into tissue and cause harm.
plos-pone-0011436:
Leandro Tarosso and co-authors mapped immune responses in 2010 in the rare people who control HIV without any drugs. These controllers keep the virus at very low levels for years, and scientists study them for clues to a cure or vaccine. The team focused on T-cell responses against two viral proteins that had received less attention than the usual targets.

They found responses against Nef and Vif that were strikingly diverse from person to person, with no single shared pattern. That variety warns vaccine designers against chasing one universal controller formula. Control of HIV may be reached by many different immune roads, not one. Broadening vaccine targets to include these proteins, and expecting variety rather than uniformity, may bring designs closer to how natural control actually works.
plos-pone-0011536:
Nicolas Christoforou and co-authors implanted heart progenitor cells in 2010 into mice whose hearts had been damaged by infarction, the death of muscle after a blocked artery. A heart attack leaves scar where muscle died, and the weakened heart often slides into failure over time. The implanted cells were cardiac progenitors grown from mouse embryonic stem cells, young cells primed to become heart tissue.

After implantation, the infarcted hearts preserved more of their function than untreated hearts. A stem-cell patch helping the heart keep working, rather than merely surviving in place, is the result the field needs. Human translation remains distant, with safety and scale unsolved. Even so, each animal study in which lab-grown heart cells measurably protect function strengthens the case that repair, not just palliation, is a reachable goal for heart attack care.
plos-pone-0011636:
Daniel Buchanan and colleagues studied cancer risk in people with many serrated colon polyps, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Patients with multiple polyps of this type face a higher chance of colorectal cancer. Recent reports had also linked smoking to the cancers that grow from such polyps, raising the question of which patients need closest watching.

Gathering cases from genetics clinics, the team compared patients to identify factors tied to cancer. Their cross-sectional analysis profiles who among polyp patients carries the greatest risk. Clinics can use that profile to focus screening and follow-up on the patients most likely to benefit.
plos-pone-0011736:
Maria Goretti Fonseca and co-authors modelled a future HIV vaccine for Brazil, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Brazil's AIDS cases are centred in groups with high exposure to HIV, and a vaccine could add a strong new layer of protection there. Before one exists, planners need to know what a vaccine of a given strength would be worth.

Their model projected how a vaccine could change new infections, deaths and the count of people on antiretroviral drugs. The results give health planners a preview of the gains under varied vaccine strengths. Such forecasts guide spending and trial design in a country with a long-running epidemic.
plos-pone-0011936:
Douglas Tsao, Allen Minton, and Nikolay Dokholyan presented in 2010 a teaching model of how crowding inside cells changes protein folding. The cell interior is packed with large molecules, and that crowding pushes proteins toward compact shapes. Full mathematical treatments of the effect are hard for students to grasp.

Their didactic model walks through the physics in a simplified form, using current theory and discrete simulations that can be followed step by step. A model built for teaching still has to be right, and this one shows how excluded space alone can speed folding and binding. It gives instructors a way to make an invisible physical effect feel concrete in the classroom.
plos-pone-0012036:
Shuangge Ma and co-workers built in 2010 a statistical model for a widely used heart risk score. The score, named for Agatston, sums calcium in the coronary arteries seen on scans; more calcium means more artery disease. Their data came from MESA, a multi-ethnic study of early cardiovascular disease in the United States.

Calcium scores are awkward data: many people score zero, and the rest spread widely. A model built for that shape sharpens how risk factors are tied to artery calcium across ethnic groups. Better modeling of a popular score matters because treatment decisions for millions of symptom-free adults lean on it.
plos-pone-0012236:
Erik Corona, Joel Dudley, and Atul Butte compared natural selection's fingerprints across seven complex diseases in PLOS ONE in 2010. When environments shift fast, as they have through human history, helpful gene variants sweep upward, leaving marks that genome scans can read. Disease studies had found thousands of risk variants, but whether evolution pushed them unevenly across diseases was unexplored.

The team measured signs of positive selection around the risk variants of each disease and found extreme differences between them. Some diseases sit on heavily selected ground, others on barely touched ground. That contrast hints that modern diseases differ in how deeply they are tangled with human adaptation, a clue for both medicine and evolutionary biology.
plos-pone-0012336:
Marine Jeanmougin, Aurelien de Reynies, Laetitia Marisa, and co-authors asked if gene studies should drop the classic t-test, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Labs compare two groups gene by gene with a t-test. It is the routine first pass over microarray data. Yet the test draws criticism in this setting. Each gene's spread is measured from few samples. At the same time, thousands of tests run at once.

They compared the plain test with smarter strategies. The new strategies model gene variance with more care. They borrow strength across genes to do so. The verdict guides daily choices in thousands of labs. Small choices at this scale have huge effects. They decide which genes get years of follow-up work. An answer based on proof has outsized value here.
plos-pone-0012436:
Ian Stevenson, Beau Cronin, Mriganka Sur and colleagues modeled how the brain tidies its own sensory signals, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Sensory neurons change their readiness on many time scales, which adds noise and could cause perception errors. Yet perception stays fairly steady, so the brain must correct for its own drift.

The authors frame adaptation and short-term plasticity as Bayesian correction — the brain updating its bets as conditions change. Their model shows how this updating can cancel self-made noise. The idea links brain physiology to statistics and may guide designs for artificial sensors that must stay accurate while their parts drift.
plos-pone-0012536:
R. Scott Cornman surveyed two small protein motifs across fruit fly proteins, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Arthropod cuticle, the shell of insects, is built from chitin plus many structural proteins that self-assemble into a tough matrix. Two short motifs, GYR and YLP, recur in those proteins, but their wider distribution and roles were not mapped.

Cornman found the motifs spread well beyond cuticle proteins, suggesting a general role in assembly and protein-protein contact. A shared molecular Velcro across many proteins would be a basic building trick of insect biology. The survey gives protein engineers new, simple parts to test in designed materials.
plos-pone-0012636:
Cai and Robertson examined how chemical tags control a tumour-blocking protein called VHL. When VHL fails, several cancers can grow, including a common kidney cancer. The tags in question, ubiquitin and SUMO, usually mark proteins for destruction or move them between cell compartments.

Their 2010 work shows these tags govern both how long VHL lasts and whether it sits in the nucleus or the outer cell body. A protein's place can matter as much as its amount, since it can only act where it is. The findings add detail to how cancer cells disable a key guard.
plos-pone-0012736:
Bakszt, Wernimont, Allali-Hassani and co-authors solved the crystal shape of an enzyme from the toxoplasma parasite. Pyruvate kinase runs the last step of sugar burning and acts as a central control of cell energy. Their 2010 structure covers the parasite's first form of this enzyme.

A precise shape shows where drugs could grip the parasite enzyme without touching the human one. Toxoplasma infects a large share of humanity and endangers unborn babies and weak immune systems. Parasite-specific shapes like this one anchor future drug design.  The team deposited the structure for other groups to use freely.
plos-pone-0012836:
Yap, Luo, Chung and co-authors solved the shape of the dengue virus cap-making enzyme holding its RNA. Flaviviruses cap their RNA messages so they look like host messages. The enzyme, part of the NS5 protein, adds two methyl marks to the cap in a set order.

Their 2010 crystal structure shows the enzyme gripping a short capped RNA piece of eight building blocks. Seeing the grip in detail exposes pockets a drug could block. Dengue infects millions yearly, and its cap machinery is a clean drug target.  The RNA piece used was a capped eight-unit stretch.
plos-pone-0321836:
Nalan Ozen and coauthors published a study in PLOS ONE developing a questionnaire to measure how adults perceive the risks of the global climate crisis. Public views on climate danger are divided, and without a standard ruler, researchers cannot compare those views cleanly. The team built the scale through eight stages. They ran from defining the concept and drafting items to expert review and a pilot. Then came a large face-to-face application with well over seven hundred people, plus a repeat application to test stability.

Analysis settled on five underlying factors explaining a strong share of answer differences, and model fit indices landed within accepted ranges. Internal consistency was very high, and scores barely shifted on retesting, marking the scale as reliable. It is offered as a first multidimensional framework for climate risk perception in adults, to be confirmed in more diverse populations before guiding communication and policy.
plos-pone-0329436:
Wu Zuoqi and four co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One mining study on coal pillars in flooded mines. Pillars are the blocks of coal left behind to hold up the roof in mined-out rooms. Long soaking in water can weaken the rock and threaten collapse. The team ran squeeze tests on coal samples under water pressure and stress. They then built a safety rule. They also simulated how mining choices affect the stability of the worked-out area.

Higher squeezing pressure raised sample strength but cut water flow through the rock. Higher water pressure did the reverse. The simulations set a safety factor below which pillars cannot be trusted long-term. Leaving a moderate share of coal unmined kept the roof supported. The authors offer the rules as guidance for preventing roof disasters in similar mines.
plos-pone-0331236:
Didier Mbombo Ndombe and Ester Lucia Rizzi studied women in two parts of the Congo. Many of these women wish to space or stop births. Yet they are not using birth control. The team used survey data from 2021 and 2022. It held near fourteen hundred women, aged fifteen to forty-nine, all in unions.

Women hurt by a partner's sexual force in the past year were more apt to lack birth control. The link grew much worse when the partner also blocked or broke their birth control. That hidden control is the key point of the study. The team urges clinics to ask about force and control, not just hand out supplies.
plos-pone-0335036:
Taheripour, Sadjadi, and Amiri built a stock portfolio method that reads company reports in a 2026 study. Quarterly reports carry mood about a firm's health that prices may not yet reflect. Their three-stage method scores report mood with a finance-tuned language model, forecasts prices with a memory network, then builds a portfolio balancing several goals at once.

Mood scores feed expected return estimates alongside forecast-based risk measures. No earlier work had joined report sentiment to portfolio building in this way, the authors note. The approach suits investors drowning in filings: machines read the tone, then optimizers weigh return, risk, and mood together.
plos-pone-0336836:
Akash Patel, Gauri Agarwal, and co-authors tell how one student-led nutrition lecture at a Miami medical school grew into a push for lasting curriculum change. Diet is a leading driver of early death worldwide, yet most American medical schools still teach far less nutrition than advised decades ago. Their 2026 case study describes a single clinical nutrition session and what followed it.

Surveys around the lecture showed real gains in knowledge and in students' confidence about advising patients on diet. Enthusiasm then snowballed into a taskforce of about fifty members working to weave nutrition teaching through the whole program. The authors argue that even a small pilot can start institutional change when students lead it, and they share the elements they believe made the effort work.
plos-pone-0340336:
Li and colleagues, in a 2026 paper, tackle route planning for mobile robots in busy, changing spaces. A robot needs a good overall route, but it must also dodge moving obstacles up close. Older ant colony methods, which copy how ants lay scent trails, can be slow and not safe enough near obstacles.

Their method joins an improved ant colony search with a local steering approach that tests short moves in real time. Changes include a guiding pull toward the goal, rewards and penalties on scent trails, and removal of needless turns to shorten the path. In computer tests, the joined method found shorter routes in far fewer rounds, with far fewer turns, than the classic ant method. It also steered around surprise obstacles in the tests, which supports its use for safe robot travel.
plos-pone-0342136:
Ta-Wei Guu and colleagues present the protocol for a small feasibility study in rural Taiwan using wearable devices with dementia patient and caregiver pairs. The behavioral symptoms of dementia, such as agitation, apathy, and broken sleep, burden families more than memory loss itself. Yet standard assessments lean on caregiver questionnaires that can be biased and only snapshot one moment.

Ten patients and ten caregivers will join. Patients wear a research activity tracker for eight weeks and use a light-therapy device daily for a month, since light treatment may ease sleep and mood. The study tests whether this dyadic, device-based approach is acceptable and workable before any larger trial. Objective, continuous measures could change how these symptoms are tracked.
plos-pone-0345236:
Kevin Mulcahy published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It re-examines Uintatherium anceps, a huge horned mammal that lived in North America tens of millions of years ago. The question is whether males and females differed strongly in body form, which is called sexual dimorphism.

The tool is linear morphometrics, simple length measurements of fossil bones and skulls. As the title states, these measurements fail to support strong differences between the sexes. That result pushes back on claims built from a few dramatic skulls, and it reminds paleontologists how easily size variation within one sex can be mistaken for two distinct forms.
plos-pone-0346236:
Ji-Eun Lee, Yuno Do, and Jun-Kyu Park moved black-spotted pond frogs from the wild into captivity, the standard rescue move for threatened amphibians, and watched what changed inside them. Gut bacteria from droppings, blood chemistry, body composition, and immune measures were tracked through the transition, and half the frogs received probiotic treatment meant to soften the shock.

Captivity itself, not the probiotic, did the heavy lifting. Gut bacterial membership shifted under both influences, but diversity held steady, and the probiotic brought no measurable gain in immunity or body condition over the short term. Blood chemistry flagged strain even under standard good husbandry. The authors advise zoos to monitor captive frogs physiologically and to design enclosures from the species' ecology, rather than trusting supplements to fix the stress of the move.
plos-pone-0346336:
Paul O'Brien, Natasha Carr, and Jeff Bowman tackle a gap in park planning. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Parks are often picked for their land alone. Few plans ask how well wildlife can move between parks. The case study is the park network of Ontario, Canada. The backdrop is the global goal of guarding thirty percent of land by 2030.

The team placed fake parks at many spots in a model. Each time, they measured how the network's links changed. Compact parks near the center helped most. Parks near an existing node also scored well. Quiet land inside the park mattered too. The model can rank real sites for land trusts and planners.
plos-pone-0347436:
Lydia Nakiyingi and coauthors published a cohort study in PLOS ONE on a hard call in Ugandan HIV care: a patient looks like tuberculosis but the sputum molecular test says no. Treat anyway, or wait? Three hundred test-negative adults with presumed TB at two Kampala facilities were enrolled, worked up with chest imaging and cultures, and followed for a year.

Just under a quarter received empiric TB treatment. The year proved deadly: nearly a third died, most within three months. Cultures confirmed TB in only one participant in twenty, while a serious fungal marker and blood infections explained other cases. The treated group died more often, but after accounting for how sick they were at entry, treatment showed no clear link to mortality. The deaths, they argue, signal severe, often non-TB illness that empiric TB drugs cannot fix; better diagnosis is the urgent need.
plos-pone-0347736:
Glenn T Schumacher and colleagues read the life histories of Arctic charr and brook trout written inside their own eye lenses. A fish's lens grows in layers, and the chemistry of each layer records what the fish ate at that age. The team applied this lens method, rare in fresh water, to fish from four lakes in Maine, near the southern edge of the charr's range.

Lens chemistry matched the expected climb from tiny prey to larger food as fish grow. Charr leaned on open-water food more than brook trout throughout life. In some lakes charr climbed the food chain steadily, while in others they barely shifted, a difference the authors link to lake conditions. Knowing how each population feeds may help protect these cold-water fish as the climate warms.
plos-pone-0348436:
Jia Xu, Guangdong Wang, and Yongfeng Ni study a blood sugar index in patients with bleeding inside the brain. The index compares a long-term sugar marker with what a one-time sugar reading would predict, capturing how a person's body sugars proteins unusually. Their 2026 study reviews more than thirteen hundred intensive care patients and tracks deaths over one and three months.

Patients in the lowest index group died most often, while higher index values went with lower risk. The link bent into an L shape, with risk falling steeply at first and then leveling. The pattern held after adjusting for other factors. A cheap index from routine labs might help doctors judge early risk after brain bleeding.
plos-pone-0348536:
EDITORIAL NOTE: The PLOS One Editors give fresh word on a past note of concern. The note was about a study that used a test to find plague germs in old teeth. The study used teeth from live dental patients in France. It also used old teeth from digs in France and Italy. The journal probed the study's ethics proof and rights to the teeth.

Gaps stayed wide. The study gave no code for its ethics pass and no dates for when teeth were took. It showed no leave from Italy to break down old relics, which the law there seems to need. The authors and their school sent no more proof. The note of concern stands.
plos-pone-0349236:
Phoebe Smith and Chris Guiver developed control rules for protecting wild populations when managers cannot know exactly what each action will do. Conservation choices, like cutting or adding animals, have uncertain effects, yet the goal is to keep the population from dying out. Their 2026 study treats the problem with math for systems that stay positive, such as animal counts over time.

They propose switching schemes that try different management actions and settle on one that keeps the population persisting, if such an action exists. The switching rules can be adjusted to change how the population behaves along the way, suiting different user needs. Worked examples show the schemes in action. The approach gives conservation planners a principled backup when knowledge is incomplete.
plos-pone-0349336:
Napasorn Sakulteera and colleagues surveyed anaesthesia staff across Thailand about burnout, a state of exhaustion that endangers both clinicians and patients. Nearly six hundred doctors and nurses in the specialty completed standard measures of burnout, personality, and resilience. High-risk burnout was defined by strong emotional exhaustion combined with growing detachment from patients.

More than two in five respondents landed in the high-risk group. That group scored higher on a tendency to worry. It scored lower on being organised, on outgoingness, and on warmth toward others, while most of its members sat in the lowest band for bouncing back. Workload measures and self-rated burnout severity also fed into the risk picture. The authors argue that screening and support in these departments should weigh personality and resilience alongside rosters, since the same shift load breaks some clinicians faster than others.
plos-pone-0349436:
Yu Zhang and co-authors dissected a viral livestreaming tour, in which an American influencer's broadcasts from China drew huge cross-cultural audiences on the Bilibili platform, to learn how emotion travels online. Their 2026 case study combined network mapping of user interactions, automated sentiment reading of comments, and epidemic-style models of how feelings spread from viewer to viewer.

Three mechanisms stood out. Platform algorithms spread clips through loose, decentralized networks, sights and sounds together triggered strong positive emotion, and viewers who already felt alike passed the feeling onward in cascades. Together they formed an emotion-first pattern of communication that crossed cultural lines with ease. The authors build a general framework from the single case, linking platform infrastructure, emotional pathways, and shared identity.
plos-pone-0349936:
Jean-Philippe Emond, Christina Wolfson, and co-authors asked a deceptively simple question: how often do standard vital sign cutoffs flag healthy, stable adults as abnormal, and does that change with age and sex? A cutoff that flags too many well people invites needless tests and treatment. Their 2026 study drew on records for more than one hundred twenty thousand patients at a Montreal hospital over a decade, using final readings before discharge.

The standard upper limit for systolic blood pressure flagged about thirteen percent of women in their late forties but nearly forty percent of women over eighty-five. Temperature and low blood pressure limits, by contrast, flagged almost no one. The team derived age- and sex-specific reference ranges from the data. They argue that one-size thresholds misread older patients in particular.
plos-pone-0350236:
Md Atik Hasan Nishat and coauthors published a 2026 engineering study in PLOS ONE on powering farm sensors with radio waves already in the air. Precision agriculture scatters wireless sensors across fields where changing batteries is costly and wasteful.
