Their harvester collects energy from broadcast and mobile phone bands through a custom antenna and matching circuits, then doubles the voltage with a rectifier built around germanium diodes.

Across thirty repeated trials the device produced a steady few volts of open-circuit output, though the usable power under load was tiny, measured in microwatts, enough only for very frugal sensors. Diode choice mattered enormously, the germanium type beating two silicon alternatives. A gradient boosting model predicted output voltage accurately, and explanation analysis pointed to diode forward voltage and ambient radio power as dominant factors. The authors present the system as a validated step toward battery-free field monitoring.
plos-pone-0350736:
Sabrine Attia and Shimat V Joseph tested four insect growth regulators against a newly detected cotton leafhopper pest in the United States. Regulators are seen as gentler insecticides that wreck moulting and development. Young, middle, and late nymphs and adults were exposed on treated leaves at field rates, alone and with two spreader additives, while survival, moult success, and lifespan were logged.

Two chitin blocking regulators killed over ninety percent of youngest nymphs and halved moulting in many groups, acting fast. Two other regulators acted weakly and late, with little effect on adults. Additives helped only slightly. Early stage timing is everything: spray while nymphs are young or growth regulators will disappoint.
plos-pone-0350936:
Zhang and colleagues studied how recycled road material sticks together as it ages in a 2026 paper. The mix reuses old pavement and steel slag, a waste product from steel making, to cut the need for fresh stone. For such roads to last, the glue-like tar must hold tight to each kind of stone over years of use.

Steel slag bonded with tar through chemical links and a rough, pitted surface that grips well. Plain rock relied mostly on surface clinging instead. As reused tar aged again, its grip fell in a steady pattern, with a clear turning point after about thirty hours of lab aging. The linked tests give road builders a fuller way to judge recycled mixes.
plos-pone-0351136:
Road crashes are a leading cause of brain injury in children, and Esther Jimbih and colleagues reviewed outcomes for school-aged patients in Malaysia. Their 2026 PLOS One study drew on records of about five hundred forty children aged seven to seventeen after first-time crash injuries.

Most patients were boys, and motorcycles figured in three quarters of the crashes, especially among teenagers. Recovery was classed as good or poor on a standard child outcome scale. The team examined which traits, injury features, and complications lined up with poor recovery. Data from Southeast Asia are rare in this field, which makes the Malaysian record valuable.
plos-pone-0351336:
Andrea Nucita and colleagues staged a coding contest between human experts and artificial intelligence on thousands of Facebook posts from two Italian universities. Sociologists increasingly face data too big to code by hand, but categories like the purpose of an institutional post are slippery. Three researchers coded the posts independently, creating the human benchmark against which machine classifications were judged.

Ambiguity plagued several categories, and humans disagreed with each other plenty. Against that honest baseline, the automated systems agreed with human coding about as well as the humans agreed among themselves. The authors propose a hybrid bench: AI as one more coder in the team, its disagreements reviewed like anyone's. For social science facing platform-scale data, the study reframes the question from whether machines code perfectly to whether they code as reliably as we do.
plos-pone-0351736:
Meng Lu and six colleagues ask whether years in a freezer quietly rewrite the blood samples biobanks trade on. Their 2026 study compares four hundred human serum samples from a Shenzhen health surveillance project. Half had been stored long-term, half short-term. Ten metals were measured with high-precision spectrometry. Protein profiling catalogued nearly seven hundred proteins in each sample type. The donors were all healthy adults, so storage itself was the variable on trial.

Storage left fingerprints everywhere. Almost two hundred fifty proteins shifted significantly in abundance. The changed proteins clustered in immune, metabolic, and antioxidant work. Six metals, including iron and zinc, also moved. Even the correlation web between elements was rewired. Biobanks underpin thousands of studies that never think about freezer time. This audit says they should: quality control must treat storage duration as a real biological confound, or risk chasing ghosts in old samples.
plos-pone-0351836:
Abdullah Antaria and colleagues weigh in 2026 whether a shorter drug course for hard to treat tuberculosis should be scaled up in Indonesia. The newer course lasts far less time than the older long course and had done well in trials. Their study compared recent patients at a Jakarta hospital with earlier patients treated the old way.

Success rose, cost per patient fell by about two thirds, and hospital stays and missed doses dropped sharply. The extra cost for each added success was modest in their figures. The authors urge funding through national health cover and wider testing close to home to speed progress.
plos-pone-0351936:
Japan's population is aging fast, and Xiaohui Li, Gang Wu, and Zhimin Ding traced how lung infections and tuberculosis changed there from 2010 to 2023. Their 2026 PLOS One paper used national and prefecture-level estimates, split by age and sex, to separate illness counts from deaths.

Total cases fell from about thirty-one million to about twenty-eight million, and deaths also declined. Yet case counts among people aged seventy-five and older grew, because there are simply more older people. Rates fell even where raw numbers rose. The authors say planning must follow the older group's needs, not just the national trend.
plos-pone-0352436:
Maria Chiara Fabbri and seven colleagues track microbes through sheep, seasons, and soil in this 2026 study. The setting is a commercial farm in Tuscany, Italy. Grazing sheep link two microbial worlds: their guts and the pasture beneath them. Samples were gathered across the whole of 2024. Over two hundred fecal samples and forty-six soil samples were compared. The soils came from grazed pasture and ungrazed meadow.

Microbial variety in both sample types grew from winter toward autumn. Gut samples held richer communities than soils did. Clustering analysis kept animal and soil communities clearly apart, despite daily contact through grazing and droppings. Grazing management still shaped each side of the interface. The work matters for farms chasing sustainability. Healthy gut microbes signal animal welfare, while soil microbes underpin the land those animals depend on.
plos-pone-0353736:
Danny Hooftman and seven colleagues adapt a widely used soil-erosion model so it can run credibly across a whole country, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The model, built on the InVEST platform, estimates how much soil washes into rivers from farmland and other ground. They rebuilt it with British data, British rainfall patterns, several crop types, and satellite measures of plant cover through the seasons.

Checked against real sediment measured in rivers, their version ranked erosion hotspots fairly well and classified risk areas with decent accuracy. Yet it badly overestimated the total load, partly because river gauges miss peak flood flows. The authors are candid: good for targeting action, not for quoting tonnages.
plos-pone-0353836:
Lois Choi-Kain and seven colleagues pilot an online first step of care for people newly diagnosed with borderline personality disorder, in this 2026 trial. Specialist therapy often involves long waits, yet guidelines say assessment and education should come first. Eighty-two participants were randomized to watch short videos about the disorder or about general mental health, and half of the disorder group also received personalized feedback on their symptom and thinking scores.

The online program proved safe: emergency visits and hospitalizations did not differ between groups, and satisfaction ran higher among those who got disorder-specific videos. Knowledge about the condition improved more in the education groups. Symptoms themselves did not fall significantly, but participants who received both education and feedback improved in self-functioning, and their time alone stopped tracking with worse symptoms. The authors see a feasible bridge while patients await full therapy.
plos-pone-0353936:
Teng Li and three colleagues model how vibrating thin films, like those used on spacecraft, can trap energy in one spot, in this 2026 PLOS ONE physics study. When a membrane's tension pulses at the right rhythm, ripples can concentrate instead of spreading evenly. The team built a nonlinear model including stretching, damping, and interacting vibration modes, then checked its predictions against detailed computer simulations.

Energy piled up strongly when two vibration frequencies combined near a resonance and tension swings passed a modest threshold. Weak coupling between modes produced standing, breathing patterns; stronger coupling set patterns travelling. The patterns persisted over thousands of cycles. Engineers designing solar sails and membrane antennas need to know when such bunching could fatigue a film.
plos-pone-0354036:
Monteiro and colleagues, in a 2026 survey study, ask what kept Brazilian adults from being active during COVID-19 lockdown, and what helped them move. Lockdowns cut daily activity for many people, but the reasons differed by age, sex, mood, and daily routine. The team used machine learning to group people by shared barriers.

Answers from an online survey were sorted by an unsupervised method that finds clusters, groups of people with like patterns. Grouping by barriers worked well and gave eight clear profiles. Grouping by helpers did not hold together, so the team set it aside. Two groups marked by low mood carried the most barriers each. Activity and sitting time differed across the groups. The authors say home and outdoor programs should be shaped for each profile, with special care for people with low mood or tight time.
plos-pone-0354136:
Eunha Jeong follows Korean teenagers across five years. The aim is to chart how aggression develops. The study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. It draws on a national panel survey. More than two thousand adolescents took part. On average, aggression declined from 2018 to 2022. But averages hide the story. Modelling separated three distinct paths.

One group started moderate and declined. One started low but crept upward. One started high and fell steeply. Many factors predicted which path a teenager followed. They included sex, impulsivity, and depression. Smartphone dependence mattered too. So did parenting style and friendships. Prevention, Jeong argues, should be aimed by path. The quietly rising group is the easiest to miss. It is also the most important to catch.
plos-pone-0354236:
Theresa Wöllner, Tim Schweisfurth, and Alexander Brem ran two field experiments on how anonymity shapes brainstorming, reported in PLOS ONE in 2026. Participants generated ideas alone, either with their names hidden, fully attached, or under a mixed rule: ideas stayed anonymous, but the people behind the best-rated ones were later named. Outcomes were judged on how many ideas appeared, how new they were, and how useful they seemed.

The first experiment, with just over two hundred people, found no clear differences between the three rules. In the second, where each person tried all three, the mixed rule produced noticeably more novel ideas. The results suggest that promising recognition later, without exposing everyone, can sharpen creative work.
plos-pone-0354336: Malaysian university students who vape — their physical activity interlinks with e-cigarette use. This cross-sectional study examined that relationship. The findings reveal whether vaping accompanies active or sedentary lifestyles — informing campus health interventions.
plos-pone-0354736:
Yirui Shao and colleagues measured black locust trees across sixty-seven plantation plots in Weifang, China, asking how altitude and slope shape the growth of one of northern China's main planting species. Their 2026 field study compared plains, hills, and low mountains, recording trunk thickness and height and testing how the two scale together on each landform.

Plain-grown trees were clearly thickest and tallest. Both measures sagged steadily as altitude and slope rose, with altitude explaining slightly more of the variation than slope, while the basic height-to-thickness relationship stayed stable everywhere. For afforestation planners chasing timber and carbon, the practical advice is blunt: plant locust on gentle low ground where it thrives, and expect leaner returns uphill.
plos-pone-0355236:
Sichen Zou and three colleagues build and test a system for charging underwater devices with sound instead of cables, in this 2026 engineering paper. Unmanned underwater vehicles and seafloor sensors are limited by battery life, and sending divers or cables to recharge them is expensive. Sound travels well through water, so the team designed matched transmitter and receiver arrays that beam acoustic energy across a distance.

Their prototype uses a composite rod design to produce strong, tightly directed sound beams, aiming to deliver useful power without contact. The system was checked in an anechoic water tank, a test pool designed to remove echoes, to validate the approach under controlled conditions. The authors present it as a step toward underwater vehicles and sensors that can stay on long missions without surfacing for power.
plos-pone-0355836:
Yazeed Temraz and colleagues asked which hospital patients regain their earlier level of daily function by discharge. They studied adults receiving physical or occupational therapy during an acute hospital stay. Their 2026 review of records at one large hospital used admission notes to predict who returns to their pre-admission category.

About four in ten patients in the main group got back to their earlier category. Each step worse a patient's function was on admission sharply lowered the chance of full return. Among patients who had walked independently before, worse admission function raised the risk of leaving below that level. Temraz and colleagues say routine admission records can help therapists target support early.
plos-pone-0355936:
David Freudenstein and five colleagues investigate how an approved multiple sclerosis drug protects nerve tissue, in this 2026 mouse study. The drug, diroximel fumarate, is related to a widely used treatment whose immune and antioxidant actions are only partly understood. The team gave it orally to mice with an induced autoimmune disease that mimics MS, then scored symptoms and examined spinal cord tissue, immune cells, and gene activity.

Treated mice fared markedly better clinically. Fewer immune cells invaded the spinal cord, particularly the aggressive Th1 type, myelin and nerve fibers were better preserved, and blood immune cells produced less of two inflammatory signals. Genes in a key antioxidant defense pathway switched on in central nervous tissue. The authors conclude the drug combines immune calming with antioxidant protection, supporting its benefit in neuroinflammation.
plos-pone-0356236:
Maximilian Karl Scharf and colleagues asked what a computer model needs to hear to predict the Lombard effect in a tonal language. The Lombard effect is how much clearer speech becomes when talkers raise their voices in noise. Their 2026 study tested two intelligibility models on Mandarin Chinese recordings from eleven speakers. Some models were fed only frequency snapshots. Richer ones also tracked how sounds evolve in time.

For predicting the Lombard benefit itself, the simpler spectral snapshots sufficed in both models. That held despite Mandarin's meaning-carrying tones. But predicting each speaker's absolute clarity demanded the time-varying detail. That detail captured big individual differences. The distinction matters for hearing technology design. Some predictions can stay cheap, while personalized ones need the full signal.
plos-pone-0356536:
Tingting Ma and Mengyun Yang explore why fashion designers adopt, or resist, generative AI tools, in this 2026 survey of Chinese practitioners. Just over three hundred designers answered questions covering perceived risk, social influence, and the conditions that support use, alongside whether the tools satisfy their needs for autonomy, competence, and connection. The analysis follows a stimulus-organism-response chain, testing how outside pressures flow through inner states into choices.

Perceived risk dragged down all three inner needs, while social influence and supportive conditions lifted them. Feeling competent was the single strongest driver of the intention to use the tools, ahead of autonomy and connection, and every indirect pathway from the outside factors through the needs proved significant. The authors translate the results into practical advice on copyright rules, prompt training, and designer-AI teamwork.
plos-pone-0357036:
Maria Cristina Herrera Valerio and three colleagues ask how much drill weight construction workers judge acceptable overhead, with and without a shoulder exoskeleton, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Passive exoskeletons that cradle the arm promise relief on overhead jobs, but guidelines for safe loads while wearing one are missing. Twenty-nine workers drilled repeatedly at three shoulder heights for five minutes at a time and picked the heaviest drill they felt they could sustain.

Wearing the exoskeleton raised the weight workers chose by roughly a fifth. Body build mattered too: smaller framed workers chose noticeably less than larger ones, while medium builds matched the large group. Men chose heavier drills than women. Shoulder height, surprisingly, changed nothing. The results give safety planners concrete adjustment factors for body size and sex when setting overhead load limits with exoskeleton support.
plos-pone-0357836:
Makoto Yamaguchi led a team of eight authors studying relapse in a vessel disease, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. ANCA-associated vasculitis attacks blood vessels and organs, and rituximab maintenance therapy is meant to keep it quiet. Some patients still relapse during that maintenance. The team reviewed outcomes after such relapses at a single center.

Yamaguchi's retrospective cohort shows what happened next for those patients and how they fared. Doctors facing a relapse on maintenance need exactly this: evidence on what the next move tends to achieve. Single-center studies are small, but they record real practice in detail. For a rare disease, each careful series adds to a shared picture no one center can build alone.
plos-pone-0358036:
Haojie Long, Longji Li, and Lifeng Zhang published a 2026 sports analytics study in PLOS ONE on flagging elite female soccer players whose readiness is about to dip. Clubs collect daily readiness, workload, and wellness data, but staff cannot review everyone every day. Using a public monitoring dataset covering thousands of athlete-days from fifty players, the team trained models on one season and tested them on the next.

Adding workload and wellness data to readiness clearly improved the model's aim compared with readiness alone, and a calibration step made its risk estimates more honest without changing the ranking. Reviewing only the riskiest fifth of athlete-days would have caught nearly half of all next-day declines. This is retrospective evidence for prioritizing staff attention, not proof of better outcomes, and prospective external testing is needed before clubs rely on it.
plos-pone-0358136:
Adugna Olani led a team of five authors checking vaccination skills in western Ethiopia, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Vaccines protect only when they are stored, handled, and given correctly at each step. The team observed health workers in facilities across East Wollega, in the Oromia region, and assessed their competency directly.

Olani's study found gaps that show exactly where training should go. Observational checks catch problems that paper records hide, such as poor technique or broken cold chains. District managers can target scarce training money at the weakest steps. For children in the area, the benefit is direct: a well-given vaccine works, while a mishandled one may fail silently and leave a child unprotected.
plos-pone-0358536:
Anvar Sadath led a team of six authors setting out a review protocol on self-harm among Indigenous youth in the United States, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Adolescents who are Alaska Native or American Indian face very high rates of suicide and non-suicidal self-injury. The planned systematic review will gather evidence on risk factors and methods in this population.

Sadath's protocol, published in advance, defines how studies will be found and judged. That rigor matters because prevention programs built on weak evidence waste trust as well as money. The population's needs are specific, shaped by history and community, so a focused review serves better than generic youth data. The stakes are as high as research questions get.
plos-pone-0359236: Julca Avalos and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on mothers' weight and children's blood health in Peru. Using a national cross-sectional survey, they linked a mother's body mass index with her child's haemoglobin level. Low haemoglobin signals anemia, which can slow a child's growth and learning. A national link of this kind can aim nutrition programs at the right households.
plos-pone-0359336:
Tianyang Li and three colleagues sift osteoarthritis data for a gene signature tied to a chemical mark on RNA, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The mark, called ac4C, is placed by an enzyme that may help drive the joint disease, but its role is unproven. The team used a ready made list of mark related genes only as a filter, then mined five public datasets of joint tissue for genes that also shift in osteoarthritis.

Eight genes passed both screens. The group then built over a hundred machine learning pipelines and ranked them across three patient cohorts; the best combinations sorted patients from healthy controls with strong scores. Five kept genes were also checked in mouse cartilage cells inflamed in the dish. The authors present the signature as an exploratory lead for sorting patients into subgroups, not a ready test.
plos-pone-0359436: Hakami and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE review on remote dentistry in Saudi Arabia. Through computer simulations and real sequencing tests, the team judged how well species and strains can be told apart. Full-length reads do far better than the short fragments long in use. Some close relatives still blur together. The results guide labs choosing between cheap short surveys and richer full-gene studies. Mock communities with known members gave the team ground truth for judging each approach.
pmc-6919336:
Regina Guthold, Gretchen Stevens, Leanne Riley, and coauthors pooled data on teen physical activity in 2020. Activity brings many health gains for young people. The World Health Organization set a target to cut inactivity among teens by a set share within a decade.

Pooling hundreds of school-based surveys, the team finds most adolescents worldwide do not move enough. Girls are less active than boys in nearly every country. Trends barely improved over the study years. The authors call for urgent action in schools and city design, since adult habits often start in these years.
pmc-6954236:
Gommaar D'Hulst and colleagues reported how the oxygen sensor PHD1 controls muscle growth signaling in 2020. The mTORC1 pathway is a key regulator of muscle mass. How oxygen and nutrients tune it was not fully understood.

In mice lacking PHD1 in muscle, growth signaling faltered and muscle mass fell. The effect ran through stabilization of an enzyme that charges transfer RNA with leucine, not through the classic oxygen route. Leucine is itself a growth trigger, so the link closes a neat loop. The work reveals an unexpected way oxygen sensing shapes muscle.
pmc-7243036:
Annemarie Docherty and a large team of co-authors reported in 2020 on more than twenty thousand patients admitted to hospitals in the United Kingdom with COVID-19. Their prospective cohort study used a shared clinical protocol from an international respiratory infections consortium and the World Health Organization. The patients were enrolled during the fast growing first wave of the outbreak.

The authors describe who these patients were, what symptoms they arrived with, what other health problems they carried, and how their hospital stays unfolded. Because every site recorded the same details in the same way, the study gives one of the earliest clear pictures of severe COVID-19 in Britain. It helped doctors and planners judge what hospital care the pandemic would demand.
practical-phrenology-1836: Practical Phrenology, 1836. The practical bumps. This book preserves that work. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
pushkin-captains-daughter-1836:
Alexander Pushkin published The Captain's Daughter in 1836, his perfect historical tale of Pugachev's rebellion in Russia. The tale tests young Pyotr Grinyov's honor in the Cossack rising of 1773 to 1775. Pushkin researched the rebellion in archives and on the ground, then distilled it into limpid prose fiction.

Grinyov, sent to a remote fort, is saved in a blizzard by a guide he rewards with a coat. That guide is Pugachev, who later spares the fort's survivors for the young officer's sake in war. Grinyov's love for Marya, the captain's daughter, drives rescues, trials, and a plea to the empress herself. Pugachev is drawn with respect, a rebel of charm, cruelty, and a strange rough honor in arms. The tale's economy and fairness set the pattern for the Russian historical novel.
qu-est-ce-que-la-phrenologie-ou-essai-su: Qu'est-ce que la phrénologie? 1836. What is phrenology? This book preserves that essay. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. It waits for future eyes. The library keeps the document safe.
remarks-on-the-erroneous-impressions-and: Remarks on the Erroneous Impressions, 1836. The hostile spirit. This book preserves that work. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
richardson-dictionary-1836:
Charles Richardson published his New Dictionary of the English Language in 1836, built on a bold new method. Where Johnson had defined words in his own phrases, Richardson built every entry out of quotations from real writers. The historical method, showing a word's life through its uses, here reached English lexicography a generation before the Oxford English Dictionary was planned.

Each word is followed by dated quotations that trace its meanings from early use toward Richardson's own day. The reader sees the definition emerge from evidence rather than from one man's authority. The book was the nineteenth century's great rival to Johnson, and its two heavy volumes sat in every serious library. Our words are explained here by the writers who used them best. Richardson's faith in quotation became the method of all later historical dictionaries.
selections-from-the-phrenological-journa: Selections from the Phrenological Journal, 1836. The forty articles. This book preserves that selection. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
senior-outline-science-political-economy:
Senior published his Outline of the Science of Political Economy in 1836, the fullest system of his teaching. The book began as an encyclopaedia article and grew into the clearest classical treatise after Ricardo. Senior aimed to state what the science is, what it assumes, and what it may conclude.

He builds the whole doctrine from four plain premises about wealth and human desire, reasoning by strict logic. Value, wages, rent, and profit are drawn out in order, each term defined before it is used. Senior also separates the science from the art of policy, a distinction later economists prized. The Outline became the handbook of the deductive school and a model of economic reasoning for a generation. Mill's great treatise followed its plan more closely than Mill ever quite admitted.
soviet-constitution-1936:
The Soviet Union adopted a new constitution in 1936, with Joseph Stalin as its presiding name. Soviet spokesmen praised it as the most democratic constitution in the world. It arrived at the very height of the Great Terror, when show trials and arrests were sweeping the country. The gap between text and terror was the point its critics seized on.

On paper the charter guarantees work, rest, education, free speech, and the vote for every citizen, priests included. It describes a federation of republics with an elected Supreme Soviet at its head. In practice, the Communist Party's grip, mentioned in a single article, overrode every promise. Foreign admirers quoted the rights; Soviet citizens learned not to test them. The constitution of the purges' apogee remains the classic case of rights proclaimed by a state that honored none of them.
statistics-of-phrenology-being-a-sketch-: Statistics of Phrenology, 1836. The phrenology statistics. This book preserves that work. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
texas-declaration-independence-1836: Texas' 1836 Declaration of Independence broke it from Mexico. The Alamo had fallen. The Tower library holds the full text. It claimed lone star. Mexico refused. Guns decided. Republic rose. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
the-harmony-of-phrenology-with-scripture: The Harmony of Phrenology with Scripture, 1836. The biblical harmony. This book preserves that work. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
the-two-gentlemen-of-verona-pg2236: In this edition of Shakespeare's early comedy, Launce and his dog Crab steal the show from the two gentlemen's romantic tangle. Valentine, Proteus, and the ladies of Milan play out love's follies while the clown and his cur get the biggest laughs. Youthful, sunny, and full of charm.
tholosan-ut-magorum-et-maleficiorum-erro:
Claude Tholosan lays down the law on witches in his Latin tract of near 1436. Tholosan was a judge in the Dauphine, in the hills of France. His tract's name means on the false claims of mages and witches. It is one of the first to make a bold claim. Witches, it says, fly to a sabbath rite and make pacts with the Devil.

He writes from trials at his own bench. The claims here fed the great hunts that came next. The text, in Latin, is a root source of the hunts. Its cold tone chills.
timon-of-athens-pg1536: The great hater of mankind takes center stage in this edition of Shakespeare's bleakest play. Ruined by false friends, Timon flees Athens to curse the whole race from a cave, digging up gold only to find more reasons for scorn. Strange, savage, and oddly modern in its disgust.
tob-0036:
James McAndrew of the United States Air Force wrote the 1997 report that closed the service's Roswell file. Fifty years after debris was found in New Mexico in 1947, the report gives the official answer to the most famous flying saucer story of all.

The wreckage, it says, came from Project Mogul, a secret balloon train built to listen for Soviet atomic tests. The alien bodies of later tales are matched to crash-test dummies dropped in tests years afterward. Witness memory, stretched across decades, did the rest. Doubters were not persuaded, but the report stands as the government's fullest public account, document by document.
tob-10036:
William Ralph Inge delivered the lectures in Christian Mysticism as the Bampton Lectures at Oxford. Inge was an English theologian interested in what mystics claim to know directly about God. His study moves from the early church through the Middle Ages.

Along the way he examines leading mystics, defines terms that are often used loosely, and weighs where mystical claims hold up under criticism. V1 evidence calls the survey demanding but rewarding, and one that shaped a century of scholarship. Readers who want history and judgment together, rather than devotion alone, will find Inge a careful and sometimes stern guide.
tob-10236:
W. E. Soothill's English version of the Lotus Sutra follows the old Chinese text linked with Kumarajiva. Called the Lotus of the Wonderful Law, it is the most loved scripture of East Asian Buddhism. Its teaching comes through tales and scenes more than through dry argument.

A house on fire, a lost son who does not know his rich father, and a false city made for tired men all point one way. All beings, the sutra says, hold the seed of Buddhahood and can wake at last. That hope of a saved world for all made the book the heart of schools from Tiantai to Nichiren.
tob-10836:
King James VI of Scotland, later James I of England, wrote Daemonologie in 1597 after personally interrogating accused witches in the North Berwick trials. Cast as a dialogue, the treatise sets out to prove that witchcraft and demonology are real. James argues from Scripture, law, and reported cases.

Kinds of spirits, the devil's pacts, and how witches may be detected and punished all receive the king's attention. The book served as part legal manual, part theology, and helped fuel witch prosecutions on both sides of the Scottish border. Readers meet a learned monarch's mind on demons in his own words, chilling precisely because he was intelligent.
tob-13136:
Seven Hermetic laws for the practical occultist stand at the center of The Kybalion, credited to the anonymous Three Initiates. Mind rules matter, rhythms rise and fall, and every cause has its effect. The laws are presented as one connected system, not a miscellany of sayings, and as principles meant to be applied.

A century of New Thought readers has treated the slim volume as a working manual for mastering one's own mental world. Passages explain polarity, gender, and vibration as patterns running through nature and thought alike. Readers can finish it quickly, but its admirers tend to reread and annotate it for years.
tob-13336:
Lectures by Swami Vivekananda, the monk who carried Vedanta to the West, stand behind How to Be a Yogi. He taught that yoga is a practical discipline, not a set of beliefs. The book speaks to beginners who want instruction they can use.

It sets out the main yogas side by side: work done without selfish aim, devotion to God, control of the mind, and knowledge of the self. Each path suits a different temper, and all aim at the same freedom. As a teacher's handbook from the man who brought these ideas to America, it keeps the plain, direct manner of his talks.
tob-13736:
Annie Besant and C. W. Leadbeater claimed clairvoyant sight of thoughts themselves, and Thought-Forms publishes what they said they saw. Feelings, in their account, build colored forms in subtle matter around the thinker. Anger appears as scarlet spikes, devotion as rising blue forms, and music as elaborate structures.

Dozens of illustrations accompany the explanations, making the book as much picture gallery as text. Leadbeater and Besant presented their observations as research, with methods and cautions. Whether readers judge the work science or fantasy, its images shaped a century of New Age art and the very idea that emotions have visible auras and colors.
tob-4136:
Waite argued in The Secret Tradition in Freemasonry, volume one of 1911, that a hidden initiatory tradition runs behind the public life of the lodges. Rituals, grades, and symbols become, on his reading, the outer dress of an inner path toward divine union.

He pursues the claim through archives and rites with dogged learning. Other Masonic scholars hotly disputed his case, and the quarrel made the book famous. Waite writes as both insider and mystic, which is the source of its charm and its trouble. Verified from the 1919 edition, volume one made him Masonry's most debated scholar of his generation.
tob-4236:
John Burnet mapped the birth of Western philosophy in Early Greek Philosophy, here in its revised second edition of 1908. Thales, who said all is water, opens the line that runs through Heraclitus, Parmenides, and Empedocles to the Atomists. Burnet prints the surviving fragments in Greek and English.

His strong claim, that the Greeks invented scientific thought by asking how the world works without myth, shaped teaching for decades. Later scholars argue with Burnet often, which proves his place. Verified public-domain text supports the entry. For a standard, learned road into the Presocratics, Burnet's book still leads.
un-ga-res-3236:
Palestinian rights took a landmark turn in Resolution 3236, adopted by the General Assembly in 1974. The Assembly had heard the Palestine Liberation Organization, named in the text as the voice of the Palestinian people. It voices deep concern that no just fix to the Palestine problem had yet been found, and that the open sore still put world peace at risk.

The text states again the fixed rights of the Palestinian people in Palestine. Those rights are spelled out: self-rule free of outside meddling, and a national state of their own. The vote, passed 89 to 8, is still cited as the moment the UN put Palestinian statehood at the heart of its terms.
un-ga-res-36: Who gets in, and by what rules? Resolution 36 of the General Assembly, from November 1946, asks the Security Council to name a team to meet with an Assembly team on that question. The two teams were to draft entry rules both bodies could accept. The Assembly later named Australia, Cuba, India, Norway, and the Soviet Union to its side; the Council sent China, Brazil, and Poland.
un-ga-res-49-236:
Guatemala's new UN mission took the field under Resolution 49/236, passed in the fall of 1994. The Mission for the Verification of Human Rights in Guatemala had been set up that September, for a first term of six months. It would check that the state and the rebel URNG kept the pledges of their rights deal. A December vote had asked the Secretary-General to keep backing the peace with his own staff as well.

The start and full spread of the mission across the land are welcomed. The help and joint work of both the state and the URNG are praised. A status deal between Guatemala and the Secretary-General, which set the mission's rights on the ground, had just been signed.
un-ga-res-a-69-36:
Central Asia's ban on nuclear arms is welcomed in Resolution A/69/36, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. Five states of the region had signed a treaty that made their lands a zone free of nuclear weapons. The pact took force on 21 March 2009. The Assembly calls it a real step for the world ban on the spread of such arms, and a guard against atomic goods falling into the hands of terror groups.

The text also welcomes the signing, on 6 May 2014, of the treaty's protocol by the nuclear-armed states. They are called on to ratify it fast. Note is taken of talks among the five states. They met in Ashgabat in 2009 and in Almaty in 2014. Joint work to clean lands hurt by past atomic tests and mines is also noted.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 3236 (XXIX), adopted at the twenty-ninth session in 1974, is titled Question of Palestine. The Assembly heard the Palestine Liberation Organization as the voice of the Palestinian people. It voiced deep concern that no just settlement had been reached, while the problem still put world peace at risk.

The text restates the firm rights of the Palestinian people in Palestine. Above all, it restates self-rule free of outside meddling, and national freedom and sovereignty. It also restates the right of Palestinians driven from their homes and land to return. It calls on all states to back their fight to regain their rights. It asks the Secretary-General to deal with the Palestine Liberation Organization on the matter.

General Assembly Resolution 36, adopted on 19 November 1946 at the forty-ninth plenary meeting, is a brief procedural step on admissions. The Assembly asked the Security Council to name a committee to meet with an Assembly committee on procedure, so the two bodies could draft shared rules for admitting new members. A note in the text records the members later named to each side's committee.

General Assembly Resolution 49/236, adopted on 31 March 1995, renewed the human rights verification mission in Guatemala for six more months. The Assembly welcomed the mission's opening and full deployment. It welcomed its status agreement passed by Guatemala's Congress. It welcomed its director's report on the first three months of work.

Both the Government of Guatemala and the Unidad Revolucionaria Nacional Guatemalteca were called on to follow the mission's advice. They were called on to keep their promises under the Comprehensive Agreement on Human Rights. The Assembly also voiced concern that the peace talks had slowed in the second half of 1994, missing agreed target dates. It urged fresh drive toward a full peace package.

Resolution 69/36 of the General Assembly welcomes the Treaty on a Nuclear-Weapon-Free Zone in Central Asia, in force since 21 March 2009. It welcomes the signing of its protocol by the nuclear-weapon states on 6 May 2014, calling for early ratification. The Assembly treats the treaty as a step for non-proliferation and regional security. It treats it as a step for keeping nuclear materials from terrorists. It notes the Central Asian states' consultative meetings. It notes their action plan on nuclear security and on dealing with radioactive contamination from uranium mining.
un-sc-res-1036:
Georgia and Abkhazia are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1036, adopted on 12 January 1996. Georgia had held presidential elections in November 1995. The cease-fire broadly held, yet talks on a full settlement dragged on. Conditions in the Gali region had grown worse, with killings and rights abuses reported.

The text extends the United Nations Observer Mission in Georgia, called UNOMIG, until 12 July 1996. It condemns ethnic killings and demands that the Abkhaz side keep people under its control safe. Both sides must work with the observers and let them inspect heavy weapons stores. Refugees keep their right to return, and the Abkhaz side must stop blocking that return.
un-sc-res-1336:
A team that watched for sanctions-busting in Angola's civil war received more time on 23 January 2001. The team had been set up in 2000 to track how the UNITA rebel movement got around sanctions. Those sanctions, on arms and on diamonds, dated back to Resolution 864 of 1993. The team's final report was before the Council. Resolution 1336 was adopted unanimously.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council took note of the monitors' final report. It extended the team's mandate for three more months. The Secretary-General was told to reappoint up to five of the experts. The team had to send the sanctions committee a written follow-up by 19 April 2001. All states were called on to cooperate fully with the monitors. The work mattered because diamonds and arms kept UNITA's war alive, long after the Council had banned both trades.
un-sc-res-1436: One entry in the Council's numbered series is Resolution 1436, catalogued for 2002 by this library. Formal decisions of this sort guide UN staff, peacekeeping forces, and governments in the years that follow. What is preserved is the exact formal wording, transcribed on English Wikisource from the official record of the Council. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-1536:
Afghanistan's assistance mission was renewed for the election year on 26 March 2004. The Loya Jirga had adopted a constitution on 4 January 2004. The Berlin conference was about to open, on 31 March, to renew the world's long-term pledge. Elections under the Bonn Agreement were the next great test.

The Council extended UNAMA for twelve more months from the day of adoption. It welcomed the Secretary-General's report of 23 March and the advice it carried. Security and donor support were named vital if the coming national elections were to be credible. Afghan authorities were urged to shape a vote open to all parts of the population. UNAMA and Kabul had to speed voter registration together. The Council welcomed the disarmament program's progress since October 2003. It also backed the national drug control strategy and pressed Kabul to apply it with force.
un-sc-res-1636:
Formal Council action on the killing of Rafiq Hariri arrived as Resolution 1636, adopted on 31 October 2005. A bomb in Beirut on 14 February 2005 killed the former Lebanese prime minister and twenty-two others. An international investigation pointed to joint Lebanese and Syrian official involvement. The inquiry was not finished, and some Syrian officials had misled investigators.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council orders travel bans and asset freezes on people the investigators name as suspects. A new committee will run the list of names. Syria must hand over suspects for questioning and cooperate fully and without conditions. The investigation's mandate runs to 15 December 2005, with reports due to the Council by then.
un-sc-res-1736: Resolution 1736, from 2006, is preserved here as a Security Council decision in official-record wording. English Wikisource is the transcription source. The entry gives the complete act: the preamble's account of the situation, then the numbered decisions. In the Council's world, those decisions are the unit of action, and each one is filed like this.
un-sc-res-1836:
UNMIL was extended with endorsed cuts on 29 September 2008. The Secretary-General's report of 15 August 2008 set out his advice. Liberia's government was improving governance and security and fighting corruption. Its first poverty reduction strategy, for 2008 to 2011, had been adopted. Police rebuilding and army restructuring moved forward. United Nations police advisers were still needed beside the national force.

The Council extended UNMIL's mandate until 30 September 2009. It restated its plan to let the Secretary-General shift troops between UNMIL and the Côte d'Ivoire mission as needed. His advice for a reduction in the mission's military strength was endorsed. A change to the police element, with immediate effect, was endorsed as well. He would track progress against the mission's benchmarks and report. The Council planned to review his findings by 31 March 2009. Liberia's own forces would take a further step toward holding the country alone.
un-sc-res-1936:
Iraq's assistance mission was renewed on 5 August 2010. Security had improved through joint political and security work, the Council welcomed. Yet challenges to safety remained, and the gains had to be held by dialogue and national unity. All communities had to share in the political process. A fair answer on resources and on the disputed internal boundaries was still owed.

The Council extended UNAMI's mandate for twelve months. The special representative and the mission would keep advising and helping Iraq's people and government. Their work covered elections, dialogue, human rights, and the return of refugees. The safety of United Nations staff was named essential to the mission's work. Member states' contributions of staff, funds, and logistics were welcomed. The Secretary-General had to report to the Council every four months on the mission's progress. The Council meant to review the mandate again within twelve months.
un-sc-res-236:
Resolution 236 addressed the Israel-Syria ceasefire when the Council adopted it unanimously on 11 June 1967. The Six-Day War had just ended. A ceasefire was in force but reports of breaches kept coming. The Secretary-General had briefed the Council across four meetings.

The Council condemns each and every breach of the ceasefire. It says the halt bars any forward move by troops after the truce took hold. Any troops that pushed forward after 1630 GMT on 10 June must pull back to the ceasefire lines. Both sides must give the UN truce observers full freedom to work. The Secretary-General must keep probing and report back soon.
un-sc-res-36:
Indonesia's ceasefire of August 1947 had not fully taken hold by autumn. A consular commission reported that neither side had tried to agree on how to apply it. On 1 November 1947 the Security Council told the parties to consult at once. They could talk directly or through the Committee of Good Offices. Until they agreed, all hostile acts and incitement had to stop. The committee would help them reach a workable arrangement.

The consular commission and its military staff had to aid the committee. The Council also explained its August resolution. Force could not be used to extend control over land not held when the ceasefire began. That reading closed a loophole both sides had tested.
un-sc-res-736:
Security Council Resolution 736, adopted on January 29, 1992, recommended Kyrgyzstan for membership in the United Nations. Some older notes attach this number to Slovenia, but Slovenia's turn came later that spring under a different text. Kyrgyzstan, a mountain land in central Asia, had declared independence from the failing Soviet Union the previous August and sought quick entry to the world body.

The Assembly seated Kyrgyzstan on March 2, alongside several other former Soviet republics. The council's wording is the standard form for admissions. Read in sequence, these brief votes of early 1992 record the map of Eurasia being remade in peace, republic by republic, after the Soviet collapse.
un-sc-res-936: Filed in the official record under number 936, this Council resolution is catalogued with a 1994 date. Resolutions are the way the Council states its decisions, and member states are expected to take them seriously. Preserving the text in this form keeps a small piece of diplomatic history open to any reader. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Georgia's frozen Abkhazia conflict is the subject of Resolution 1036, adopted on 12 January 1996. The 1994 Moscow ceasefire broadly held, watched by UNOMIG and the CIS peacekeeping force. Talks on a political settlement, including Abkhazia's status, were deadlocked. The Abkhaz authorities kept blocking refugee returns, and killings in the Gali region were reported. Georgia had held elections in November 1995.

The Council extends the UN Observer Mission in Georgia, UNOMIG, to 12 July 1996. It calls on the parties, above all the Abkhaz side, to make substantive progress without delay and cooperate with the Secretary-General's efforts, assisted by Russia as facilitator and the OSCE. It demands the Abkhaz side speed up voluntary returns, starting with the Gali region, and guarantee the safety of those already back. It backs a concrete human rights programme for Abkhazia and asks for a report in three months.

Resolution 1336 is a UN Security Council extension of sanctions monitoring on Angola, adopted unanimously on 23 January 2001 under Chapter VII. Angola's long civil war was fueled by UNITA's defiance of sanctions, and a monitoring mechanism of experts had just delivered its final report on how the sanctions were being broken.

The resolution takes note of that report, promises it full consideration, and extends the monitors' mandate for three months, asking for an addendum by 19 April 2001. The Secretary-General is to reappoint up to five experts, and all states are called on to cooperate. The expert panels' naming-and-shaming reports were the Council's tool for squeezing UNITA's diamond and arms networks.

Togo, a narrow West African state, gained independence from France in April 1960. Its government quickly applied to join the United Nations. Resolution 136, adopted unanimously on 31 May 1960, took up that request. The Council had the application papers before it, filed as document S/4318.

The members recommended the Togolese Republic for membership. Final approval belonged to the General Assembly. It admitted Togo later that year, in the famous wave of new members. Seventeen states joined in 1960 alone. Most were newly free African nations. Their arrival changed the UN's balance. Debates tilted toward decolonization and development from then on.

Peaceful elections in May 2002, held with the mission's support, frame this Sierra Leone text of 24 September 2002. UNAMSIL's mandate is extended, and at the same time its drawdown begins. The Special Court for Sierra Leone had also just opened, though war in neighbouring Liberia still threatened the region.

The mandate is renewed for six months from 30 September 2002. The mission is directed to complete the first phases of the Secretary-General's plan, including cutting 4,500 troops within eight months, as Sierra Leone's own forces take on more responsibility. Extending state authority, controlling the diamond fields, and reintegrating former fighters remain central goals.

Resolution 1536, adopted on 26 March 2004, extends help to Afghanistan as it moves toward its first elections. A new constitution had been adopted that January, and a voter sign-up effort was under way. The Bonn Agreement set the path from interim rule to elected government. A Berlin conference on long-term support was about to open.

The Council extends the UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan, UNAMA, for twelve more months. It stresses that safety and donor support are vital for a believable vote and urges Afghans, including women and refugees, to take part in full. It welcomes headway in disarming armed factions since October 2003. It also presses action on the drug trade and asks UNAMA to keep backing human rights work and a fair court system.

The Hariri assassination investigation hardens into sanctions in Resolution 1636, adopted on 31 October 2005. The international investigation commission had reported converging evidence that Lebanese and Syrian officials were involved in the 14 February 2005 Beirut bombing that killed former Prime Minister Rafiq Hariri and 22 others. It found Syrian officials had misled investigators, while Lebanon asked that the commission's mandate be extended.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council sets up a committee to designate individuals suspected of involvement; those designated face a travel ban and asset freeze and must be made available for interview. It decides Syria must detain the Syrian officials and individuals the commission suspects and give the commission full, unconditional cooperation, including the right to choose where and how interviews happen. It insists Syria not interfere in Lebanon's affairs. The commission, extended to 15 December 2005, must report by then, sooner if Syria's cooperation falls short.

Troops move between the Burundi and Congo operations under this text of 22 December 2006. Fifty military observers serving under the Burundi operation's strength in Congo had watched the electoral process and were due to leave by the end of December. Fighting by militias and foreign armed groups in eastern Congo still threatened civilians.

The Secretary-General is authorized, from 1 January 2007 until the Congo mission's current mandate expires, to redeploy troops between the two missions as needed. The arrangement lets the United Nations shift scarce peacekeepers across the two neighbouring operations without new authorizations each time. Congolese citizens are praised again for their commitment to the democratic process shown in the 2006 elections.

Resolution 1836, adopted on 29 September 2008, extends the UN Mission in Liberia, UNMIL, while shrinking it. Liberia's government was fighting corruption, taking firmer control of its natural wealth, and working from its first national poverty plan. Police and army rebuilding had moved ahead, and ex-fighters were being settled back into civilian life, though courts and state authority still needed work.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends UNMIL until 30 September 2009. It approves cutting 1,460 more troops between October 2008 and March 2009 and merging four sectors into two. At the same time it adds 240 police staff for expert advice and rapid response. It asks for progress reports tied to clear benchmarks, plus long-range plans for a phased pullout that does not put Liberia's safety at risk.

Iraq's politics after the March 2010 parliamentary election frame Resolution 1936, adopted on 5 August 2010. The results had been certified, and the Council called on Iraq's leaders to form a broad government quickly. Safety had improved, though terrorism and sectarian violence remained. The UN Assistance Mission for Iraq, UNAMI, advised on elections, rights, and talks among Iraq's communities.

The Council extends UNAMI until 31 July 2011, keeping the mandate set in Resolution 1883. It asks Iraq's government and member states to keep giving UNAMI the safety cover and supply support it needs. It stresses aid for refugees and displaced people and the need for their safe, willing return. It notes Iraq's steps toward regaining the standing it held before Resolution 661 and urges it to close the Oil-for-Food programme with speed. Reports are due every four months.

The Six-Day War had just ended when Resolution 236 passed unanimously on 11 June 1967. Fighting between Israel and Syria had flared again after the ceasefire call. The Secretary-General briefed members across four straight meetings. His reports described troops moving and guns still firing on the Syrian front.

The Council condemned every violation of the ceasefire. It banned any forward military movement after the truce. Troops that had advanced past their lines after 4:30 p.m. Greenwich time on 10 June had to pull back. UN truce observers were promised full cooperation. They needed freedom of movement and working communications to watch the lines.

On 18 July 1973 the Council adopted Resolution 336, recommending the Commonwealth of the Bahamas for United Nations membership. The application, filed as document S/10966, had just been examined. The Bahamas had become independent from Britain eight days earlier, ending more than three centuries of colonial rule over the Atlantic archipelago.

The decision itself is one sentence long: the General Assembly is asked to admit the Bahamas. That formality was required, since no country joins the UN without the Council first recommending it. The resolution stands as the paper trail of a new Caribbean state stepping into the international system in the summer of 1973, alongside other former colonies doing the same.

A truce in Indonesia was failing in the fall of 1947. Consuls on the ground sent a report on 14 October. It said the August ceasefire call had not worked in full. Neither side had tried to meet the other halfway. Resolution 36 passed on 1 November 1947. Seven members voted yes. Poland voted no. Three held back.

Both sides were told to talk at once. They could meet face to face or use the UN good offices team. All acts against the truce had to stop. Lives and goods had to be kept safe. One key point was spelled out. Seizing land not held on 4 August broke the truce. If troops had to pull back, a pact on that had to come fast.

Two Central Asian bids moved side by side in January 1992, and this is one. On the twenty-ninth, the Council adopted Resolution 736 without a vote. The Republic of Kyrgyzstan had claimed freedom the August before. It made that freedom final as the Soviet Union dissolved in December. The new state was suddenly on its own.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit Kyrgyzstan. Admission followed in early March 1992. Uzbekistan's bid was handled the same day, in a twin meeting. The paired steps form a small paper trail. They mark Central Asia's arrival on the world map as a set of sovereign states.

The top legal post at the Yugoslavia war crimes court was filled on 8 July 1994. Resolution 936 appoints the prosecutor of the International Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. The man named in the text is Richard J. Goldstone. The Secretary-General had put his name forward. Under the court's statute, the Council appoints the prosecutor from that nomination. The appointment put a chief prosecutor in place to bring charges for grave crimes committed in the former Yugoslavia since 1991.
un-un-res-united-nations-emergency-force:
The eighth report of the Secretary-General on the United Nations Emergency Force, document A/5736, covers the force in its later years, in 1963 and 1964. UNEF had stood on the Egypt-Israel frontier since the Suez Crisis of 1956. By now its patrols were routine, and its presence was part of the region's uneasy calm.

The report reviews troop strength, costs, incidents along the line, and talks with the host state. It notes how a force sent for a crisis had become a long-term fixture. Within three years the force would be withdrawn at Egypt's demand, days before a new war.
worm-runir-danica-1636:
Ole Worm, a Danish scholar and doctor, gave the runes their first full learned study in this Latin book of 1636. The text here is from the 1651 second edition. Worm gathered rune stones and carved sticks from across the north lands. He was a keen hoarder of old things, and his rooms held a famed store of them.

He set out each rune sign, its name, and its sound, and matched them with old verse. He also drew the stones so readers far away could see the cuts for themselves. The book marks the birth of rune study as a true field of learning.
